pages.label: Book I · Section 1
pages.original: Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from all anger and passion. From the fame and memory of him that begot me I have learned both shamefastness and manlike behaviour. Of my mother I have learned to be religious, and bountiful; and to forbear, not only to do, but to intend any evil; to content myself with a spare diet, and to fly all such excess as is incidental to great wealth. Of my great-grandfather, both to frequent public schools and auditories, and to get me good and able teachers at home; and that I ought not to think much, if upon such occasions, I were at excessive charges.
pages.familiar: From my grandfather Verus I learned gentleness, self-control, and freedom from anger. From my father's reputation and example I learned modesty, dignity, and courage. From my mother I learned devotion, generosity, and restraint—not only from doing harm, but even from intending it. I learned to be content with simple food and to avoid the excesses that often come with wealth. From my great-grandfather I learned to attend good schools, find capable teachers, and not resent the expense of a proper education.
pages.abbreviated: From his family he learned gentleness, self-control, modesty, courage, generosity, restraint even in intention, contentment with simple living, and the value of good education.

pages.label: Book I · Section 2
pages.original: Of him that brought me up, not to be fondly addicted to either of the two great factions of the coursers in the circus, called Prasini, and Veneti: nor in the amphitheatre partially to favour any of the gladiators, or fencers, as either the Parmularii, or the Secutores. Moreover, to endure labour; nor to need many things; when I have anything to do, to do it myself rather than by others; not to meddle with many businesses; and not easily to admit of any slander.
pages.familiar: From the man who raised me I learned not to become blindly loyal to either of the great racing factions, nor to take sides for particular gladiators. I learned to endure hard work, live without needing many things, and do necessary tasks myself instead of passing them to others. I learned not to scatter my attention across too many concerns and not to believe accusations easily.
pages.abbreviated: From his guardian he learned not to take sides blindly, to endure work, live simply, handle necessary tasks himself, focus his attention, and avoid believing accusations too readily.

pages.label: Book I · Section 3
pages.original: Of Diognetus, not to busy myself about vain things, and not easily to believe those things, which are commonly spoken, by such as take upon them to work wonders, and by sorcerers, or prestidigitators, and impostors; concerning the power of charms, and their driving out of demons, or evil spirits; and the like. Not to keep quails for the game; nor to be mad after such things. Not to be offended with other men's liberty of speech, and to apply myself unto philosophy. Him also I must thank, that ever I heard first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus, and that I did write dialogues in my youth; and that I took liking to the philosophers' little couch and skins, and such other things, which by the Grecian discipline are proper to those who profess philosophy.
pages.familiar: From Diognetus I learned not to waste myself on empty pursuits or quickly believe the claims of wonder-workers, magicians, tricksters, and frauds about charms that drive out spirits and similar nonsense. I learned not to obsess over sporting birds or games. I learned not to resent other people's freedom to speak plainly, and to devote myself to philosophy. I also owe him my first encounters with serious teachers, my youthful practice of writing dialogues, and my appreciation for the simple life of those who genuinely study philosophy.
pages.abbreviated: Diognetus taught him to reject empty pursuits, superstition, fraud, and obsessive entertainments; to tolerate frank speech; and to pursue philosophy, serious study, writing, and a simple life.

pages.label: Book I · Section 4
pages.original: To Rusticus I am beholding, that I first entered into the conceit that my life wanted some redress and cure. And then, that I did not fall into the ambition of ordinary sophists, either to write tracts concerning the common theorems, or to exhort men unto virtue and the study of philosophy by public orations; as also that I never by way of ostentation did affect to show myself an active able man, for any kind of bodily exercises. And that I gave over the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of elegant neat language. That I did not use to walk about the house in my long robe, nor to do any such things. Moreover I learned of him to write letters without any affectation, or curiosity; such as that was, which by him was written to my mother from Sinuessa: and to be easy and ready to be reconciled, and well pleased again with them that had offended me, as soon as any of them would be content to seek unto me again. To read with diligence; not to rest satisfied with a light and superficial knowledge, nor quickly to assent to things commonly spoken of: whom also I must thank that ever I lighted upon Epictetus his _Hypomnemata_, or moral commentaries and common-factions: which also he gave me of his own.
pages.familiar: I owe Rusticus the realization that my life needed correction and healing. He kept me from chasing the ambitions of ordinary intellectual performers—writing treatises on familiar theories or giving public speeches urging people toward virtue and philosophy. He kept me from showing off my physical abilities. I gave up performing rhetoric and poetry, polishing every sentence, dressing theatrically at home, and similar displays. He taught me to write plainly and naturally, as in the letter he sent my mother from Sinuessa. He taught me to reconcile easily with anyone willing to make peace, and to welcome them back without holding a grudge. He taught me to read carefully, never settling for shallow understanding or accepting common claims too quickly. And he gave me Epictetus's notes and moral teachings.
pages.abbreviated: Rusticus showed him that his life needed correction and turned him away from intellectual showmanship, rhetorical and physical display, and shallow reading. He taught plain writing, reconciliation, careful understanding, and Epictetus's moral teachings.

pages.label: Book I · Section 5
pages.original: From Apollonius, true liberty, and unvariable steadfastness, and not to regard anything at all, though never so little, but right and reason: and always, whether in the sharpest pains, or after the loss of a child, or in long diseases, to be still the same man; who also was a present and visible example unto me, that it was possible for the same man to be both vehement and remiss: a man not subject to be vexed, and offended with the incapacity of his scholars and auditors in his lectures and expositions; and a true pattern of a man who of all his good gifts and faculties, least esteemed in himself, that his excellent skill and ability to teach and persuade others the common theorems and maxims of the Stoic philosophy. Of him also I learned how to receive favours and kindnesses (as commonly they are accounted:) from friends, so that I might not become obnoxious unto them, for them, nor more yielding upon occasion, than in right I ought; and yet so that I should not pass them neither, as an unsensible and unthankful man.
pages.familiar: From Apollonius I learned genuine freedom, steady character, and complete loyalty to reason, even in the smallest matters. I saw him remain himself through severe pain, the loss of a child, and prolonged illness. He showed that one person could be intense when needed and relaxed when appropriate. He was never irritated by the slowness of his students, and he valued his own teaching ability less than any of his other gifts. From him I learned to accept kindness from friends gratefully without becoming dependent on them or surrendering my judgment, while also never ignoring or forgetting what they had done.
pages.abbreviated: Apollonius taught him freedom, steadiness, and loyalty to reason through pain, loss, and illness, while adapting appropriately to circumstances. He also taught gratitude for friends' kindness without dependence, and faithful remembrance of it.

pages.label: Book I · Section 6
pages.original: Of Sextus, mildness and the pattern of a family governed with paternal affection; and a purpose to live according to nature: to be grave without affectation: to observe carefully the several dispositions of my friends, not to be offended with idiots, nor unseasonably to set upon those that are carried with the vulgar opinions, with the theorems, and tenets of philosophers: his conversation being an example how a man might accommodate himself to all men and companies; so that though his company were sweeter and more pleasing than any flatterer's cogging and fawning; yet was it at the same time most respected and reverenced: who also had a proper happiness and faculty, rationally and methodically to find out, and set in order all necessary determinations and instructions for a man's life. A man without ever the least appearance of anger, or any other passion; able at the same time most exactly to observe the Stoic _Apathia_, or unpassionateness, and yet to be most tender-hearted: ever of good credit; and yet almost without any noise, or rumour: very learned, and yet making little show.
pages.familiar: From Sextus I learned gentleness, and I saw the example of a household guided by fatherly care. I learned to live according to nature, to be serious without pretending, and to pay close attention to each friend's character. I learned not to be annoyed by foolish people or to confront those trapped in popular opinions at the wrong moment. His conversation showed how to adapt wisely to every kind of person. He was more pleasant than a flatterer, yet more respected than one. He could reason clearly and organize the guidance needed for a good life. He showed no anger or uncontrolled passion, yet remained deeply compassionate; he was trusted without seeking attention, learned without showing off.
pages.abbreviated: Sextus taught him gentleness, natural living, serious but unpretentious conduct, careful attention to character, and patience with foolish or mistaken people. He modeled adaptable, clear guidance, compassion without passion, trustworthiness, learning without display, and helpful leadership.

pages.label: Book I · Section 7
pages.original: From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
pages.familiar: From Alexander the Grammarian I learned to make my own speech correct without humiliating anyone for a mistake in grammar, sentence structure, or pronunciation. Instead, while responding to the meaning, I could naturally use the correct form myself, or offer a tactful, indirect correction that preserved the other person's dignity.
pages.abbreviated: Alexander taught him to correct his own speech without embarrassing others, using the correct form naturally or offering a tactful indirect correction while responding to their meaning.

pages.label: Book I · Section 8
pages.original: Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called εὐπατρίδαι, _i.e._ nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural affection.
pages.familiar: From Fronto I learned how much envy, deceit, and hypocrisy surround a tyrant's position, and how people born into privilege can sometimes be strangely lacking in ordinary human affection.
pages.abbreviated: Fronto taught him how much envy, deceit, and hypocrisy surround tyrants, and how privilege can coexist with a surprising lack of ordinary human affection.

pages.label: Book I · Section 9
pages.original: Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends and acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent affairs.
pages.familiar: From Alexander the Platonist I learned not to tell someone in a letter, 'I don't have time,' unless there is a real necessity. I should not continually use urgent business as an excuse to postpone the duties I owe my friends and acquaintances, each according to the relationship.
pages.abbreviated: Alexander taught him not to claim lack of time unless truly necessary, and not to use urgent business repeatedly to postpone duties owed to friends and acquaintances.

pages.label: Book I · Section 10
pages.original: Of Catulus, not to contemn any friend's expostulation, though unjust, but to strive to reduce him to his former disposition: freely and heartily to speak well of all my masters upon any occasion, as it is reported of Domitius, and Athenodotus: and to love my children with true affection.
pages.familiar: From Catulus I learned not to dismiss a friend's complaint, even when it is unfair, but to work patiently to restore the friendship to its former warmth. I learned to speak freely and sincerely in praise of all my teachers whenever there was a fitting occasion, as Domitius and Athenodotus were known to do. And I learned to love my children with genuine affection.
pages.abbreviated: Catulus taught him to take even unfair complaints seriously and patiently restore friendship, to praise his teachers openly when appropriate, and to love his children sincerely.

pages.label: Book I · Section 11
pages.original: From my brother Severus, to be kind and loving to all them of my house and family; by whom also I came to the knowledge of Thrasea and Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus. He it was also that did put me in the first conceit and desire of an equal commonwealth, administered by justice and equality; and of a kingdom wherein should be regarded nothing more than the good and welfare of the subjects. Of him also, to observe a constant tenor, (not interrupted, with any other cares and distractions,) in the study and esteem of philosophy: to be bountiful and liberal in the largest measure; always to hope the best; and to be confident that my friends love me. In whom I moreover observed open dealing towards those whom he reproved at any time, and that his friends might without all doubt or much observation know what he would, or would not, so open and plain was he.
pages.familiar: From my brother Severus, I learned to be kind and loving toward everyone in my household and family. Through him I came to know the examples of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus. He first awakened in me the desire for a commonwealth governed by justice and equality, and for a rule concerned with nothing more than the good of its people. From him I learned to keep my study and respect for philosophy steady, without letting other worries distract me; to be generous in the fullest measure; to hope for the best; and to trust that my friends loved me. I also saw in him how openly he dealt with people when he had to correct them, and how plainly he made his wishes known, so that his friends never had to guess what he wanted or did not want.
pages.abbreviated: Severus taught him kindness toward family, commitment to justice and equal government devoted to the people's good, steady philosophical study, generosity, hope, and trust in friends. He also modeled direct correction and plainly expressed preferences.

pages.label: Book I · Section 12
pages.original: From Claudius Maximus, in all things to endeavour to have power of myself, and in nothing to be carried about; to be cheerful and courageous in all sudden chances and accidents, as in sicknesses: to love mildness, and moderation, and gravity: and to do my business, whatsoever it be, thoroughly, and without querulousness. Whatsoever he said, all men believed him that as he spake, so he thought, and whatsoever he did, that he did it with a good intent. His manner was, never to wonder at anything; never to be in haste, and yet never slow: nor to be perplexed, or dejected, or at any time unseemly, or excessively to laugh: nor to be angry, or suspicious, but ever ready to do good, and to forgive, and to speak truth; and all this, as one that seemed rather of himself to have been straight and right, than ever to have been rectified or redressed; neither was there any man that ever thought himself undervalued by him, or that could find in his heart, to think himself a better man than he. He would also be very pleasant and gracious.
pages.familiar: From Claudius Maximus, I learned to govern myself and not be swept along by circumstances; to remain cheerful and brave when sudden trouble came, even illness; to value gentleness, moderation, and dignity; and to do whatever work was before me thoroughly, without complaining. People believed everything he said because his words clearly matched his thoughts, and they trusted that whatever he did, he did with good intentions. He never acted astonished, never rushed, yet was never sluggish. He was not confused, discouraged, awkward, excessively merry, angry, or suspicious. He was always ready to help, forgive, and speak the truth. He seemed naturally upright, as though he had never needed correction. No one felt looked down on by him, yet no one could sincerely think himself better than Maximus. He was also warm, pleasant, and gracious.
pages.abbreviated: Claudius Maximus modeled self-command, courage and cheerfulness in trouble, gentleness, moderation, dignity, thorough work without complaint, and calm, truthful, helpful, forgiving conduct. His words matched his thoughts, his intentions were trusted, and he was warm without being either servile or overbearing.

pages.label: Book I · Section 13
pages.original: In my father, I observed his meekness; his constancy without wavering in those things, which after a due examination and deliberation, he had determined. How free from all vanity he carried himself in matter of honour and dignity, (as they are esteemed:) his laboriousness and assiduity, his readiness to hear any man, that had aught to say tending to any common good: how generally and impartially he would give every man his due; his skill and knowledge, when rigour or extremity, or when remissness or moderation was in season; how he did abstain from all unchaste love of youths; his moderate condescending to other men's occasions as an ordinary man, neither absolutely requiring of his friends, that they should wait upon him at his ordinary meals, nor that they should of necessity accompany him in his journeys; and that whensoever any business upon some necessary occasions was to be put off and omitted before it could be ended, he was ever found when he went about it again, the same man that he was before. His accurate examination of things in consultations, and patient hearing of others. He would not hastily give over the search of the matter, as one easy to be satisfied with sudden notions and apprehensions. His care to preserve his friends; how neither at any time he would carry himself towards them with disdainful neglect, and grow weary of them; nor yet at any time be madly fond of them. His contented mind in all things, his cheerful countenance, his care to foresee things afar off, and to take order for the least, without any noise or clamour. Moreover how all acclamations and flattery were repressed by him: how carefully he observed all things necessary to the government, and kept an account of the common expenses, and how patiently he did abide that he was reprehended by some for this his strict and rigid kind of dealing. How he was neither a superstitious worshipper of the gods, nor an ambitious pleaser of men, or studious of popular applause; but sober in all things, and everywhere observant of that which was fitting; no affecter of novelties: in those things which conduced to his ease and convenience, (plenty whereof his fortune did afford him,) without pride and bragging, yet with all freedom and liberty: so that as he did freely enjoy them without any anxiety or affectation when they were present; so when absent, he found no want of them. Moreover, that he was never commended by any man, as either a learned acute man, or an obsequious officious man, or a fine orator; but as a ripe mature man, a perfect sound man; one that could not endure to be flattered; able to govern both himself and others. Moreover, how much he did honour all true philosophers, without upbraiding those that were not so; his sociableness, his gracious and delightful conversation, but never unto satiety; his care of his body within bounds and measure, not as one that desired to live long, or over-studious of neatness, and elegancy; and yet not as one that did not regard it: so that through his own care and providence, he seldom needed any inward physic, or outward applications: but especially how ingeniously he would yield to any that had obtained any peculiar faculty, as either eloquence, or the knowledge of the laws, or of ancient customs, or the like; and how he concurred with them, in his best care and endeavour that every one of them might in his kind, for that wherein he excelled, be regarded and esteemed: and although he did all things carefully after the ancient customs of his forefathers, yet even of this was he not desirous that men should take notice, that he did imitate ancient customs. Again, how he was not easily moved and tossed up and down, but loved to be constant, both in the same places and businesses; and how after his great fits of headache he would return fresh and vigorous to his wonted affairs. Again, that secrets he neither had many, nor often, and such only as concerned public matters: his discretion and moderation, in exhibiting of the public sights and shows for the pleasure and pastime of the people: in public buildings. congiaries, and the like. In all these things, having a respect unto men only as men, and to the equity of the things themselves, and not unto the glory that might follow. Never wont to use the baths at unseasonable hours; no builder; never curious, or solicitous, either about his meat, or about the workmanship, or colour of his clothes, or about anything that belonged to external beauty. In all his conversation, far from all inhumanity, all boldness, and incivility, all greediness and impetuosity; never doing anything with such earnestness, and intention, that a man could say of him, that he did sweat about it: but contrariwise, all things distinctly, as at leisure; without trouble; orderly, soundly, and agreeably. A man might have applied that to him, which is recorded of Socrates, that he knew how to want, and to enjoy those things, in the want whereof, most men show themselves weak; and in the fruition, intemperate: but to hold out firm and constant, and to keep within the compass of true moderation and sobriety in either estate, is proper to a man, who hath a perfect and invincible soul; such as he showed himself in the sickness of Maximus.
pages.familiar:
In my father I saw gentleness and steadfastness in decisions he had reached after careful examination and thought. He was free from vanity about honor and status. He was hardworking and persistent, ready to listen to anyone who had something useful to say for the common good. He gave everyone what was due to them, fairly and without favoritism. He knew when strictness was needed and when patience or leniency was better. He avoided improper relations with young men. He made reasonable allowances for other people's needs as an ordinary person would, without demanding that friends attend every meal or accompany him on every journey. If necessary business had to be postponed, he returned to it later with the same steady attention.

In discussion he examined matters carefully and listened patiently to others. He did not abandon an inquiry quickly or settle for a first impression. He took care of his friends without neglecting them contemptuously or becoming tired of them, and without becoming foolishly attached. He was contented in every situation, cheerful in appearance, and quietly prepared for distant possibilities and small practical needs alike. He restrained applause and flattery. He carefully managed the responsibilities of government and kept track of public expenses, patiently accepting criticism for being strict about them.

He was neither superstitious in religion nor eager to win popular approval. He was sober, sensible, and attentive to what was appropriate, with no appetite for novelty. When he enjoyed comforts that his fortune provided, he did so freely and without pride or fuss; when they were absent, he felt no desperation for them. No one praised him as a clever scholar, a flattering servant, or a polished speaker, but as a mature, sound, dependable person who could not be manipulated by praise and could govern both himself and others.

He respected genuine philosophers without insulting those who were not philosophers. He was sociable and delightful to talk with, but never exhausting. He cared for his body moderately—not as someone desperate to live long or obsessed with appearance, but not carelessly either. Through his prudence he rarely needed medicine or treatment. He gladly made room for people who excelled in eloquence, law, ancient customs, or other skills, and worked to ensure that each was respected for what he did best. Though he followed the customs of his ancestors carefully, he did not seek recognition for doing so.

He was not easily agitated or thrown off balance. He liked consistency in his places and duties. Even after severe headaches, he returned refreshed to his usual work. He kept few secrets, and those concerned public matters. He showed discretion and moderation in public entertainments, buildings, gifts to the people, and similar affairs, caring about people as people and about fairness itself, not about the praise that might follow.

He did not bathe at inconvenient hours. He was not a builder or someone fussy about food, clothing, colors, or outward beauty. In conversation he was never cruel, presumptuous, rude, greedy, or overbearing. He never worked with such frantic intensity that anyone would say he was sweating over it. He handled everything calmly, distinctly, orderly, competently, and pleasantly.

One could apply to him what was said of Socrates: he knew how to go without things that make most people weak when they lack them, and uncontrolled when they possess them. To remain firm and moderate in either condition belongs to a person with a complete and unconquerable soul. My father showed that strength during Maximus's illness.
pages.abbreviated: His father modeled thoughtful, steadfast, fair, hardworking, patient, and self-controlled leadership, combining careful inquiry with practical attention to people, public duties, money, and future needs. He enjoyed comforts without dependence, respected expertise, followed tradition without vanity, and remained calm, sociable, moderate, competent, and unshaken by praise, hardship, or illness.

pages.label: Book I · Section 14
pages.original: From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, and parents, a good sister, good masters, good domestics, loving kinsmen, almost all that I have; and that I never through haste and rashness transgressed against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such, as that such a thing (if occasion had been) might very well have been committed by me, but that It was the mercy of the gods, to prevent such a concurring of matters and occasions, as might make me to incur this blame. That I was not long brought up by the concubine of my father; that I preserved the flower of my youth. That I took not upon me to be a man before my time, but rather put it off longer than I needed. That I lived under the government of my lord and father, who would take away from me all pride and vainglory, and reduce me to that conceit and opinion that it was not impossible for a prince to live in the court without a troop of guards and followers, extraordinary apparel, such and such torches and statues, and other like particulars of state and magnificence; but that a man may reduce and contract himself almost to the state of a private man, and yet for all that not to become the more base and remiss in those public matters and affairs, wherein power and authority is requisite. That I have had such a brother, who by his own example might stir me up to think of myself; and by his respect and love, delight and please me. That I have got ingenuous children, and that they were not born distorted, nor with any other natural deformity. That I was no great proficient in the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of other faculties, which perchance I might have dwelt upon, if I had found myself to go on in them with success. That I did by times prefer those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and dignities, which they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not put them off with hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but young) I would do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and Rusticus, and Maximus. That I have had occasion often and effectually to consider and meditate with myself, concerning that life which is according to nature, what the nature and manner of it is: so that as for the gods and such suggestions, helps and inspirations, as might be expected from them, nothing did hinder, but that I might have begun long before to live according to nature; or that even now that I was not yet partaker and in present possession of that life, that I myself (in that I did not observe those inward motions, and suggestions, yea and almost plain and apparent instructions and admonitions of the gods,) was the only cause of it. That my body in such a life, hath been able to hold out so long. That I never had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea and afterwards when I fell into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That having been often displeased with Rusticus, I never did him anything for which afterwards I had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was to die young, yet she lived with me all her latter years. That as often as I had a purpose to help and succour any that either were poor, or fallen into some present necessity, I never was answered by my officers that there was not ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never had occasion to require the like succour from any other. That I have such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of fit and able men, to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children. That by dreams I have received help, as for other things, so in particular, how I might stay my casting of blood, and cure my dizziness, as that also that happened to thee in Cajeta, as unto Chryses when he prayed by the seashore. And when I did first apply myself to philosophy, that I did not fall into the hands of some sophists, or spent my time either in reading the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in practising myself in the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt upon the studies of the meteors, and other natural curiosities. All these things without the assistance of the gods, and fortune, could not have been.
pages.familiar:
From the gods I received good grandparents, parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household servants, loving relatives, and nearly everything else I have. I was also spared, through their mercy, from acting rashly and harming any of them, even though my temperament could easily have led me into such a mistake if circumstances had aligned badly. I was not raised for long by my father's concubine, and I preserved the innocence of my youth. I did not rush into adulthood, but delayed it longer than necessary.

I lived under my father's authority. He removed pride and vanity from me and taught me that even a ruler could live at court without a crowd of guards and attendants, elaborate clothing, torches, statues, and other signs of grandeur. A person could live almost like a private citizen without becoming weak or neglecting the public duties that require power and authority.

I had a brother whose example encouraged me to examine myself, and whose love and respect brought me joy. I had intelligent, healthy children. I did not become highly skilled in rhetoric, poetry, or other subjects that I might have pursued if I had found quick success in them. In good time I gave the people who raised me the positions and honors they seemed to want, rather than merely putting them off with promises about the future.

I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus. I was repeatedly given the opportunity to think seriously about a life according to nature—what it is and how it should be lived. Nothing prevented me from beginning much earlier, or from living it fully even now, except my own failure to follow the inner promptings and nearly unmistakable instructions I had received. My body has also held up long enough for such a life.

I was spared affairs with Benedicta and Theodotus, and when I later fell into infatuation, I recovered quickly. Though I was often displeased with Rusticus, I never did anything toward him that I later regretted. Although my mother died young, she lived with me through all her final years. Whenever I intended to help someone poor or in immediate need, my officials never told me there was not enough ready money, and I myself never needed to ask another person for similar help.

I had a wife who was obedient, loving, and intelligent. I had capable people to entrust with my children's upbringing. Dreams sometimes helped me, including with stopping a hemorrhage and curing dizziness. When I first turned to philosophy, I avoided falling into the hands of sophists, wasting time on endless books, practicing clever solutions to arguments and fallacies, or becoming absorbed in obscure natural curiosities. None of these blessings could have come without the gods and fortune.
pages.abbreviated: He credits the gods and fortune for good family, teachers, servants, health, education, opportunities, and protection from rashness, corruption, and harmful entanglements. His father's example taught him that authority can coexist with simplicity, and repeated instruction gave him every opportunity to live according to nature, though failing to do so earlier was his own fault.

pages.label: Book I · Section 15
pages.original: In the country of the Quadi at Granua, these. Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have happened unto them, through ignorance of that which is truly good and truly bad. But I that understand the nature of that which is good, that it only is to be desired, and of that which is bad, that it only is truly odious and shameful: who know moreover, that this transgressor, whosoever he be, is my kinsman, not by the same blood and seed, but by participation of the same reason, and of the same divine particle; How can I either be hurt by any of those, since it is not in their power to make me incur anything that is truly reproachful? or angry, and ill affected towards him, who by nature is so near unto me? for we are all born to be fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of the upper and under teeth: for such therefore to be in opposition, is against nature; and what is it to chafe at, and to be averse from, but to be in opposition?
pages.familiar:
At Granua, in the land of the Quadi, remember this first thing in the morning: today you will meet someone idle and meddlesome, ungrateful, abusive, deceitful, envious, or selfish. These faults come from ignorance of what is truly good and truly bad. I understand that only what is good is worth wanting, and only what is bad is genuinely shameful and hateful. I also understand that this wrongdoer is my relative—not by blood, but because we share reason and the same divine spark.

How could such a person truly harm me, when he cannot force me into anything genuinely disgraceful? And how could I hate or resent someone who is naturally close to me? We were born to work together, like the feet, hands, and eyelids, or the upper and lower rows of teeth. To oppose one another is against nature. To be angry with someone or turn away from him is to oppose the very way we were made.
pages.abbreviated: Expect to meet difficult people, recognizing that their faults come from ignorance of good and evil, while they remain your rational kin. Since people are made to cooperate, anger and withdrawal from them oppose nature, and they cannot force you into genuine wrongdoing.

pages.label: Book I · Section 16
pages.original: Whatsoever I am, is either flesh, or life, or that which we commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man; reason. Away with thy books, suffer not thy mind any more to be distracted, and carried to and fro; for it will not be; but as even now ready to die, think little of thy flesh: blood, bones, and a skin; a pretty piece of knit and twisted work, consisting of nerves, veins and arteries; think no more of it, than so. And as for thy life, consider what it is; a wind; not one constant wind neither, but every moment of an hour let out, and sucked in again. The third, is thy ruling part; and here consider; Thou art an old man; suffer not that excellent part to be brought in subjection, and to become slavish: suffer it not to be drawn up and down with unreasonable and unsociable lusts and motions, as it were with wires and nerves; suffer it not any more, either to repine at anything now present, or to fear and fly anything to come, which the destiny hath appointed thee.
pages.familiar:
Whatever I am consists of flesh, life, and what we commonly call the ruling part: reason. Set aside your books for now and stop letting your mind be pulled in every direction. Since you may die at any moment, think little of the body—blood, bones, skin, and a woven network of nerves, veins, and arteries. That is all it is.

As for life, consider what it is: a breath, not even a steady one, but air released and drawn back in from moment to moment. Then consider your ruling mind. You are an old man. Do not let this finest part of you become submissive and enslaved. Do not let it be dragged around by irrational, antisocial desires, as if pulled by strings. Do not let it complain about what is here now or fear and run from what the course of events has assigned to you.
pages.abbreviated: A person consists of body, breath, and the ruling faculty of reason, while death may come at any time. Therefore do not let reason become enslaved to irrational or antisocial desires, complain about the present, or fear what events bring.

pages.label: Book I · Section 17
pages.original: Whatsoever proceeds from the gods immediately, that any man will grant totally depends from their divine providence. As for those things that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even those must be conceived to have dependence from nature, or from that first and general connection, and concatenation of all those things, which more apparently by the divine providence are administered and brought to pass. All things flow from thence: and whatsoever it is that is, is both necessary, and conducing to the whole (part of which thou art), and whatsoever it is that is requisite and necessary for the preservation of the general, must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and behoveful. And as for the whole, it is preserved, as by the perpetual mutation and conversion of the simple elements one into another, so also by the mutation, and alteration of things mixed and compounded. Let these things suffice thee; let them be always unto thee, as thy general rules and precepts. As for thy thirst after books, away with it with all speed, that thou die not murmuring and complaining, but truly meek and well satisfied, and from thy heart thankful unto the gods.
pages.familiar:
Everyone will agree that whatever comes directly from the gods depends entirely on divine providence. Even what people call chance must be understood as connected with nature and with the first, universal chain of events through which providence orders and brings everything about. Everything flows from that source. Whatever exists is necessary and contributes to the whole, of which you are a part. What the whole needs for its preservation must therefore be useful and beneficial to each individual nature as well.

The whole is preserved through the continual transformation of the basic elements into one another, and through the changes in all mixed and compounded things. Let that be enough for you. Keep these principles as your standing rules. And as for your craving for books, let it go quickly, so that you may meet death without resentment or complaint, but gentle, satisfied, and sincerely grateful.
pages.abbreviated: Everything, including chance, flows from divine providence and universal nature; each necessary part contributes to the whole, whose preservation benefits its members. Hold to this, release excessive attachment to books, and meet death gently, contentedly, and gratefully.

pages.label: Book II · Section 1
pages.original: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it. It is high time for thee to understand the true nature both of the world, whereof thou art a part; and of that Lord and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, thou thyself didst flow: and that there is but a certain limit of time appointed unto thee, which if thou shalt not make use of to calm and allay the many distempers of thy soul, it will pass away and thou with it, and never after return.
pages.familiar: Remember how long you have already postponed these matters, and how often you have ignored the day and hour that seemed to have been set for you. It is time to understand the true nature of the world, of which you are a part, and of the ruler and source of the world, from whom you came as water flows from a spring. Your time has a fixed limit. If you do not use it to calm and heal the disorders of your soul, it will pass away—and you with it—and you will not return.
pages.abbreviated: Stop postponing the work of understanding the world, your place in it, and its divine source, because your time is limited. If you do not use it to heal your soul, life will pass and cannot be recovered.

pages.label: Book II · Section 2
pages.original: Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which thou shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action, free from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason, and from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things, which by the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee. Thou seest that those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous course, and to live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not many, for the gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep and observe these things.
pages.familiar:
Make it your constant and serious aim, as a human being and a citizen, to do whatever you are doing with genuine dignity, natural affection, freedom, and justice. Release yourself from every other worry and fantasy. You can do this by approaching each action as though it were your last: free from vanity, emotional rebellion against reason, hypocrisy, selfishness, and resentment toward whatever fate or God has placed before you.

You can see that the requirements for a successful life and a life in harmony with the divine are not many. The gods ask no more of anyone who simply keeps these principles.
pages.abbreviated: Make every action dignified, affectionate, free, and just, as though it were your last, without vanity, rebellion against reason, hypocrisy, selfishness, or resentment toward fate. These few principles are sufficient for a good and godly life.

pages.label: Book II · Section 3
pages.original: Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.
pages.familiar: Come on, soul—do what must be done. Stop mistreating and belittling yourself. Soon there will be no time left to respect yourself. Every person's happiness depends on himself, yet your life is nearly over while you keep denying yourself that respect and make your happiness depend on the opinions and judgments of other people.
pages.abbreviated: Stop mistreating and belittling yourself, because life is nearly over and happiness depends on your own judgment rather than other people's opinions.

pages.label: Book II · Section 4
pages.original: Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another kind of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and labour in this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all their motions, and desires.
pages.familiar: Why let outside events distract you so much? Make time to learn something worthwhile, and stop rushing aimlessly from one thing to another. There is another kind of wandering too: people can spend their whole lives working hard without any clear purpose guiding their actions and desires.
pages.abbreviated: Do not let external events or aimless busyness distract you from learning something worthwhile. People can also wander through life by working hard without any clear purpose guiding their actions and desires.

pages.label: Book II · Section 5
pages.original: For not observing the state of another man's soul, scarce was ever any man known to be unhappy. Tell whosoever they be that intend not, and guide not by reason and discretion the motions of their own souls, they must of necessity be unhappy.
pages.familiar: Almost no one has ever been made unhappy simply by failing to understand another person's state of mind. But anyone who neither directs nor governs the movements of their own soul with reason and good judgment must inevitably be unhappy.
pages.abbreviated: Failing to understand another person's mind rarely causes unhappiness, but failing to govern one's own soul through reason and sound judgment inevitably does.

pages.label: Book II · Section 6
pages.original: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.
pages.familiar: Keep these questions before you: What is the nature of the universe, and what is my own nature? How am I related to it, and what part do I play in the whole? Remember that no one can prevent you from doing and saying what fits the nature of the universe, of which you are a part.
pages.abbreviated: Consider the nature of the universe, your own nature, your relationship to the whole, and your role within it. No one can prevent you from speaking and acting according to the universe's nature.

pages.label: Book II · Section 7
pages.original: Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust, than those which are committed through anger. For he that is angry seems with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn away from reason; but he that sins through lust, being overcome by pleasure, doth in his very sin bewray a more impotent, and unmanlike disposition. Well then and like a philosopher doth he say, that he of the two is the more to be condemned, that sins with pleasure, than he that sins with grief. For indeed this latter may seem first to have been wronged, and so in some manner through grief thereof to have been forced to be angry, whereas he who through lust doth commit anything, did of himself merely resolve upon that action.
pages.familiar: Theophrastus made a sound philosophical comparison between wrongdoing driven by desire and wrongdoing driven by anger. Anger seems to turn away from reason through pain and inner strain; desire gives in to pleasure and reveals a weaker, less disciplined character. So the person who does wrong for pleasure may deserve more blame than the person who does wrong in anguish. The angry person may first have been hurt and then pushed into anger by that pain. But the person acting from desire freely chooses the act for the sake of pleasure.
pages.abbreviated: Wrongdoing from anger begins in pain and inner strain, while wrongdoing from desire freely chooses pleasure over reason. Therefore the person who acts from desire may deserve greater blame than one driven into anger by suffering.

pages.label: Book II · Section 8
pages.original: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life. And as for death, if there be any gods, it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do thee no hurt, thou mayest be sure. But if it be so that there be no gods, or that they take no care of the world, why should I desire to live in a world void of gods, and of all divine providence? But gods there be certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those things which be truly evil, as vice and wickedness, such things they have put in a man's own power, that he might avoid them if he would: and had there been anything besides that had been truly bad and evil, they would have had a care of that also, that a man might have avoided it. But why should that be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in this world, which cannot any ways make man himself the better, or the worse in his own person? Neither must we think that the nature of the universe did either through ignorance pass these things, or if not as ignorant of them, yet as unable either to prevent, or better to order and dispose them. It cannot be that she through want either of power or skill, should have committed such a thing, so as to suffer all things both good and bad, equally and promiscuously, to happen unto all both good and bad. As for life therefore, and death, honour and dishonour, labour and pleasure, riches and poverty, all these things happen unto men indeed, both good and bad, equally; but as things which of themselves are neither good nor bad; because of themselves, neither shameful nor praiseworthy.
pages.familiar: Whatever you do or plan, do it as someone who may have to leave life at this very moment. If there are gods, leaving human company is nothing terrible; they will not harm you. If there are no gods or no care for the world, why would I want to live in a world without divine order? But there are gods, and they care for the world. They have placed what is truly evil—vice and wrongdoing—within our own power to avoid. If anything else were truly evil, they would have made that avoidable too. Why should something be thought harmful to your life if it cannot make you better or worse as a person? Life and death, honor and disgrace, work and pleasure, wealth and poverty happen to good and bad people alike. In themselves, they are neither good nor bad, shameful nor praiseworthy.
pages.abbreviated: Act as though death may come immediately: if gods exist, they will receive you, and if not, a godless life would have no reason to be preferred. The gods place true evil, vice, within our control to avoid; life, death, honor, disgrace, work, pleasure, wealth, and poverty affect good and bad people alike and are neither good nor bad in themselves.

pages.label: Book II · Section 9
pages.original: Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world. Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things; of those especially, which either ensnare by pleasure, or for their irksomeness are dreadful, or for their outward lustre and show are in great esteem and request, how vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of all true life and being they are.
pages.familiar: Consider how quickly everything breaks down and returns to its source: bodies and physical things become part of the world's matter, and memories dissolve into the world's long passage of time. Look closely at everything that affects the senses, especially what traps people through pleasure, frightens them through discomfort, or wins admiration through outward brilliance and display. See how cheap, fragile, corruptible, and lacking in any lasting life these things really are.
pages.abbreviated: Everything quickly dissolves into matter and time, including bodies, memories, and sensory attractions. Pleasure, fear, and outward splendor are fragile, corruptible, and without lasting life.

pages.label: Book II · Section 10
pages.original: It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty, to consider what they themselves are in very deed, from whose bare conceits and voices, honour and credit do proceed: as also what it is to die, and how if a man shall consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate from it in his mind all those things which with it usually represent themselves unto us, he can conceive of it no otherwise, than as of a work of nature, and he that fears any work of nature, is a very child. Now death, it is not only a work of nature, but also conducing to nature.
pages.familiar: A person with sound understanding should ask what those people are really like whose opinions and voices create honor and reputation. Consider death by itself. If you mentally remove all the images and fears usually attached to it, death appears simply as an act of nature. Anyone afraid of an act of nature is still like a child. Death is not only natural; it also serves nature.
pages.abbreviated: A sound mind should examine the people whose opinions create honor and reputation. Stripped of its usual fears and images, death is simply a natural act—and fearing nature is childish; death also serves nature.

pages.label: Book II · Section 11
pages.original: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible, that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is within him, and truly and really to serve him. His service doth consist in this, that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, either in regard of the gods or men. For indeed whatsoever proceeds from the gods, deserves respect for their worth and excellency; and whatsoever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be entertained, with love, always; sometimes, as proceeding from their ignorance, of that which is truly good and bad, (a blindness no less, than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black:) with a kind of pity and compassion also.
pages.familiar: Consider how a person is joined to the divine, and what happens to that part of us when it is allowed to spread outward. Nothing is more miserable than a soul that searches everywhere—even into the depths of the earth—and tries to uncover other people's thoughts, yet fails to understand that it is enough to devote all its attention and care to the guiding spirit within. To serve that spirit means keeping free of violent passions and harmful desires, rashness and vanity, and every kind of resentment toward gods or people. Whatever comes from the gods deserves respect for their excellence. Whatever comes from people should be met with love because they are our kin—and sometimes with pity, because their ignorance of good and evil is like our inability to tell white from black.
pages.abbreviated: The soul should stop searching through others and devote itself to its inner guiding spirit by rejecting violent passions, harmful desires, rashness, vanity, and resentment. Respect what comes from the gods, and meet people with love as kin, or pity when their ignorance harms them.

pages.label: Book II · Section 12
pages.original: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being, is equal unto all men. And that being it which we part with whensoever we die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he hath not? These two things therefore thou must remember. First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with, is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present, is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.
pages.familiar: You may live three thousand years or ten thousand, but remember that you can give up only the small portion of life you are living right now. That is all anyone ever gives up. The longest life and the shortest therefore come to the same end. The past may differ in length, but the present moment is equal for everyone. When we die, we surrender only that moment, because we cannot truly give up what has already passed or what has not yet come. Remember two things. First, everything in the world has always moved through recurring cycles, with the same kinds of events arising again and again, so seeing them for a hundred years, two hundred years, or forever makes little difference. Second, the life surrendered by the longest-lived and the shortest-lived is equal in duration, because each can lose only the present moment—the only thing either actually possesses.
pages.abbreviated: No matter how long one lives, one can give up only the present moment, so the longest and shortest lives end equally in this respect. Since events recur through cycles and neither past nor future is possessed, length of life makes little difference.

pages.label: Book II · Section 13
pages.original: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.
pages.familiar: Remember that everything is shaped by opinion and interpretation. The points made to Monimus the Cynic were clear, and so is the practical lesson in them, if you accept the serious truth along with whatever is pleasant or amusing.
pages.abbreviated: Everything is shaped by opinion and interpretation. The lesson of Monimus the Cynic is clear if one accepts its serious truth along with its pleasant or amusing aspects.

pages.label: Book II · Section 14
pages.original: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are. Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are the souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done, without relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures is, to follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of this great city, and ancient commonwealth.
pages.familiar: A person's soul first wrongs and dishonors itself when, as far as it can, it makes itself an isolated growth detached from the world. To resent what happens in the world is to rebel against the nature of the universe, of which every individual nature is a part. Second, it wrongs itself when it turns against another person or is driven by desires that would harm them, as happens in anger. Third, when it lets pleasure or pain master it. Fourth, when it hides behind false words or actions. Fifth, when it pursues something without a clear purpose, acting rashly and without considering whether it serves the common good. Nothing should be done without reference to that end, because the purpose of rational beings is to follow and obey reason—the law of this great city and ancient commonwealth.
pages.abbreviated: The soul wrongs itself by rejecting its place in the universe, harming others, surrendering to pleasure or pain, using deceit, or acting rashly without regard for the common good. Rational beings should therefore follow reason, the law of the universal community.

pages.label: Book II · Section 15
pages.original: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful; to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the body; as a dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul. Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing, philosophy. And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to preserve that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies and injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from himself and his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to embrace contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those elements, of which every creature is composed. And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into another, that dissolution, and alteration, which is so common unto all, why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature can be evil. _Whilst I was at Carnuntum._
pages.familiar: A human life is a point; its substance is always flowing away, its senses are dim, and the body is steadily moving toward decay. The soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and reputation unreliable. In short, bodily things are like a stream; things of the soul like a dream or smoke. Life is a campaign and a journey. Fame after death is little better than being forgotten. What, then, remains with us? Only philosophy. And philosophy means preserving the spirit within us from insult and injury, and from being ruled by pain or pleasure; never acting rashly, deceptively, or hypocritically; relying on our own actions; accepting whatever happens with contentment, since it comes from the same source as we do; and above all, meeting death gently and cheerfully, as nothing more than the breaking apart of the elements from which every creature is made. If the elements suffer nothing by constantly changing into one another, why should we fear this dissolution and change, which happens to everything? Is it not natural? And nothing natural can be evil. Written at Carnuntum.
pages.abbreviated: Life, the body, fortune, and reputation are fleeting, leaving philosophy as the lasting guide. Philosophy preserves the spirit from passion, deceit, and self-injury, accepts what happens, and meets death cheerfully as a natural transformation of elements, which cannot be evil.

pages.label: Book III · Section 1
pages.original: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend. For if once he shall begin to dote, his respiration, nutrition, his imaginative, and appetitive, and other natural faculties, may still continue the same: he shall find no want of them. But how to make that right use of himself that he should, how to observe exactly in all things that which is right and just, how to redress and rectify all wrong, or sudden apprehensions and imaginations, and even of this particular, whether he should live any longer or no, to consider duly; for all such things, wherein the best strength and vigour of the mind is most requisite; his power and ability will be past and gone. Thou must hasten therefore; not only because thou art every day nearer unto death than other, but also because that intellective faculty in thee, whereby thou art enabled to know the true nature of things, and to order all thy actions by that knowledge, doth daily waste and decay: or, may fail thee before thou die.
pages.familiar: You must consider not only how your life is shrinking each day, but also that, even if you live a long time, you cannot know whether your understanding will remain strong enough for sound judgment in practical matters or for reflection—the very abilities on which true knowledge of human and divine things depends. If your mind begins to fail, your breathing, digestion, imagination, appetite, and other natural functions may continue normally. But the ability to use yourself properly, to recognize what is right and just, to correct mistakes and sudden impressions, and even to judge whether continuing to live is worthwhile—all this requires the mind at its best, and that strength may be gone. Hurry, then—not only because death comes closer every day, but because the faculty that lets you understand reality and order your actions by it is wasting away, and may fail before you die.
pages.abbreviated: Life is shrinking, and the mind may lose its ability to judge, reflect, correct impressions, and determine how to live before the body fails. Hurry to understand reality and order your actions by it while that faculty remains.

pages.label: Book III · Section 2
pages.original: This also thou must observe, that whatsoever it is that naturally doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing and delightful: as a great loaf when it is baked, some parts of it cleave as it were, and part asunder, and make the crust of it rugged and unequal, and yet those parts of it, though in some sort it be against the art and intention of baking itself, that they are thus cleft and parted, which should have been and were first made all even and uniform, they become it well nevertheless, and have a certain peculiar property, to stir the appetite. So figs are accounted fairest and ripest then, when they begin to shrink, and wither as it were. So ripe olives, when they are next to putrefaction, then are they in their proper beauty. The hanging down of grapes--the brow of a lion, the froth of a foaming wild boar, and many other like things, though by themselves considered, they are far from any beauty, yet because they happen naturally, they both are comely, and delightful; so that if a man shall with a profound mind and apprehension, consider all things in the world, even among all those things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were, there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find matter of pleasure and delight. So will he behold with as much pleasure the true _rictus_ of wild beasts, as those which by skilful painters and other artificers are imitated. So will he be able to perceive the proper ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman: and whatsoever else it is that is beautiful and alluring in whatsoever is, with chaste and continent eyes he will soon find out and discern. Those and many other things will he discern, not credible unto every one, but unto them only who are truly and familiarly acquainted, both with nature itself, and all natural things.
pages.familiar: Notice also that whatever happens naturally to natural things contains something pleasing in it. When a large loaf is baked, parts of it split and leave the crust rough and uneven. Though this goes against the baker's original plan for a smooth, uniform loaf, it still suits the bread and gives it a special power to awaken appetite. Figs are considered most beautiful and ripe when they begin to shrivel. Ripe olives are at their proper beauty when they are almost spoiled. The drooping grapes, a lion's wrinkled brow, the foam around a wild boar's mouth, and many other things may seem ugly by themselves, yet because they arise naturally, they are fitting and appealing. If you look deeply at everything in the world, even its incidental details, you will find little that cannot give pleasure. You will see the real snarl of a wild animal with as much appreciation as a painter's imitation. You will recognize the particular ripeness and beauty of old age in a man or woman, and you will quickly notice whatever else is naturally beautiful and attractive—with clean, disciplined eyes. Many people will not believe this; it is visible only to those truly familiar with nature and all natural things.
pages.abbreviated: Natural things are pleasing even when they seem rough, withered, wrinkled, or ugly, because their natural condition gives them fitting beauty. Deep familiarity with nature reveals this beauty in aging, animals, and every incidental detail.

pages.label: Book III · Section 3
pages.original: Hippocrates having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologians having foretold the deaths of divers, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates. Alexander and Pompeius, and Caius Cæsar, having destroyed so many towns, and cut off in the field so many thousands both of horse and foot, yet they themselves at last were fain to part with their own lives. Heraclitus having written so many natural tracts concerning the last and general conflagration of the world, died afterwards all filled with water within, and all bedaubed with dirt and dung without. Lice killed Democritus; and Socrates, another sort of vermin, wicked ungodly men. How then stands the case? Thou hast taken ship, thou hast sailed, thou art come to land, go out, if to another life, there also shalt thou find gods, who are everywhere. If all life and sense shall cease, then shalt thou cease also to be subject to either pains or pleasures; and to serve and tend this vile cottage; so much the viler, by how much that which ministers unto it doth excel; the one being a rational substance, and a spirit, the other nothing but earth and blood.
pages.familiar: Hippocrates cured many illnesses, then became ill himself and died. Astrologers predicted the deaths of others, then were themselves caught by fate. Alexander, Pompey, and Caesar destroyed cities and killed thousands of soldiers, yet in the end they too had to surrender their lives. Heraclitus wrote about the world's final conflagration, then died swollen with water inside and covered with mud and filth outside. Lice killed Democritus; Socrates was killed by another kind of pest—wicked men. So what is the situation? You have boarded the ship, sailed, and reached land. Get off. If there is another life, you will find gods there too, for they are everywhere. If life and consciousness end, then you will no longer be subject to pain or pleasure, nor serve and care for this miserable body—made more miserable by the greatness of what serves it, since one is rational spirit and the other only earth and blood.
pages.abbreviated: Even healers, prophets, conquerors, philosophers, and wise people eventually die. Having sailed through life and reached land, one should leave calmly: either the gods await beyond, or consciousness ends and there is no further pain, pleasure, or burden of the body.

pages.label: Book III · Section 4
pages.original: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work. That is, spend not thy time in thinking, what such a man doth, and to what end: what he saith, and what he thinks, and what he is about, and such other things or curiosities, which make a man to rove and wander from the care and observation of that part of himself, which is rational, and overruling. See therefore in the whole series and connection of thy thoughts, that thou be careful to prevent whatsoever is idle and impertinent: but especially, whatsoever is curious and malicious: and thou must use thyself to think only of such things, of which if a man upon a sudden should ask thee, what it is that thou art now thinking, thou mayest answer This, and That, freely and boldly, that so by thy thoughts it may presently appear that in all thee is sincere, and peaceable; as becometh one that is made for society, and regards not pleasures, nor gives way to any voluptuous imaginations at all: free from all contentiousness, envy, and suspicion, and from whatsoever else thou wouldest blush to confess thy thoughts were set upon. He that is such, is he surely that doth not put off to lay hold on that which is best indeed, a very priest and minister of the gods, well acquainted and in good correspondence with him especially that is seated and placed within himself, as in a temple and sacrary: to whom also he keeps and preserves himself unspotted by pleasure, undaunted by pain; free from any manner of wrong, or contumely, by himself offered unto himself: not capable of any evil from others: a wrestler of the best sort, and for the highest prize, that he may not be cast down by any passion or affection of his own; deeply dyed and drenched in righteousness, embracing and accepting with his whole heart whatsoever either happeneth or is allotted unto him. One who not often, nor without some great necessity tending to some public good, mindeth what any other, either speaks, or doth, or purposeth: for those things only that are in his own power, or that are truly his own, are the objects of his employments, and his thoughts are ever taken up with those things, which of the whole universe are by the fates or Providence destinated and appropriated unto himself. Those things that are his own, and in his own power, he himself takes order, for that they be good: and as for those that happen unto him, he believes them to be so. For that lot and portion which is assigned to every one, as it is unavoidable and necessary, so is it always profitable. He remembers besides that whatsoever partakes of reason, is akin unto him, and that to care for all men generally, is agreeing to the nature of a man: but as for honour and praise, that they ought not generally to be admitted and accepted of from all, but from such only, who live according to nature. As for them that do not, what manner of men they be at home, or abroad; day or night, how conditioned themselves with what manner of conditions, or with men of what conditions they moil and pass away the time together, he knoweth, and remembers right well, he therefore regards not such praise and approbation, as proceeding from them, who cannot like and approve themselves.
pages.familiar: Do not spend the rest of your days thinking about other people unless it serves the common good. Otherwise it keeps you from better work. Do not waste time wondering what someone is doing, why, what they are saying, thinking, or planning, or following similar curiosities that pull you away from caring for and guiding your rational self. Watch the whole chain of your thoughts and cut off whatever is idle or irrelevant—especially what is prying or malicious. Train yourself to think only about things you could name openly if someone suddenly asked what was on your mind. Let your thoughts show a sincere and peaceful person, made for society, untouched by envy, suspicion, quarrelsomeness, or pleasures you would be ashamed to confess. Such a person does not delay in reaching for what is truly best. They are like a priest serving the gods, in close relationship with the divine presence within, keeping themselves unstained by pleasure, unshaken by pain, and free from wronging themselves. Nothing others do can truly harm them. They are a first-rate wrestler competing for the highest prize, not thrown down by their own passions, deeply committed to justice, and wholeheartedly accepting whatever happens or is assigned to them. They rarely concern themselves with what others say, do, or intend, unless some serious public good requires it. Their work and thoughts concern what is in their own power and what fate has assigned them.
