They make their own actions good and trust that what happens to them is good as well, because each person's allotted share is unavoidable and therefore useful. They remember that every rational being is kin, and that caring for humanity is natural. But they accept honor and praise only from people who live according to nature. They know what the others are like, at home or away, day or night, and what company they keep; so they do not care about approval from people who cannot even respect themselves.
pages.abbreviated: Do not dwell on others unless the common good requires it; guard your thoughts from idle curiosity, envy, suspicion, and malice. Focus on your own power and assigned duties, act justly, accept what happens as useful, care for humanity as kin, and disregard praise from people who do not live according to nature.

pages.label: Book III · Section 5
pages.original: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy. Affect not to set out thy thoughts with curious neat language. Be neither a great talker, nor a great undertaker. Moreover, let thy God that is in thee to rule over thee, find by thee, that he hath to do with a man; an aged man; a sociable man; a Roman; a prince; one that hath ordered his life, as one that expecteth, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet, sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all expedition. One who for his word or actions neither needs an oath, nor any man to be a witness.
pages.familiar: Do nothing against your will, against the community, without careful examination, or with inner resistance. Do not decorate your thoughts with overly clever language. Do not talk endlessly or take on everything. Let the divine presence within you find that it is dealing with a human being—an older man, a social being, a Roman, a prince—someone who has arranged his life as if he were waiting only for the trumpet calling him to leave this life promptly. Let your word and actions need neither an oath nor a witness.
pages.abbreviated: Act willingly, socially, thoughtfully, and without inner resistance; avoid clever ornament, endless speech, and overcommitment. Live as a rational, social person ready to leave life immediately, with words and actions needing no oath or witness.

pages.label: Book III · Section 6
pages.original: To be cheerful, and to stand in no need, either of other men's help or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity, which thou must be beholding to others for. Rather like one that is straight of himself, or hath ever been straight, than one that hath been rectified.
pages.familiar: Be cheerful, and do not depend on other people's help, attention, or the peace and rest they provide. Be like someone who stands straight by nature, not someone who had to be straightened.
pages.abbreviated: Be cheerful and independent of other people's help, attention, peace, or rest. Stand upright naturally, rather than needing to be forced into integrity.

pages.label: Book III · Section 7
pages.original: If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better than a mind contented both with those things which according to right and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart, and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.
pages.familiar: If you find anything in this mortal life better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and a mind content with both its own right actions and whatever happens beyond its control by providence, then devote yourself to it completely and enjoy it freely. But if nothing is better than the spirit within you—than mastering your desires, refusing to follow an impression before examining it, withdrawing from sensual excess, submitting yourself to the gods, and caring for everyone—then do not let anything else distract you. Once popular applause, honor, wealth, or pleasure begins to attract you, it quickly takes over and turns your mind from the right path. Choose what is best plainly and freely, and hold to it. What is best is what is most useful. If useful means useful to a rational human being, stand by it and defend it; if it means useful only to an animal, reject it. Keep attractive appearances and persuasive pretenses from clouding your judgment, so you can see things clearly.
pages.abbreviated: If anything surpasses justice, truth, self-control, courage, and a contented rational spirit, pursue it completely; otherwise devote yourself to the inner spirit and its virtues. Reject applause, honor, wealth, pleasure, and attractive appearances when they distract from what is genuinely useful to a rational human being.

pages.label: Book III · Section 8
pages.original: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action, which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long, this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
pages.familiar: Never call anything beneficial if it forces you to break your word, lose your modesty, hate someone, become suspicious, curse, deceive, or desire something that must be hidden behind walls or curtains. Anyone who puts their rational spirit and the sacred work of virtue above everything else will never spend life lamenting or complaining. They will need neither isolation nor constant company. Most importantly, they will live without fear or craving. Whether life is long or short, they will be indifferent, because if they had to leave right now, they would be as ready as for any other action that could be done decently and honorably. Their lifelong concern is simply to keep their mind occupied with purposes and subjects fitting for a rational, social being.
pages.abbreviated: Nothing is beneficial if it requires breaking promises, losing modesty, hating, suspecting, cursing, deceiving, or hiding desires. Someone devoted to virtue can live without complaint, fear, craving, or dependence on life’s length, remaining ready to die and focused on rational, social purposes.

pages.label: Book III · Section 9
pages.original: In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered: nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man might speak.
pages.familiar: In a mind that has truly been disciplined and cleansed, you will find nothing foul, corrupt, or festering; nothing servile or artificial; no divided loyalties, malicious hostility, vulnerability, or hidden corner. Such a person’s life can never be caught unfinished by death, like an actor dying before the scene or the play is over.
pages.abbreviated: A disciplined and purified mind contains no corruption, artificiality, hostility, divided loyalty, hidden weakness, or concealed motive. Such a life is complete and cannot be caught unfinished by death.

pages.label: Book III · Section 10
pages.original: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods. Casting therefore all other things aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time. Whatsoever is besides either is already past, or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead and gone.
pages.familiar: Treat your power of judgment with the highest respect, because everything depends on it. Do not let your opinions place anything in your mind that conflicts with nature or with the proper character of a rational being. A rational being exists to act without recklessness, to treat people with kindness, and to willingly accept what the gods bring. Set everything else aside and hold to these few principles. Remember, too, that no one truly lives beyond the present moment, which is only an instant. Everything else is either already gone or uncertain. Our whole lifetime is brief, our place on earth is tiny, and even the greatest fame after death is small. And while it lasts, that fame is preserved by short-lived people who soon die themselves and do not really understand even their own lives, much less someone who died long ago.
pages.abbreviated: Guard your judgment, since everything depends on it, and hold to the rational duties of avoiding recklessness, treating people kindly, and accepting what the gods bring. Since only the present exists and fame is brief and poorly understood, set everything else aside.

pages.label: Book III · Section 11
pages.original: To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added, ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked; wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but houses and families?
pages.familiar: Add one more practice to these constant reminders: whenever something appears before your mind, describe it clearly and completely. Look at it in its own nature, stripped bare; examine it as a whole and in every part. Then name it, and name the things from which it is made and into which it will dissolve, using their true names. Nothing creates real courage more effectively than examining everything that happens in life carefully and methodically, penetrating its nature, and asking at the same time: What is this really for? What place does it have in the nature of the universe? How important is it to the whole? How important is it to a human being, a citizen of the great commonwealth, compared with which every other city is only a household?
pages.abbreviated: Examine every impression clearly, completely, and in its true nature, including what it is made of and what it will become. Ask its purpose, place in the universe, and significance to the whole and to a human citizen, because this method produces courage.

pages.label: Book III · Section 12
pages.original: What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth, faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God, this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.
pages.familiar: What is my mind fixed on right now? What is it made of? How long can it last? Which virtue is needed here—gentleness, courage, honesty, trust, sincerity, contentment, or another? With everything that happens, train yourself to say: This comes from God; this follows from the chain of causes; or, which amounts to nearly the same thing, it happened by chance. As for this person, it comes from my neighbor, my relative, my fellow human being—through ignorance, because he does not understand what is natural for him. But I do understand, so I will treat him according to the natural law we share: with kindness and justice. As for things that are indifferent in themselves, I will respond to each according to the value I reasonably judge it to have.
pages.abbreviated: Ask what occupies the mind, how long it will last, and which virtue the situation requires. Attribute events to God, causes, or chance; treat others kindly and justly as fellow humans, and respond to indifferent things according to their reasonably judged value.

pages.label: Book III · Section 13
pages.original: If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak, contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
pages.familiar: If you focus on what is happening now, carefully following right reason with steadiness and gentleness; if you do not mix in other concerns, but devote yourself to keeping your spirit clean and undisturbed; if you hold to it without hoping for or fearing anything, and in everything you do or say are satisfied with honest truth, you will live happily. No one can prevent this.
pages.abbreviated: By attending steadily and gently to the present, keeping the spirit clean and undisturbed, expecting and fearing nothing, and speaking and acting honestly, one can live happily. No one can prevent this.

pages.label: Book III · Section 14
pages.original: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
pages.familiar: Doctors and surgeons keep their instruments ready for sudden emergencies. Keep your principles equally ready, so you understand both divine and human matters. In everything you do, even the smallest thing, remember the connection between them. Without regard for God, you will not succeed in human affairs; and without regard for human realities, you will not succeed in anything divine.
pages.abbreviated: Keep your principles ready for emergencies as doctors keep instruments prepared. Every act connects divine and human matters: without regard for God, human affairs fail, and without regard for human realities, nothing divine succeeds.

pages.label: Book III · Section 15
pages.original: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
pages.familiar: Do not fool yourself: you will not live long enough to read all the moral writings, histories of famous Romans and Greeks, and selections from the books you have saved for old age. So get to the point. Give up empty hopes and help yourself while you still can, if you truly care about yourself as you should.
pages.abbreviated: You will not live long enough to read everything saved for later, so abandon empty hopes and address the essential work of improving yourself while you still can.

pages.label: Book III · Section 16
pages.original: To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
pages.familiar: To steal, to plant, to buy, to rest, to see what must be done—which does not mean seeing with the eyes but with another kind of vision—people do not understand what these words mean or how many ways they can be understood. There is the body, the soul, and the mind. The senses naturally belong to the body, desires and emotions to the soul, and principles to the mind.
pages.abbreviated: Common actions such as stealing, planting, buying, resting, and seeing can have different meanings depending on the faculty involved. The body has senses, the soul has desires and emotions, and the mind has principles.

pages.label: Book III · Section 17
pages.original: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything. If therefore all things else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably, or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion.
pages.familiar: The ability to form images and impressions is shared by humans and animals. Being violently dragged around by desire belongs to wild beasts and monsters such as Phalaris and Nero. Following reason in ordinary duties is also possible for people who deny the gods and, for their own advantage, would betray their country—people who, once the doors are closed, dare to do anything. If all these qualities are shared, then the distinctive quality of a good person must be this: to welcome everything that happens and is assigned to him; not to disturb the spirit within his own heart with a crowd of empty fantasies; but to keep that spirit calm, obey it as something divine, and never say what is false or do what is unjust. Even if no one believes that he lives sincerely, conscientiously, cheerfully, or contentedly, he does not become angry with anyone or abandon the path toward the end of life. He continues on it pure, always ready to leave, and willingly adapting himself to the portion allotted to him.
pages.abbreviated: Imagination, desire, and ordinary reason are shared with animals, monsters, and even dishonest atheists, so a good person is distinguished by welcoming what happens, keeping the inner spirit calm, and refusing falsehood and injustice. Such a person remains sincere, cheerful, contented, pure, ready to die, and willing to adapt to their allotted share even without recognition.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 1
pages.original: That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those very things it is made greater and greater.
pages.familiar: When a person’s ruling mind is in its natural condition, it responds to every event in the world by easily turning toward whatever is possible and within its power, whenever its first intention cannot be carried out. It never binds itself completely to one outcome. Whatever it pursues, it pursues with a reservation: if things turn out differently, that new situation becomes its next object. It is like a fire. Small flames may be put out by what falls onto them, but a great fire quickly changes whatever reaches it into fire and uses it to grow stronger.
pages.abbreviated: When its first intention fails, a naturally ordered mind turns easily toward whatever remains possible and within its power, treating the changed situation as its new aim. Like a great fire, it transforms obstacles into material for greater strength.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 2
pages.original: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
pages.familiar: Do nothing hastily or randomly. Let everything you do follow careful, practiced principles.
pages.abbreviated: Act neither hastily nor randomly; let everything you do follow careful, practiced principles.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 3
pages.original: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end. As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee? How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
pages.familiar: People look for quiet retreats in the countryside, by the sea, or in the mountains, and you often long for them too. But this desire comes from not realizing what is always available to you. Whenever you choose, you can withdraw into yourself, settle down, and be free from outside demands. No place offers a better retreat than your own mind—especially when you have prepared it with thoughts that can give you immediate peace whenever you turn inward. By peace, I mean a steady, orderly way of being, free from confusion and turmoil. Give yourself this retreat often, and use it to restore yourself. Keep a few short, basic principles ready; remembering them should be enough to clear your mind and send you back satisfied with whatever you must return to. What are you upset about? Other people's wrongdoing? Remember that reasonable beings are made to help one another, that patience with them is part of justice, and that they often act against their better judgment. Remember how many people who once hated, suspected, and fought one another are now gone and forgotten. It is time to stop dwelling on it. Are you troubled by whatever circumstances have fallen to your share? Remember the two possibilities: either the world follows a larger order, or it is simply the result of chance—and remember all the arguments that show humanity is still one community. Are you worried about your body? What can it ultimately threaten, once your mind has gathered itself and understood its own power? Whether your breathing is easy or difficult, your mind need not surrender itself to either pain or pleasure. Are you distracted by concern for your reputation? Look back and see how quickly everything is forgotten, how endless time stretches before and after us, how empty praise is, how changeable people's opinions are, and how small the place is where anyone can know you. The whole earth is a point; the inhabited part is smaller still; and among its people, how many will ever praise you—and what are they really worth? So practice returning to this small inner space. Above all, avoid distraction. Do not cling fiercely to any one thing. Consider everything as a person whose aim is virtue, whose nature is kindness and cooperation, a citizen, and a mortal being. When you withdraw into yourself, keep two thoughts close. First, things themselves do not enter your mind and disturb it; they remain outside. The turmoil comes from the judgment you form about them. Second, everything you see will soon change and disappear. Remember how many changes you have already witnessed. The world is change, and life is shaped by our judgments.
pages.abbreviated: Your own prepared mind is a better retreat than any place, offering peace whenever you turn inward. Return to it by remembering that judgments cause turmoil, people are interconnected and mortal, circumstances follow order or chance, reputation fades, and everything changes.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 4
pages.original: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath proceeded.
pages.familiar: If understanding and reason are shared by all people, then the reason that makes us rational is shared by all as well. If reason is shared, then the principles that tell us what to do and what to avoid are shared too. If those principles are shared, we have a common law. If we have common law, we are fellow citizens. If we are fellow citizens, we belong to one common society. The world, then, is like one city. What other society could all people belong to? From this common city come our understanding, reason, and law—for where else could they come from? Just as the earth in me comes from the common earth, moisture from the common waters, and breath and life from their own sources—and just as nothing comes from nowhere or disappears into nothing—there must also be a common source from which my understanding comes.
pages.abbreviated: Because all people share reason and the principles of action, they share a common law and belong to one universal society. Their understanding must likewise come from a common rational source, just as their physical elements come from common natural sources.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 5
pages.original: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.
pages.familiar: Birth happens according to nature's wisdom, and so does death: the elements are mixed together, then separated and returned to the same elements. There is nothing shameful in that. It is one event in a chain of necessary consequences to which every rational creature is subject, and it is neither unnatural nor contrary to what a human being is.
pages.abbreviated: Birth and death naturally mix and separate the elements, returning them to their sources. This is neither shameful nor contrary to human nature, but part of the necessary order affecting every rational creature.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 6
pages.original: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.
pages.familiar: Certain things must follow from certain causes. Someone who refuses to accept them is like someone who wants a fig tree to grow without sap or moisture. Remember this: in a very short time, both you and the person who troubles you will be dead. A little later, even your names and memories will be gone.
pages.abbreviated: Certain causes necessarily produce certain effects, just as a fig tree cannot grow without what sustains it. Remember that you and the person troubling you will soon die, and later even your names and memories will disappear.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 7
pages.original: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.
pages.familiar: Remove the judgment that you have been wronged, and the feeling of being wronged disappears. Without that judgment, there is no wrong as far as you are concerned. Whatever does not make you a worse person cannot make your life worse, and cannot truly harm you either inwardly or outwardly. Nature allowed it to happen, so it belongs to the necessary order of things.
pages.abbreviated: Remove the judgment that you have been wronged, and the feeling of being wronged vanishes. Whatever does not make you a worse person cannot truly harm your life, and whatever happens belongs to nature's necessary order.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 8
pages.original: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun, and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.
pages.familiar: Everything that happens in the world happens according to an order that is just, if you pay close attention. I do not mean merely that events follow one another inevitably, but that they are distributed according to what things truly deserve. Keep noticing this, as you have begun to do. And whatever you do, make sure it is something a genuinely good person could do. Apply that test carefully to every action.
pages.abbreviated: World events are not merely inevitable but distributed according to a just order when understood clearly. Keep observing this, and test every action against what a genuinely good person could do.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 9
pages.original: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.
pages.familiar: Do not accept the story the person who wronged you tells himself, or wants you to accept. Look at the matter itself and see what it really is.
pages.abbreviated: Do not accept the offender's account of his own wrongdoing or the version he wants you to believe; examine the matter itself.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 10
pages.original: These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be furthered; or from some other such inducement.
pages.familiar: Keep two rules ready at all times. First, do only what reason, coming from the highest part of you, recommends for the good of other people. Second, if someone present can correct you or turn you away from a mistaken belief, be ready to change your mind. Let that change come not from the pleasure or praise you might gain, but from clear evidence of what is just, what serves the common good, or some similarly sound reason.
pages.abbreviated: Do what your highest reason recommends for others' good, and be ready to change your mind when sound evidence shows you are mistaken. Change for justice, the common good, or another rational basis—not for praise or pleasure.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 11
pages.original: Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
pages.familiar: Do you have reason? I do. Then why not use it? If your reason is doing its work, what more could you need?
pages.abbreviated: If you possess reason and it is functioning, use it; nothing more is required.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 12
pages.original: As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
pages.familiar: For a while, you have existed as a separate part; soon you will return to the common substance of the One who gave you life—or, more precisely, to the original rational nature from which everything comes. Pieces of incense are placed on the same altar: one burns first, another later, but they all end in the same place.
pages.abbreviated: You exist briefly as a separate part before returning to the common rational nature from which all things come. Like incense placed on one altar, individuals may finish at different times but end in the same place.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 13
pages.original: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.
pages.familiar: Within ten days, if circumstances allow, people may be calling you god—people who, if you return to your principles and respect reason, would regard you as no better than an animal or an ape.
pages.abbreviated: Within ten days, circumstances may cause people to treat you as divine, though if you follow reason and your principles they would otherwise consider you no better than an animal or ape.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 14
pages.original: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
pages.familiar: Do not act as though you have thousands of years ahead of you. Death is already over you. While you are alive and still able to choose, be good.
pages.abbreviated: Do not live as though you have unlimited time; death is already near. While you can still choose, live well.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 15
pages.original: Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.
pages.familiar: A person gains enormous time and peace by refusing to pry into what others say, do, or attempt, and focusing only on whether his own actions are just and honorable. As Agathos put it: do not keep looking at other people's faults; run straight along your own path without pointless wandering.
pages.abbreviated: You gain time and peace by ignoring others' words and actions except when judging your own conduct. Focus on your own just and honorable path instead of wandering through other people's faults.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 16
pages.original: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?
pages.familiar: Anyone who craves fame after death forgets that the people who remember him will soon die too, followed by those who come after them, until every chain of memory finally disappears. But even suppose your admirers and your reputation lasted forever—what would their praise give you, even while you are alive? Nothing, except perhaps some practical advantage. Anything genuinely beautiful or good is good in itself; praise does not improve it, and neglect does not diminish it. An emerald does not become less valuable because nobody compliments it. Neither do gold, ivory, purple cloth, a knife, a flower, or a tree. What truly deserves the name good needs no more than justice, truth, kindness, and modesty. Does praise make these virtues better? Does criticism damage them?
pages.abbreviated: Fame after death is temporary because everyone who remembers you will also die, and even lasting praise would offer little benefit. Genuine goodness—justice, truth, kindness, and modesty—has value in itself, unaffected by praise or criticism.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 17
pages.original: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed: and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto bodies, now begin to subsist single. This, upon a supposition that the souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.
pages.familiar: If souls remain after death, as some believe, how could the air have room for all of them forever? And how has the earth held all the bodies buried in it? Dead bodies change into other forms, making room for new ones; souls, if they exist separately for a time, may likewise change, merge, or return to the original rational nature from which everything comes. The same idea appears in what happens to animals: countless creatures are eaten every day, yet their substance is transformed into blood, air, and fire rather than simply vanishing. What matters in considering such questions is to distinguish what receives change—the material and passive—from what directs it—the active and formative principle.
pages.abbreviated: If souls persist after death, they may change, merge, or return to the original rational nature, just as bodies and animal substances transform rather than vanish. Distinguish the passive material that changes from the active principle that directs and forms it.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 18
pages.original: Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
pages.familiar: Do not stray from your path. With every impulse and desire, do what is just, and take care to understand clearly each impression that comes before your mind.
pages.abbreviated: Stay on your path by acting justly in every impulse and desire, while clearly understanding each impression that enters your mind.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 19
pages.original: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me; nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the world, Thou lovely city of God?
pages.familiar: Whatever is useful to the world is useful to me. Nothing that suits the world can be badly timed or outdated for me. Whatever your seasons produce, I will regard as a welcome harvest. Nature, everything comes from you, exists within you, and returns to you. If someone could praise Athens as the beautiful city of Cecrops, should you not praise the whole world as the beautiful city of God?
pages.abbreviated: Whatever benefits the world benefits you, and nothing produced by its seasons is mistimed or outdated. Since all things come from nature, exist within it, and return to it, the whole world deserves praise as a beautiful divine city.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 20
pages.original: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble, and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.
pages.familiar: People often say, “Do fewer things if you want to live happily.” They are right. Nothing is better than limiting yourself to necessary actions—only those that reason commands of a creature born to live among others. This brings the calm that comes from goodness, and also the calm that comes from having less to do. Since most of what we say and do is unnecessary, cutting it away gives us time and spares us trouble. Before each action, ask yourself privately: “Does this really need to be done?” Do the same with unnecessary thoughts and fantasies, because fewer useless thoughts will lead to fewer useless actions.
pages.abbreviated: Happiness comes from limiting yourself to necessary actions—those reason requires of a social being—which brings calm and reduces trouble. Before acting or indulging a thought, ask whether it is truly necessary, since fewer useless thoughts produce fewer useless actions.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 21
pages.original: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity. Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.
pages.familiar: Try living as a good person does: content with whatever falls to his share amid the world's changes, satisfied that his present action is just and that his character is prepared for what comes next. You have experienced the opposite way of living; now test this one. Return to complete simplicity. Has someone wronged you? He has harmed himself—why should that disturb you? Has something happened to you? Then accept it; among all the events unfolding through the world, this one was the portion assigned to you. In short, life is brief, so use the present wisely and justly. Take recreation, but do it with moderation.
pages.abbreviated: Live contentedly amid change, satisfied that your present action is just and your character ready for what follows. Treat others' wrongdoing as their own harm, accept what happens as your assigned portion, use the brief present wisely, and enjoy recreation moderately.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 22
pages.original: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy, one to another united, as they are?
pages.familiar: Either the world is an ordered and beautiful whole, or it is a confused mixture that still forms a whole. Could there be beauty in you while the universe contains nothing but disorder? Its parts differ by their natural qualities, yet they are spread throughout and joined together by a natural sympathy.
pages.abbreviated: The universe is either an ordered, beautiful whole or a confused mixture that still forms a whole. Its diverse parts are nevertheless joined and distributed by natural sympathy, so beauty in a person cannot coexist with a wholly disordered universe.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 23
pages.original: A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world, that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well, that wonders at the things that are done in it?
pages.familiar: A dark or malicious character; a weak or soft one; a harsh, unyielding one; a wild, inhuman one; a timid one; a childish one; a dull, deceitful, vulgar, scheming, or tyrannical one. What then? If someone is a stranger who does not understand the world, why should he not also be a stranger who is amazed by what happens in it?
pages.abbreviated: People may be malicious, weak, harsh, wild, timid, childish, dull, deceitful, vulgar, scheming, or tyrannical. Someone who does not understand the world is naturally also a stranger to and bewildered by what happens in it.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 24
pages.original: He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding. He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world, doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
pages.familiar: The true fugitive is the person who runs from reason, the thing that makes human beings social. The blind person is the one who cannot see with understanding. The poor person is the one who depends on others and lacks what life requires within himself. The person who resents what happens is like a wound in the world, separating himself from nature's rational order. Yet the same nature that brought you into the world brings whatever happens to you. And anyone who acts irrationally and withdraws his soul from the shared reason of humanity is stirring rebellion in the city of life.
pages.abbreviated: The true fugitive, blind person, and poor person are those who flee reason, cannot understand, or depend on others for what they lack within themselves. Resenting events wounds the world's rational order, and irrationally withdrawing from shared human reason rebels against the city of life.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 25
pages.original: There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I depart not from reason.
pages.familiar: Some people practice philosophy with nothing but the clothes on their backs; others do it without even a book. One says, “I have hardly any clothes and no bread, yet I do not abandon reason.” I say, “I lack good teaching and instruction, yet I still do not abandon reason.”
pages.abbreviated: Some practice philosophy with almost no clothing or food, while others lack books or instruction. Both maintain that deprivation does not justify abandoning reason.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 26
pages.original: What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either tyrannically or servilely towards any.
pages.familiar: Whatever skill or profession you have learned, practice it well and take comfort in it. Spend the rest of your life giving yourself, and everything entrusted to you, wholeheartedly to the gods. And toward other people, be neither a tyrant nor a slave.
pages.abbreviated: Practice your learned skill or profession well and take comfort in doing it. Devote the rest of your life wholeheartedly to yourself, your responsibilities, and the gods, while being neither tyrannical nor servile toward others.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 27
pages.original: Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian: thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that their age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of Trajan. There likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that age also is now over and ended. In the like manner consider other periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after they had with all their might and main intended and prosecuted some one worldly thing or other did soon after drop away, and were resolved into the elements. But especially thou must call to mind them, whom thou thyself in thy lifetime hast known much distracted about vain things, and in the meantime neglecting to do that, and closely and unseparably (as fully satisfied with it) to adhere unto it, which their own proper constitution did require. And here thou must remember, that thy carriage in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired out and vexed, if thou shalt not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.
pages.familiar: Think of the time of Vespasian and you will see the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling ill, dying, fighting, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, boasting, suspecting, scheming, wishing for death, complaining about their circumstances, courting, hoarding, seeking office, and seeking power. That whole age has passed away. Think of Trajan's time: the same things again, and that age too is gone. Do the same with other periods and nations. See how many people pursued some worldly goal with all their strength, only to soon disappear and return to the elements. Especially remember people you have known who were consumed by trivial concerns while neglecting the one thing their nature required them to do and hold firmly to. In every task, give it the attention and effort it deserves. Then small matters will not exhaust or trouble you by taking more of your life than they should.
pages.abbreviated: Across every age, people repeat the same pursuits and soon disappear. Give each task the attention it deserves so trivial matters do not consume more of your life than they should.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 28
pages.original: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is vanity. What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou thyself and all things are. Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.
pages.familiar: Words that were once ordinary become obscure and outdated; so do the names of people once famous. Camillus, Caesar, Scipio, Cato, Augustus, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius—all will soon be forgotten, like stories from another world. And that is true even of those who once amazed their age; everyone else is forgotten almost as soon as they die. What, then, will always be remembered? Everything is vanity. What deserves our care? This alone: that our thoughts and choices are just, our actions kind, our speech honest, our understanding clear, and our attitude ready to accept whatever happens as necessary, familiar, ordinary, and arising from the same source that brought us and all things into being. So willingly and completely give yourself to the chain of events, letting fate arrange your life as it will.
pages.abbreviated: Fame and memory quickly vanish, so they are vanity. Care instead that your thoughts and choices are just, your actions kind, your speech honest, your understanding clear, and your attitude willingly accepting of whatever happens.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 29
pages.original: Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence; all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves, incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.
pages.familiar: Everything that exists now and day after day, every memory and every mind that holds memories, is constantly changing. Train yourself to remember that the universe delights in changing what exists and producing something like it in its place. Everything that exists is, in a sense, the seed of what will come. It is childish to think that only what the earth or a womb receives can be called a seed.
pages.abbreviated: Everything, including memories and minds, constantly changes, and each existing thing becomes the seed of what follows. It is childish to limit the idea of a seed to what earth or a womb receives.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 30
pages.original: Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to be just in all his actions.
pages.familiar: You are ready to die, yet you have not reached complete simplicity. You are still troubled and unsettled, still afraid and suspicious of things outside your control. You are not yet as gentle toward everyone as you should be, nor as devoted to justice as someone whose only study and wisdom is to act justly.
pages.abbreviated: Although ready to die, you remain troubled, fearful, suspicious, and insufficiently gentle and just. You have not yet attained the complete simplicity and justice that wisdom requires.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 31
pages.original: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
pages.familiar: Look closely at the state of the wise people's minds. See what the world calls wise people avoid and fear, and what they chase after.
pages.abbreviated: Examine the minds of those considered wise, especially what they avoid and fear and what they pursue.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 32
pages.original: In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction, yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil. For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature, and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.
pages.familiar: Your suffering does not exist in another person's mind, nor in your body's natural condition, which is only the outer shelter of your soul. It exists only in the part of you that judges something to be miserable. Do not let that part form such a judgment, and you remain whole. Even if your body is cut, burned, injured, or decays, let the judging part stay calm. Anything that can happen equally to a good person and a bad person is neither good nor bad in itself. What happens alike to someone living according to nature and someone who is not cannot by itself be either in harmony with nature or against it.
pages.abbreviated: Suffering exists in your judgment that something is miserable, not in another mind or in the body's natural condition. Keep that judgment calm, since what can happen equally to good and bad people is neither good nor bad in itself.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 33
pages.original: Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen.
pages.familiar: Keep seeing the world as one living whole, with one shared life and one power of awareness. Everything moves together, as if guided by one common purpose. All things contribute to one another's existence, and everything that happens is linked through an unbroken chain of causes.
pages.abbreviated: See the world as one living whole with one shared life and awareness. Everything contributes to everything else and unfolds through an unbroken chain of causes.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 34
pages.original: What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?
pages.familiar: Apart from the better, divine part of you, what are you but a troubled soul carrying a body around?
pages.abbreviated: Apart from your better, divine part, you are merely a troubled soul carrying a body.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 35
pages.original: To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
pages.familiar: Change cannot harm you, just as becoming something new is not itself a benefit. The world's time is like a rushing river carrying everything along. As soon as one thing appears and passes away, another takes its place, and that too soon disappears.
pages.abbreviated: Change itself cannot harm you, and becoming something new is not automatically a benefit. Everything is swept along by time, appearing and disappearing in succession.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 36
pages.original: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession, but an admirable correspondence and affinity.
pages.familiar: Everything that happens in the world is as natural and ordinary as roses in spring or fruit in summer. Illness and death are no different, nor are insults, deception, or any other things that foolish people treat as reasons for joy or grief. Whatever comes next follows naturally from what came before. Do not see the world as a disconnected series of necessary events, but as an orderly and harmonious network in which everything belongs to everything else. There is not merely succession, but a remarkable correspondence among things.
pages.abbreviated: Illness, death, insults, and deception are as natural as seasonal growth and follow from what came before. See them not as disconnected events but as parts of an orderly, harmonious network in which everything corresponds.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 37
pages.original: Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being the thing by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which daily happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and that we should not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep, by opinion and bare imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example; for best reason alleging their bare καθότι παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.
pages.familiar: Remember Heraclitus: earth becomes water, water becomes air, air becomes fire, and the process runs in reverse as well. Remember, too, the person who did not know where the road led. Reason governs everything in the world, and we are constantly in contact with it, yet people usually resist it most. The things that happen among us every day still seem strange to us. So do not speak or act half-asleep, guided only by assumptions and imagination. Do not merely copy your parents or ancestors and call that wisdom. Think for yourself.
pages.abbreviated: Reason governs the world's constant transformations, though people resist and find ordinary events strange. Do not act from inherited assumptions or imagination; think for yourself.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 38
pages.original: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.
pages.familiar: If a god told you that you would certainly die tomorrow or the day after, unless you were extremely timid you would not consider it a great advantage to die one day later. The difference is tiny. For the same reason, do not treat dying many years from now as vastly different from dying tomorrow.
pages.abbreviated: Dying one day later is only a tiny advantage, so do not regard death years from now as fundamentally different from death tomorrow.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 39
pages.original: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after that in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable are dead and gone. Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time. For herein lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile, and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes. Thus must thou according to truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.
pages.familiar: Keep remembering how many doctors who once looked severe and dramatically worried over their patients are now dead themselves. How many astrologers who proudly predicted another person's death have died; how many philosophers who wrote at length about mortality or immortality; how many commanders who caused countless deaths; how many kings and tyrants who used power as though they could never die. Entire cities have vanished too. Think also of the people you have known who disappeared one by one. Someone arranged another person's funeral and was buried soon afterward. Then another, and another. Everything passes quickly. Look at worldly things as lasting only a day and, in themselves, as insignificant. What is a human being? Recently, before birth, only a little fluid; soon, an embalmed body or ashes. Understand that life is only a brief moment, and leave it gently and contentedly, like a ripe olive falling from the tree, grateful to the earth that sustained it and the tree that produced it.
pages.abbreviated: Doctors, astrologers, philosophers, rulers, cities, and everyone you know eventually disappear, so worldly things are brief and insignificant. Life is a moment; leave it gently and gratefully, like a ripe olive falling from its tree.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 40
