pages.original: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
pages.familiar: Be like a headland in the sea. Waves strike it constantly, yet it remains firm, and the waters around it settle and grow calm.
pages.abbreviated: Be firm like a headland that withstands constant waves until the surrounding waters become calm.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 41
pages.original: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself, as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great happiness.
pages.familiar: Do not say, “How unfortunate that this happened to me.” Say instead, “How fortunate that, although this happened, I can remain free from grief—not wounded by the present or frightened of the future.” The event could happen to anyone, but not everyone could endure it without grief. Why call it misfortune rather than call your strength a blessing? Can you call something a misfortune if it does not harm human nature? Can you call it harmful if it does not prevent you from being just, brave, self-controlled, wise, careful, honest, modest, or free? Your nature is fulfilled in practicing these qualities. So whenever sorrow arises, remember: what happened is not, by itself, a misfortune. Bearing it with courage is a genuine form of good fortune.
pages.abbreviated: Do not call an event unfortunate if it does not damage your human nature or prevent you from practicing virtue. The event may happen to anyone, but enduring it without grief is a genuine good fortune.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 42
pages.original: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that which liveth three ages?
pages.familiar: A simple but effective way to ease the fear of death is to think about people who clung greedily to life for a long time. What did they gain over those who died young? In the end, they died too. People who had watched many others be buried were eventually buried themselves. Any human life is brief, and even that brief time is filled with troubles, difficult moods, and the company of unhappy people. So treat the length of life as something neither good nor bad in itself. Look back, and you see an endless stretch of time; look ahead, and you see another endless stretch. Against infinity, what real difference is there between living three days and living three generations?
pages.abbreviated: Those who cling to life eventually die just as those who die young do, and the short span of life is filled with troubles. Measured against infinite time, living three days or three generations makes no real difference.

pages.label: Book IV · Section 43
pages.original: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.
pages.familiar: Always take the shortest sound path. The shortest path is the one that follows nature: in everything you say and do, follow what is healthiest and most complete. That decision frees you from turmoil, conflict, pretending, and showing off.
pages.abbreviated: Follow the shortest path: let nature guide everything you say and do toward what is healthiest and most complete. This frees you from turmoil, conflict, pretence, and display.

pages.label: Book V · Section 1
pages.original: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants, spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe) naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that, which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy nature doth require? 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must. Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others, as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection, can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and intention?
pages.familiar: When you are reluctant to get up in the morning, remind yourself at once: I am getting up to do a human being’s work. Was I born for this, or was I made only to stay in bed and keep myself comfortable? “But it feels good.” Were you born just to feel good? Were you not born to stay active and do what needs doing? Look at everything else in the world: trees and plants, sparrows and ants, spiders and bees. Each one diligently carries out the work that belongs to it and helps preserve the order of the whole. Will you refuse to do what belongs to a human being? Will you resist what your nature requires? “But I need rest.” Of course you do. Nature allows a proper amount of rest, just as it allows a proper amount of food and drink. But you go beyond what is enough when it comes to rest, while falling short of what you are capable of in action. That shows you do not truly value yourself. If you did, you would value your nature and the purpose it gives you. People who love their trades can work themselves thin, neglect their food and sleep, and keep going for the sake of what they care about. Will you respect your nature less than a craftsperson respects a craft, a dancer respects the dance, a greedy person respects money, or an ambitious person respects applause? They will go without food and sleep to pursue what they want. Will work that serves the good of human society seem less worthy to you, or deserve less of your attention?
pages.abbreviated: Rise to do the work proper to a human being, rather than extending rest beyond what you need. Other creatures diligently fulfill their nature, and work that serves human society deserves at least as much devotion as any craft or personal desire.

pages.label: Book V · Section 2
pages.original: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!
pages.familiar: How easy it is to let go of all the agitating thoughts that come from outside you and return immediately to complete peace.
pages.abbreviated: You can quickly release agitating thoughts that come from outside and return to complete peace.

pages.label: Book V · Section 3
pages.original: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both these, is but one.
pages.familiar: Consider yourself fit and worthy to say or do anything that follows nature, and never let possible criticism or gossip stop you. If something is right and honest to say or do, do not think so little of yourself that you shrink from it. Other people have their own reasoning minds and personal tendencies. You do not need to stop and study their reactions. Go straight where your own nature and the common nature lead you. In the end, both point along the same road.
pages.abbreviated: Do what nature requires when it is right and honest, without shrinking because of criticism or gossip. Your nature and the common nature lead along the same path.

pages.label: Book V · Section 4
pages.original: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
pages.familiar: I will keep living by nature until I fall and breathe my last breath into the air I have continually breathed to stay alive. I will fall onto the earth from whose gifts my father received his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, and from which I have been fed and given drink for so many years. The earth carries me now as I walk on it, and bears with all the ways I misuse it or freely take from it for countless purposes.
pages.abbreviated: Live by nature until death, returning to the air and earth that have continually sustained you and supported every part of your life.

pages.label: Book V · Section 5
pages.original: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee; sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping downwards? Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.
pages.familiar: No one may admire you for clever, cutting speech; perhaps you simply lack that talent. So be it. But there are many other good qualities you cannot excuse yourself from having because of natural limitations. Let people see sincerity, seriousness, hard work, freedom from pleasure, a refusal to complain, contentment with little, kindness, generosity, simplicity, restraint in speech, and courage in you. Do you not see how many things you could have done despite any natural weakness, yet you keep choosing to sink lower? Will you say your natural constitution forces you to complain, act shamefully, flatter, accuse, soothe and indulge your body, boast, and let your thoughts become scattered and unstable? No. You could have freed yourself from all of that long ago. The most you would have had to accept was being called somewhat slow or dull. Even there, you should train yourself without taking the weakness too seriously or turning it into an excuse.
pages.abbreviated: You may lack clever speech, but you cannot excuse yourself from sincerity, diligence, restraint, kindness, courage, and other attainable virtues. Natural weakness does not force you to complain, flatter, indulge yourself, boast, or let your thoughts become unstable.

pages.label: Book V · Section 6
pages.original: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any, yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey, look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn: but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time. Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give over any sociable action.
pages.familiar: Some people do a good deed and immediately put it on the other person’s account, expecting repayment. Others do not demand repayment, but still think of the person as their debtor and remember exactly what they did. Others are like a vine that bears grapes: once it has produced its fruit, it is satisfied and asks for nothing more. A horse after a race, a hunting dog after the hunt, and a bee after making honey do not wait for applause. Neither does someone who understands human nature properly after doing a good deed. He simply goes on to do another, as the vine bears fruit again when its season returns. Be one of those people who act without adding any further thought, almost unaware of their own goodness. “But,” someone may object, “a rational person should understand what he is doing. A social person should recognize that he is acting for others, and should want the person helped to recognize it too.” That is partly true, but you have misunderstood the point. Thinking clearly about your action does not mean keeping a record of it or seeking recognition. Do not worry that understanding this will make you stop acting for others.
pages.abbreviated: Do good without treating others as debtors, keeping records, or seeking recognition. Understand your actions clearly while remaining like a vine that bears fruit and simply continues bearing it.

pages.label: Book V · Section 7
pages.original: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.
pages.familiar: The Athenians used to pray, “Rain, rain, good Zeus, on all the fields and farmland of Athens.” Either do not pray at all, or pray in that open and universal way—not each person asking only for what benefits himself.
pages.abbreviated: Pray openly for benefits shared by everyone, as in asking for rain on all the fields, or do not pray at all. Do not ask only for what benefits yourself.

pages.label: Book V · Section 8
pages.original: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing. For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates, and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or harmony itself is but one. And as the whole world is made up of all the particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and recovery, accept of them. Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee. First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole, therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth.
pages.familiar: We say that a doctor has prescribed exercise for one person, cold baths for another, and walking barefoot for a third. In the same way, we can say that the nature of the universe has prescribed illness, blindness, loss, or some other hardship for someone. A doctor prescribes something as a means toward health. Likewise, whatever happens to each person is part of the larger order, fitted into the course of events. Different stones can come together to form a wall or pyramid, and builders say they fit together. In the same way, different events come together in one harmony. The world is made from all its separate bodies into one complete body, and the fate of separate causes and events forms one larger fate. Even ordinary people understand this when they say, “This was brought upon him by his fate.” What happens to each person has been brought to that person in particular, as a treatment prescribed by a doctor. Accept it in the same spirit as a difficult treatment: it may be harsh, but you accept it because you hope it will restore health. Let the fulfillment of nature’s plan be like your health. Accept what happens, even when it is painful or unwelcome, because it serves the health and well-being of the whole. It would not have happened if it did not belong to the good of the universe. No ordinary part of nature produces anything that does not fit the work of the whole. For two reasons, then, be at peace with whatever happens. First, it was brought about for you and assigned to you through the entire chain of causes from the beginning. Second, the well-being and continuation of the whole depend on every part remaining connected. The whole is damaged if anything is cut away from the network that holds its parts and causes together. Whenever you resent what happens, you are, as far as you can, cutting something away from that whole.
pages.abbreviated: Hardships are like difficult treatments prescribed within the larger order of nature, and each event fits the harmony and well-being of the whole. Accept even painful events because they were assigned through the chain of causes and because resenting them cuts you away from the connected whole.

pages.label: Book V · Section 9
pages.original: Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off, return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy, return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort. And remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing? Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather, and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness; whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble? As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible, yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner. Pass from thence to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with, how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.
pages.familiar: Do not become frustrated, discouraged, or hopeless when you repeatedly fail to live exactly by sound principles. When you fall away, return to them. You cannot avoid worldly distractions and human weaknesses, so do not resent them. Keep loving the life of a philosopher and return to it as someone seeking relief from an illness—not to show off, but because reason brings comfort. Philosophy asks only what your nature asks of you. Would you really prefer what goes against nature? Pleasure may seem natural, but it often harms and destroys people. Consider instead whether courage, freedom, simplicity, steadiness, holiness, and good judgment are not more natural and lovable. The world is difficult to understand, and even our best conclusions may be mistaken. Its possessions are temporary and may belong to corrupt or shameful people. We struggle even to tolerate those we love, let alone ourselves. Everything is changing—things, time, movement, and the people who move—so what can we truly cling to, honor, or pursue? I cannot see it clearly, because these things pull in opposite directions.
pages.abbreviated: Do not despair when you fail to live by sound principles; return to them, since distraction and weakness are unavoidable. Philosophy should comfort you through reason, while courage, freedom, simplicity, steadiness, holiness, and good judgment may be more natural and worthy than pleasure, especially in an uncertain, changing world where possessions and conclusions are unreliable.

pages.label: Book V · Section 10
pages.original: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly, that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to transgress against him.
pages.familiar: Take comfort in knowing that your natural death will come, and do not suffer because it has not come yet. Rest in two facts: nothing will happen to you outside the order of nature, and no one can force you to betray your own conscience. No person has the power to make you act against the divine reason within you.
pages.abbreviated: Take comfort that natural death will come in its proper time. Nothing can happen outside nature’s order, and no one can force you to betray your conscience or the divine reason within you.

pages.label: Book V · Section 11
pages.original: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?
pages.familiar: What am I using my mind for right now? Ask yourself this often and in every situation. What is the rational part of me occupied with at this moment? Whose mind am I carrying right now—a child’s, a young person’s, a woman’s, a tyrant’s, an animal’s, or a wild beast’s?
pages.abbreviated: Keep asking what your mind is doing right now and what kind of mind you are carrying—wise, immature, tyrannical, animal-like, or otherwise.

pages.label: Book V · Section 12
pages.original: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
pages.familiar: You can tell what is truly good by how the word is used. When people hear about wisdom, self-control, justice, or courage, they recognize that these are genuinely good and do not need anything added. But when they hear wealth, pleasure, or status called good, they wait for more, as though the speaker were joking or speaking only in the popular way. Why do praise of virtue and praise of riches sound so different? Perhaps the things people celebrate—wealth, pleasure, and honor—deserve the same ridicule once made onstage about the very rich: that, despite owning everything, they did not even possess a private place to relieve themselves. Perhaps these are not truly good at all, while the qualities that make a person wise, fair, brave, and disciplined are the things worthy of real respect.
pages.abbreviated: Wisdom, self-control, justice, and courage are recognized as good without qualification, while wealth, pleasure, and status require explanation. This suggests that virtue deserves genuine respect, whereas worldly advantages may be no better than objects of ridicule.

pages.label: Book V · Section 13
pages.original: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak, though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods of time limited, and confined.
pages.familiar: Everything I am is either form or matter. Neither can be destroyed into nothing, because I did not come from nothing. Each part of me will be changed into some part of the universe, and in time into another part, endlessly. Through this kind of change I became what I am, just as my parents became who they were, and those before them. We may speak of this chain without limit, even if the life and order of the universe itself move through defined cycles.
pages.abbreviated: Everything consists of form and matter, neither arising from nor disappearing into nothing. Each part continually changes into other parts of the universe, forming an endless chain that includes us, our parents, and those before them, even within possibly defined cosmic cycles.

pages.label: Book V · Section 14
pages.original: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended. Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.
pages.familiar: Reason and the rational mind are satisfied by their own proper work. They begin from within themselves, then move directly toward whatever can actually be done, whether or not it is exactly what they first intended. That is why such actions are called upright: they follow a straight course. Nothing belongs to a person merely because he wants it; it must belong to him as a human being. Success is not required for a human life to be good. Human nature does not demand that every plan reach its intended outcome. A person’s highest good cannot consist simply in finishing everything he sets out to do. If wealth, status, and other external things truly belonged to human beings, we would not rightly criticize them or resist them, and no one who lived without them would deserve praise. Yet we see the opposite: the more someone withdraws from display and worldly greatness, or the better he bears their loss, the better we judge him.
pages.abbreviated: Reason is fulfilled by doing what can rightly be done, not necessarily by achieving an intended result. Wealth, status, and other externals are not truly human possessions, since lacking or losing them can deserve praise rather than blame.

pages.label: Book V · Section 15
pages.original: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?
pages.familiar: Your mind will gradually take the shape of your usual thoughts. Your inner life is colored by the images you repeatedly entertain, so soak it thoroughly in thoughts worth keeping. Wherever you live, you can live well and happily—even at a palace or in the middle of public pressure. Everything is made for some purpose, and naturally inclines toward that purpose. Its good lies in fulfilling it. For a rational being, that purpose is living in fellowship with others. We were made for community. What is naturally lower is generally ordered toward what is higher; the best things are made for one another; living beings are better than lifeless things; and among living beings, those with rational minds are best equipped for mutual life.
pages.abbreviated: The mind takes the shape of its repeated thoughts, so fill it with thoughts worth keeping; good living is possible anywhere. Every thing fulfills its purpose by doing what it is made for, and rational beings fulfill theirs through fellowship and community.

pages.label: Book V · Section 16
pages.original: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence? As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.
pages.familiar: Wanting the impossible is madness. It is impossible for a wicked person never to do something wicked. Whatever happens to someone in the ordinary course of nature can happen to others as well. If an ignorant person can endure an insult simply because he does not understand it, or an ambitious person can endure it to win praise, is it not shameful if ignorance or vanity prove stronger than wisdom? The events themselves cannot touch the soul. They have no direct access to it and cannot move it on their own. Only the soul can move itself, and it decides what meaning those events will have by the judgments it accepts.
pages.abbreviated: Wanting the impossible is madness, including expecting a wicked person never to act wickedly. Events cannot touch the soul directly; the soul gives them meaning through its own judgments, so wisdom should be stronger than ignorance or vanity.

pages.label: Book V · Section 17
pages.original: After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be, that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be, to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.
pages.familiar: In one sense, other people are closest to us: we are obligated to help them and tolerate them. But when someone interferes with an action that truly belongs to me, that person becomes no more significant to my character than the sun, the wind, or a wild animal. Any of them may obstruct something I am doing, but none can obstruct my mind or resolve. My mind can reserve its judgment, turn toward what is possible, and adapt its purpose to the circumstances. It can transform every obstacle into material for its own work. What once stood in the way becomes the thing it works with; what blocked the path becomes the path.
pages.abbreviated: Other people deserve help and tolerance, but obstacles cannot obstruct the mind or resolve. The mind can suspend judgment, adapt its purpose, and turn every obstruction into material for its work, making what blocked the path part of the path.

pages.label: Book V · Section 18
pages.original: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
pages.familiar: Honor the highest and most powerful force in the universe—the force that uses and governs everything. Honor that same power within yourself. It is of the same nature: the part of you that puts everything else to use and directs the course of your life.
pages.abbreviated: Honor the universe’s highest governing power and the same power within yourself: the rational part that directs your life and uses everything else.

pages.label: Book V · Section 19
pages.original: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong. Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time? Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
pages.familiar: What does not harm the city itself cannot harm any citizen. Remember this whenever you feel wronged. If the whole community is not harmed, then I am not truly harmed either. And if the whole is unharmed, why make it my personal grievance? Consider instead what the person who seems to have done wrong has failed to understand. Also remember how quickly everything that exists and everything that happens is carried away. Things flow like a river, actions are always changing, and their causes are altered in countless ways. Almost nothing can be called settled or permanent. Then consider the endless time already gone and the immense time still to come, in which everything will dissolve and disappear. Would it not be foolish, then, to become proud, anxious, or deeply distressed over things that will trouble you only briefly? Look at the whole universe: you are only a tiny part of it. Look at all of history: your life is only a brief moment. Look at all that fate contains: how little of it belongs to you. Someone has wronged me. Let him deal with that. He controls his own character and actions. For my part, I possess what common nature has given me, and I do what my own nature requires.
pages.abbreviated: If the community is unharmed, an individual is not truly harmed, so another person’s wrongdoing should not become a personal grievance. Since everything changes and your life is tiny within time and the universe, let the wrongdoer manage his character while you follow your own nature.

pages.label: Book V · Section 20
pages.original: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members. But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural. However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling, which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
pages.familiar: Do not let the ruling part of your mind be thrown off balance by bodily pain or pleasure. Do not mix the mind with them; keep each in its proper place. If bodily sensations reach the mind and understanding—as they naturally will in a unified body—do not fight the feeling itself. It is natural to feel pain or pleasure. But do not add the judgment that the feeling is good or bad in itself. Once you stop making that extra judgment, all is well.
pages.abbreviated: Feel bodily pain and pleasure without letting them disturb the ruling mind. Accept the sensations as natural, but do not add the judgment that they are inherently good or bad.

pages.label: Book V · Section 21
pages.original: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
pages.familiar: Live as if you were living with the gods. A person lives with the gods when the soul remains content with whatever is given or assigned to it, and carries out what pleases the guiding spirit within—a part of the divine nature that has been appointed to watch over and guide each person.
pages.abbreviated: To live with the gods is to remain content with what is given and to carry out what accords with the guiding divine spirit within you.

pages.label: Book V · Section 22
pages.original: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally, and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
pages.familiar: Do not be angry with someone whose breath smells bad or whose body odor is unpleasant. What can he do? His breath and body naturally produce those smells. You may say, “But he has reason and could realize that standing so close is offensive.” And you, too, have reason. Use your reason to reach his reason. Point out the problem and politely warn him. If he listens, you have helped correct it, and there is no need for anger.
pages.abbreviated: Do not be angry about someone’s unpleasant odor, since it may be natural; use reason to explain the problem and politely warn him. If he listens, the matter is corrected without need for anger.

pages.label: Book V · Section 23
pages.original: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged. Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable creature, regulated and directed.
pages.familiar: You say, “I want to live somewhere without loud, obnoxious people or people who corrupt me.” Why? Live here as you intend to live there. If they will not allow you to do that, then leave life itself rather than abandon your purpose—but leave without thinking you have been wronged. Simply say, “There is smoke here; I am going outside.” What is so difficult about that? Until something truly forces me to leave, I will remain free. No one can stop me from doing what I choose, because my choice is governed by the nature of a reasonable and social being.
pages.abbreviated: Live according to your purpose even among difficult or corrupt people; if that becomes impossible, leave without considering yourself wronged. Until then, remain free, since no one can prevent a reasonable and social person from choosing rightly.

pages.label: Book V · Section 24
pages.original: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual consent and agreement.
pages.familiar: The rational principle that governs the universe exists for community and fellowship. That is why it has arranged lesser things for the benefit of greater things, and joined the better things together in harmony. Can you not see how everything has been ordered beneath and alongside everything else, each thing receiving its proper place and worth? And those with the greatest importance have been united with one another in mutual agreement.
pages.abbreviated: The universe’s rational principle exists for fellowship, arranging lesser things for greater ones and joining the better things in harmony. Everything receives its proper place and worth, with the most important things united in mutual agreement.

pages.label: Book V · Section 25
pages.original: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised? towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself kindly, and discreetly?
pages.familiar: How have you behaved toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, your guardians, your friends, the people in your household, and those who serve you? Have you reached this point without wronging any of them by word or deed? Remember how many experiences you have already passed through and how much you have endured. Your life's record is already full, and your duty has been carried out many times over. Remember, too, how many truly good things you have recognized; how many pleasures and pains you have moved beyond without being ruled by them; how many things praised as glorious you have refused to value; and how kindly and wisely you have treated difficult and unreasonable people.
pages.abbreviated: Review how you have treated family, teachers, friends, household members, and servants, and remember what you have endured. Your life has already contained many fulfilled duties, recognized goods, overcome pleasures and pains, rejected false glory, and acts of kindness toward difficult people.

pages.label: Book V · Section 26
pages.original: Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it were this universe by certain periods of time.
pages.familiar: Why should careless, ignorant minds disturb the mind that is educated and wise? And what kind of mind is that? One that understands both the beginning and the end, and knows the rational principle moving through everything that exists and through every age, always remaining the same while ordering and distributing the universe through its appointed cycles.
pages.abbreviated: An educated and wise mind should not be disturbed by careless ignorance. Such a mind understands the universe’s beginning and end and the rational principle that continually orders it through all ages and cycles.

pages.label: Book V · Section 27
pages.original: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name. And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious, if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward children, now laughing and then crying. As for faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven. What is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such, be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are neither thine, nor in thy power.
pages.familiar: Soon you will be ashes, bones, perhaps a name—and perhaps not even that. And what is a name but an empty sound, an echo returning to silence? The things we value most in this life are, in themselves, empty, decaying, and contemptible. Even the most serious conflicts, seen clearly, are like puppies biting one another or children who laugh one moment and cry the next. Faith, modesty, justice, and truth, as the poet says, have long since left the earth and withdrawn to heaven. So what keeps you here, when everything you can touch is unstable, your senses unclear and unreliable, and your soul no more than a breath of blood? To seek approval from people like this is vanity. What are you waiting for—extinction or transformation? Either can be met with a willing and peaceful mind. Until that time comes, what can satisfy you? Nothing but honoring and praising the gods, doing good to people, bearing with them, and refusing to wrong them. As for everything external—the things belonging to your body or your life—remember that they are neither truly yours nor within your control.
pages.abbreviated: Soon you will be reduced to ashes, bones, a name, or nothing, while worldly concerns are unstable and empty. Until death or transformation arrives, fulfillment lies only in honoring the gods, helping and tolerating people, avoiding wrongdoing, and recognizing that bodily and external things are neither yours nor under your control.

pages.label: Book V · Section 28
pages.original: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.
pages.familiar: You can always make progress if you choose the right path. In both your judgments and your actions, follow a sound method. The souls of gods, human beings, and every rational creature share two qualities: nothing can prevent them from doing their proper work, and their happiness consists in choosing and practicing what is right. That is where their desire should end.
pages.abbreviated: Progress is always possible by following sound methods in judgment and action. Rational beings are happy when nothing prevents their proper work and when they choose and practice what is right; their desire should end there.

pages.label: Book V · Section 29
pages.original: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly hurt thereby: for that is not right. But as that old foster-father in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise. For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.
pages.familiar: If what happened was not caused by anything wrong I did, and it does not truly harm the community, why should it trouble me? How could the community really be harmed? Do not let appearances and popular opinion carry you away. Help people as well as you can and when the situation calls for it, even in ordinary matters where they may suffer some loss. But do not imagine that they have been truly harmed, because that is not right. Remember the old caretaker in the comedy who, saying goodbye with great ceremony, asks for his foster child’s toy top while knowing perfectly well that it is only a toy. Treat public arguments and courtroom shouting the same way. Have you forgotten what these things are? Yes, others care deeply about them and think them important. Must you become foolish too? You once were; once was enough.
pages.abbreviated: If an event was not caused by your wrongdoing and does not truly harm the community, it should not trouble you, even if public opinion says otherwise. Help people when needed, but do not treat political and legal disputes as more substantial than toys or theatrical arguments.

pages.label: Book V · Section 30
pages.original: Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless. For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
pages.familiar: Let death come whenever and wherever it will. I can still be a fortunate and fulfilled person. A fulfilled person is someone who has given himself a good portion in life: a well-disposed character, worthy desires, and good actions.
pages.abbreviated: Death may come at any time, yet you can still be fortunate and fulfilled. Fulfillment consists in a well-disposed character, worthy desires, and good actions.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 1
pages.original: The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it, hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
pages.familiar: The material that makes up the universe is naturally workable and adaptable. The rational power guiding it has no reason to do evil. It contains no evil and cannot do anything evil; nothing can truly be harmed by it. Everything happens according to its order and purpose.
pages.abbreviated: The universe’s material is adaptable, and its rational governing power has no reason or ability to do evil. Nothing is truly harmed by it; everything occurs according to its order and purpose.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 2
pages.original: Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties and actions of our lives.
pages.familiar: Treat it all the same: being half-frozen or comfortably warm, barely awake or fully rested, praised or criticized while doing your duty, alive or dying. Death, too, is one of the duties and actions that belong to a human life.
pages.abbreviated: Treat cold and warmth, tiredness and rest, praise and criticism, life and death alike while performing your duty. Death is also part of the actions belonging to human life.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 3
pages.original: Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
pages.familiar: Look beneath the surface. Do not let a thing’s real character or true value pass you by before you have understood it completely.
pages.abbreviated: Look beneath appearances and understand a thing’s actual character and value before passing it by or judging it.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 4
pages.original: All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be scattered and dispersed. As for that Rational Essence by which all things are governed, as it best understandeth itself, both its own disposition, and what it doth, and what matter it hath to do with and accordingly doth all things; so we that do not, no wonder, if we wonder at many things, the reasons whereof we cannot comprehend.
pages.familiar: Everything quickly changes form. Some say all things will eventually return to one substance, rising like vapor; others say they will scatter and dissolve. The rational power that governs everything understands itself, its own nature, its actions, and the material it works with, and acts accordingly. We do not understand these things so fully, so it is no surprise that much of life leaves us wondering.
pages.abbreviated: Everything changes form, though people disagree about whether it ultimately reunites into one substance or dissolves into parts. The rational power governing the universe understands itself, its actions, and its material completely, while our limited understanding makes life’s mysteries unsurprising.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 5
pages.original: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
pages.familiar: The best revenge is to refuse to become like the people who wronged you.
pages.abbreviated: The best revenge is refusing to become like those who wrong you.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 6
pages.original: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.
pages.familiar: Let this be your only joy and comfort: move without interruption from one act of kindness toward another, keeping the divine in your thoughts.
pages.abbreviated: Let your only joy and comfort be moving continually from one kind act to another while keeping the divine in mind.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 7
pages.original: The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth, to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
pages.familiar: The reasoning part of you alone can initiate change and redirect itself. It also decides how it will understand itself and how everything that happens will appear to it.
pages.abbreviated: Only the reasoning part of you can initiate change and redirect itself. It also determines how it understands itself and how everything appears to it.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 8
pages.original: According to the nature of the universe all things particular are determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without, depending. Either this universe is a mere confused mass, and an intricate context of things, which shall in time be scattered and dispersed again: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered by Providence. If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer in this fortuit confusion and commixtion? or why should I take care for anything else, but that as soon as may be I may be earth again? And why should I trouble myself any more whilst I seek to please the Gods? Whatsoever I do, dispersion is my end, and will come upon me whether I will or no. But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain; then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the Governor of all.
pages.familiar: Everything that happens to each individual follows the nature of the universe, whether that means being held within a greater whole, scattered throughout it, or dependent on what lies outside. Either the universe is a confused mixture that will eventually break apart, or it is an ordered whole guided by providence. If it is only confusion, why should I want to remain in it? Why care about anything except returning to earth as soon as possible? Why keep trying to please the gods? Whatever I do, dissolution will come, whether I want it or not. But if the universe is ordered, then my faith is not pointless. I can remain calm and patient, trusting the power that governs everything.
pages.abbreviated: Whatever happens follows the nature of the universe, which may be chaotic and destined to dissolve or ordered and governed by providence. If it is chaos, nothing matters; if it is ordered, faith and patient calm are justified, since the governing power directs everything.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 9
pages.original: Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out, presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
pages.familiar: Whenever some immediate difficulty throws you off balance, return to yourself as soon as you can. Do not remain upset longer than necessary. You will be better able to keep your place and preserve your inner harmony next time if you practice this continually: whenever you fall out of tune, go back and begin again.
pages.abbreviated: When difficulty unsettles you, return to yourself as soon as possible instead of remaining upset. Repeatedly practicing this return helps preserve your inner harmony the next time you lose it.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 10
pages.original: If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also; nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those things not intolerable unto others.
pages.familiar: If you had both a stepmother and your own mother living, you would respect them both, but you would keep returning to your mother for comfort. Let the court and your philosophy be like that for you. Return to them often, and take comfort in the one that makes everything else bearable—and makes you bearable to others.
pages.abbreviated: As you would respect a stepmother but return to your mother for comfort, let public duties and philosophy both matter while returning often to philosophy. It makes everything else bearable and helps you become bearable to others.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 11
pages.original: How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with the blood of a shellfish. So for coitus, it is but the attrition of an ordinary base entrail, and the excretion of a little vile snivel, with a certain kind of convulsion: according to Hippocrates his opinion. How excellent useful are these lively fancies and representations of things, thus penetrating and passing through the objects, to make their true nature known and apparent! This must thou use all thy life long, and upon all occasions: and then especially, when matters are apprehended as of great worth and respect, thy art and care must be to uncover them, and to behold their vileness, and to take away from them all those serious circumstances and expressions, under which they made so grave a show. For outward pomp and appearance is a great juggler; and then especially art thou most in danger to be beguiled by it, when (to a man's thinking) thou most seemest to be employed about matters of moment.
pages.familiar: It is remarkably useful to see things plainly. This is the body of a fish, that of a bird, that of a pig. This expensive wine is only grape juice. This fine purple clothing is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Sex is only the rubbing together of ordinary body parts followed by a bodily release. Use such clear images throughout your life, especially when something seems extremely important or impressive. Look beneath the display and see what it really is. Outward show is a great deceiver, and it is most likely to fool you when you think you are occupied with something serious.
pages.abbreviated: See things plainly beneath their impressive appearance: costly wine is grape juice, fine purple clothing is dyed wool, and sex is ordinary physical contact followed by release. Use this practice especially when something seems important, because outward show most easily deceives you when you think you are engaged in serious matters.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 12
pages.original: See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.
pages.familiar: Consider what Crates said about Xenocrates himself.
pages.abbreviated: Reflect on what Crates said about Xenocrates.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 13
pages.original: Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones, wood, figs, vines, olives. Those that be admired by them that are more moderate and restrained, are comprehended under things animated: as flocks and herds. Those that are yet more gentle and curious, their admiration is commonly confined to reasonable creatures only; not in general as they are reasonable, but as they are capable of art, or of some craft and subtile invention: or perchance barely to reasonable creatures; as they that delight in the possession of many slaves. But he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and naturally sociable, doth little regard anything else: and above all things is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and exercise both of reason and sociableness: and thereby doth co-operate with him, of whose nature he doth also participate; God.
pages.familiar: What most people admire is usually something ordinary in nature: stones, wood, figs, vines, or olives. More restrained people admire living things, such as flocks and herds. Those with finer interests may admire clever, inventive people—or simply people who own many slaves. But someone who honors reason itself, together with our natural ability to live cooperatively, cares little for anything else. Above all, such a person protects the reason and social concern within themselves, working with the nature they share with God.
pages.abbreviated: Most admired things are ordinary natural objects, living creatures, clever people, or wealth and power. The person who honors reason and our cooperative nature values these less, protecting their own reason and social concern in harmony with the nature shared with God.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 14
pages.original: Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished. Perpetual fluxes and alterations renew the world, as the perpetual course of time doth make the age of the world (of itself infinite) to appear always fresh and new. In such a flux and course of all things, what of these things that hasten so fast away should any man regard, since among all there is not any that a man may fasten and fix upon? as if a man would settle his affection upon some ordinary sparrow living by him, who is no sooner seen, than out of sight. For we must not think otherwise of our lives, than as a mere exhalation of blood, or of an ordinary respiration of air. For what in our common apprehension is, to breathe in the air and to breathe it out again, which we do daily: so much is it and no more, at once to breathe out all thy respirative faculty into that common air from whence but lately (as being but from yesterday, and to-day), thou didst first breathe it in, and with it, life.
pages.familiar: Some things are coming into existence while others are passing away. Even what exists now is already partly gone. Constant change renews the world, while time keeps making it seem fresh. In this continual flow, why cling to anything that disappears so quickly? It is like trying to hold on to a sparrow that vanishes as soon as you see it. Our lives are no more lasting than a breath of air or a little blood moving through the body. Breathing out all our breath into the common air is no more final than releasing the life we only recently drew in.
pages.abbreviated: Everything is continually coming into being and passing away, and even what exists is already disappearing. Since life is as fleeting as a breath or a moment of blood flow, clinging to temporary things is like trying to hold a vanishing sparrow.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 15
