pages.original: Not vegetative spiration, it is not surely (which plants have) that in this life should be so dear unto us; nor sensitive respiration, the proper life of beasts, both tame and wild; nor this our imaginative faculty; nor that we are subject to be led and carried up and down by the strength of our sensual appetites; or that we can gather, and live together; or that we can feed: for that in effect is no better, than that we can void the excrements of our food. What is it then that should be dear unto us? to hear a clattering noise? if not that, then neither to be applauded by the tongues of men. For the praises of many tongues, is in effect no better than the clattering of so many tongues. If then neither applause, what is there remaining that should be dear unto thee? This I think: that in all thy motions and actions thou be moved, and restrained according to thine own true natural constitution and Construction only. And to this even ordinary arts and professions do lead us. For it is that which every art doth aim at, that whatsoever it is, that is by art effected and prepared, may be fit for that work that it is prepared for. This is the end that he that dresseth the vine, and he that takes upon him either to tame colts, or to train up dogs, doth aim at. What else doth the education of children, and all learned professions tend unto? Certainly then it is that, which should be dear unto us also. If in this particular it go well with thee, care not for the obtaining of other things. But is it so, that thou canst not but respect other things also? Then canst not thou truly be free? then canst thou not have self-content: then wilt thou ever be subject to passions. For it is not possible, but that thou must be envious, and jealous, and suspicious of them whom thou knowest can bereave thee of such things; and again, a secret underminer of them, whom thou seest in present possession of that which is dear unto thee. To be short, he must of necessity be full of confusion within himself, and often accuse the Gods, whosoever stands in need of these things. But if thou shalt honour and respect thy mind only, that will make thee acceptable towards thyself, towards thy friends very tractable; and conformable and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
pages.familiar: What should matter most to you? Not merely being alive like a plant, sensing and reacting like an animal, imagining things, following appetites, gathering with others, eating, or simply removing what you have eaten. Is it the sound of praise? If not, then the applause of many people is no better than the clatter of many voices. What remains worthy of love is this: in every movement and action, follow and preserve your true nature. Every craft aims at this—the vine dresser prepares the vine to bear fruit, the trainer prepares a horse or dog for its work, and education prepares a child to become capable. That should be your aim too. If you are right in this, do not worry about gaining anything else. If you must have other things as well, you cannot be free or content. You will envy, fear, suspect, and undermine those who might take them from you or already possess them. You will be inwardly confused and blame the gods. But if you honor your own mind above all else, you will be at peace with yourself, easy with your friends, and in harmony with the gods, accepting with gratitude whatever they give you.
pages.abbreviated: What matters is not mere life, sensation, imagination, appetite, social activity, food, or praise, but preserving your true nature in every action. If you need anything else for contentment, you will become envious and fearful; if you honor your mind above all, you can be at peace with yourself, friendly with others, and grateful to the gods.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 16
pages.original: Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
pages.familiar: The elements move below, above, and around one another. Virtue moves in none of these ordinary ways; it is something higher and more divine. To advance in it, you must follow a path whose direction is not easily understood.
pages.abbreviated: The elements move in ordinary directions, but virtue moves in a higher and more divine way. Advancing in virtue therefore requires following a path whose direction is difficult to recognize.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 17
pages.original: Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived before him.
pages.familiar: How can anyone not be amazed by them? They refuse to speak well of people living beside them, yet they desperately want future generations—people they have never met and never will—to praise them. That is like grieving because people who lived before you never praised you.
pages.abbreviated: It is astonishing that people refuse to praise those around them while desperately seeking praise from future generations they will never meet. This is like grieving that people from the past never praised you.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 18
pages.original: Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that very possible unto thee also.
pages.familiar: Do not call something impossible for a human being merely because you cannot do it, or cannot do it without great effort. Whatever you can reasonably imagine another person capable of doing, consider possible for you as well.
pages.abbreviated: Do not call something impossible for humans simply because you cannot do it or can do it only with great effort. If you can reasonably imagine another person doing it, regard it as possible for you too.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 19
pages.original: Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with his nails, and hath broken thy head. Well, thou art wounded. Yet thou dost not exclaim; thou art not offended with him. Thou dost not suspect him for it afterwards, as one that watcheth to do thee a mischief. Yea even then, though thou dost thy best to save thyself from him, yet not from him as an enemy. It is not by way of any suspicious indignation, but by way of gentle and friendly declination. Keep the same mind and disposition in other parts of thy life also. For many things there be, which we must conceit and apprehend, as though we had had to do with an antagonist at the palestra. For as I said, it is very possible for us to avoid and decline, though we neither suspect, nor hate.
pages.familiar: Suppose someone at the gym tore you up with his nails and split your head open. You are hurt, but you do not shout or take offense. Later, you do not watch him suspiciously, expecting him to harm you again. Even while protecting yourself, you do not treat him as an enemy. You simply step away, calmly and without hostility. Keep that same attitude throughout your life. Many situations are like facing an opponent in practice: you can avoid harm without suspecting or hating the person.
pages.abbreviated: You can protect yourself from someone who harms you without shouting, taking offense, suspecting, or hating them, as when calmly stepping away from a rough gym opponent. Treat many conflicts the same way: avoid harm without treating the other person as an enemy.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 20
pages.original: If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me, that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
pages.familiar: If someone corrects me and clearly shows me that I am mistaken in an opinion or an action, I will gladly change. I am searching for the truth, and I know that truth never harms anyone. What harms us is clinging to error and ignorance.
pages.abbreviated: If someone clearly shows that your opinion or action is mistaken, gladly change because you seek the truth. Truth does not harm; clinging to error and ignorance does.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 21
pages.original: I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things, whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or distract me. For as for those creatures which are not endued with reason and all other things and-matters of the world whatsoever I freely, and generously, as one endued with reason, of things that have none, make use of them. And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably. But whatsoever it is that thou art about, remember to call upon the Gods. And as for the time how long thou shalt live to do these things, let it be altogether indifferent unto thee, for even three such hours are sufficient.
pages.familiar: I will do what is mine to do. Other things—whether lifeless, irrational, or rational but confused and ignorant of the right path—will not disturb or distract me. I will use lifeless things as a rational being should, and treat other people sociably because they share reason with me. Whatever you are doing, remember to call on the gods. And do not worry about how long you will have to continue; even three good hours would be enough.
pages.abbreviated: Do your own duty without being distracted by lifeless things or by confused people, using things rationally and treating fellow rational beings sociably. Call on the gods whatever you are doing, and do not worry about how long the task must continue, since even three good hours would suffice.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 22
pages.original: Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those original rational essences from whence all things in the world are propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms. XXIII Consider how many different things, whether they concern our bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and general, which we call the world.
pages.familiar: Alexander of Macedon and the man who cared for his mules, once dead, came to the same end. Both were either taken back into the rational source from which everything comes, or scattered into atoms in the same way. Consider how many different things, affecting both body and mind, happen within each of us in a single moment. Then you will not be surprised that countless things—or everything that happens—can exist together at once in the one whole we call the world.
pages.abbreviated: Alexander and the man who cared for his mules ultimately met the same end, whether absorbed into the rational source of everything or scattered into atoms. Since many different bodily and mental events occur together in each person, it is unsurprising that countless events coexist within the single whole of the world.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 24
pages.original: if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again, or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were, to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would quarrel and fall out with thee.
pages.familiar: If someone asked how to spell “Antoninus,” would you not focus on the task and say each letter in order? If they started arguing with you, would you argue back, or would you calmly continue until you had named every letter? Duties are like that. Each has its own letters and steps. Quietly follow them to the end, without getting into a fight with someone who wants to quarrel.
pages.abbreviated: As you would calmly spell a word letter by letter rather than argue with someone who interrupts, perform your duties through their distinct steps. Follow them quietly to the end instead of fighting with someone who wants to quarrel.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 25
pages.original: Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most to their own proper good and behoof? But thou after a sort deniest them this liberty, as often as thou art angry with them for their sins. For surely they are led unto those sins whatsoever they be, as to their proper good and commodity. But it is not so (thou wilt object perchance). Thou therefore teach them better, and make it appear unto them: but be not thou angry with them.
pages.familiar: Is it not cruel to forbid people from pursuing what they believe suits their nature and serves their good? Yet you do something like that whenever you become angry with them for their wrongdoing. They are drawn toward those actions because they think the actions will benefit them. You may say they are mistaken. Then teach them, show them a better way—but do not be angry with them.
pages.abbreviated: People pursue wrongdoing because they believe it suits their nature and serves their good, so becoming angry with them is like forbidding them to pursue what they think benefits them. If they are mistaken, teach and guide them toward a better way rather than responding with anger.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 26
pages.original: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
pages.familiar: Death is the end of sensory impressions, the rule of the passions, the mind’s errors, and the body’s servitude.
pages.abbreviated: Death ends sensory impressions, the rule of the passions, the mind’s errors, and the body’s servitude.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 27
pages.original: If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed. Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind, tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee. Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short. Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this earthly life.
pages.familiar: If your body can endure this life, it is shameful for your soul to give up first. Take care that, while calling yourself a philosopher, you do not gradually become merely a ruler shaped by the court. Keep yourself simple, good, sincere, serious, free of display, devoted to justice, reverent, kind, compassionate, and strong enough to endure what is required of you. Try to remain the person philosophy would have made you if you had followed it fully and consistently. Honor the gods and help people. Life is short. Compassionate actions and a holy character are its only lasting harvest.
pages.abbreviated: If the body can endure life, the soul should not give up first; remain simple, sincere, just, reverent, compassionate, and strong rather than becoming corrupted by power or display. Honor the gods and help people, because life is short and compassionate acts and a holy character are its only lasting harvest.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 28
pages.original: Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius. Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything, nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men. Again, how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing, and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition. All these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the possession of a good conscience.
pages.familiar: Live as a student of Antoninus Pius. Remember his firm commitment to reason, his calmness in everything, his reverence, his cheerful face, his gentleness, and his complete freedom from vanity. Remember how carefully he sought exact knowledge, refusing to stop until he understood the whole matter; how patiently he endured unjust blame; how he was never hasty, never guided by rumors or accusations, and carefully observed people’s actions and character. He did not gossip, frighten easily, or live suspiciously. His speech was natural, not showy or affected. He was satisfied with little: a simple home, bed, clothing, food, and service. He could endure work and remain steady on a spare diet. He was constant in friendship, welcomed people who challenged him, and even rejoiced when someone could offer better advice. He was reverent without superstition. Remember all this, so that when your final hour comes, it finds you as it found him: ready, with a clear conscience.
pages.abbreviated: Remember Antoninus Pius as rational, calm, reverent, cheerful, gentle, unvain, careful in seeking knowledge, patient with blame, and free from rumor, suspicion, gossip, and display. He lived simply, endured work and little food, welcomed correction, maintained friendship, and remained reverent without superstition; keep these qualities so your final hour finds you ready and clear-conscienced.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 29
pages.original: Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly awakened out of another kind of sleep look upon these worldly things with the same mind as thou didst upon those, that thou sawest in thy sleep.
pages.familiar: Wake your mind and gather your thoughts again from its natural dreams and visions. Once fully awake, recognize that the dreams troubling you were only dreams. Then look at worldly things with the same attitude you had toward what you saw while asleep.
pages.abbreviated: Wake your mind from its natural dreams and recognize that the troubling visions were only dreams. Then view worldly things with the same detachment you had toward what you saw while asleep.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 30
pages.original: I consist of body and soul. Unto my body all things are indifferent, for of itself it cannot affect one thing more than another with apprehension of any difference; as for my mind, all things which are not within the verge of her own operation, are indifferent unto her, and for her own operations, those altogether depend of her; neither does she busy herself about any, but those that are present; for as for future and past operations, those also are now at this present indifferent unto her.
pages.familiar: I am made of body and mind. What happens to my body, by itself, is neither good nor bad; it cannot judge one thing better than another. My mind is concerned only with what lies within its own activity, and its activity is always happening now. The past and future are not available to it as actions, so they do not belong to its present work.
pages.abbreviated: I consist of body and mind: bodily events are neither good nor bad, while the mind concerns only its present activity, since past and future are not actions available to it now.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 31
pages.original: As long as the foot doth that which belongeth unto it to do, and the hand that which belongs unto it, their labour, whatsoever it be, is not unnatural. So a man as long as he doth that which is proper unto a man, his labour cannot be against nature; and if it be not against nature, then neither is it hurtful unto him. But if it were so that happiness did consist in pleasure: how came notorious robbers, impure abominable livers, parricides, and tyrants, in so large a measure to have their part of pleasures?
pages.familiar: A foot is doing what belongs to a foot, and a hand what belongs to a hand, whenever each does its proper work. In the same way, a person is acting naturally when doing what belongs to a human being. If that work follows human nature, it cannot truly harm us. And if happiness were simply pleasure, how could thieves, abusers, killers of their own parents, and tyrants have enjoyed so much of it?
pages.abbreviated: A person acts naturally by doing what belongs to human beings, and work that follows human nature cannot truly harm us. Happiness cannot simply be pleasure, since even thieves, abusers, murderers, and tyrants have experienced pleasure.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 32
pages.original: Dost thou not see, how even those that profess mechanic arts, though in some respect they be no better than mere idiots, yet they stick close to the course of their trade, neither can they find in their heart to decline from it: and is it not a grievous thing that an architect, or a physician shall respect the course and mysteries of their profession, more than a man the proper course and condition of his own nature, reason, which is common to him and to the Gods?
pages.familiar: Look at people who practice ordinary trades. Even when they understand little beyond their craft, they remain committed to its methods and refuse to abandon them. Is it not shameful that an architect or doctor respects the principles of a profession more deeply than a human being respects the proper order of human nature—the reason shared with the divine?
pages.abbreviated: People in ordinary trades faithfully follow the principles of their craft. It is shameful if professionals respect their methods more than human beings respect the rational order shared with the divine.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 33
pages.original: Asia, Europe; what are they, but as corners of the whole world; of which the whole sea, is but as one drop; and the great Mount Athos, but as a clod, as all present time is but as one point of eternity. All, petty things; all things that are soon altered, soon perished. And all things come from one beginning; either all severally and particularly deliberated and resolved upon, by the general ruler and governor of all; or all by necessary consequence. So that the dreadful hiatus of a gaping lion, and all poison, and all hurtful things, are but (as the thorn and the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things. Think not of these therefore, as things contrary to those which thou dost much honour, and respect; but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all. XXXIV He that seeth the things that are now, hath Seen all that either was ever, or ever shall be, for all things are of one kind; and all like one unto another. Meditate often upon the connection of all things in the world; and upon the mutual relation that they have one unto another. For all things are after a sort folded and involved one within another, and by these means all agree well together. For one thing is consequent unto another, by local motion, by natural conspiration and agreement, and by substantial union, or, reduction of all substances into one.
pages.familiar: Asia and Europe are only small corners of the world. The entire ocean is a drop, Mount Athos a clod, and all present time a point in eternity. Everything is small, quickly changed, and quickly gone. Everything comes from one beginning, whether each event is deliberately ordered by the ruler of all or follows by necessary consequence. The lion's open jaws, poison, and every harmful thing are consequences woven into the same world that produces what is beautiful. Do not treat them as enemies of what you honor; look instead to the common source of everything. Whoever sees what exists now has seen everything that ever was or will be, because all things follow the same patterns. Often consider how everything is connected: how one thing leads to another through movement, natural cooperation, and the unity into which all matter is gathered.
pages.abbreviated: Everything is small, temporary, interconnected, and arises from one common source, whether by deliberate order or necessity. Harmful things are woven into the same world as beautiful things, so contemplate how all events connect and how the present reflects all time.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 35
pages.original: Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee; and love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly. An instrument, a tool, an utensil, whatsoever it be, if it be fit for the purpose it was made for, it is as it should be though he perchance that made and fitted it, be out of sight and gone. But in things natural, that power which hath framed and fitted them, is and abideth within them still: for which reason she ought also the more to be respected, and we are the more obliged (if we may live and pass our time according to her purpose and intention) to think that all is well with us, and according to our own minds. After this manner also, and in this respect it is, that he that is all in all doth enjoy his happiness.
pages.familiar: Adjust yourself to the circumstances and events that have come with your life, and genuinely love the people you are meant to live among. A tool is right when it serves the purpose it was made for, even if its maker is no longer present. In living things, the power that shaped them remains within them. For that reason it deserves even greater respect. If we live according to our nature and purpose, we should recognize that our lives are in order. In this way, the power within everything fulfills its own happiness.
pages.abbreviated: Adapt to your circumstances and genuinely love the people among whom you live. A thing is rightly fulfilling its purpose when it serves its nature, so living according to our nature puts our lives in order and fulfills the power within us.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 36
pages.original: What things soever are not within the proper power and jurisdiction of thine own will either to compass or avoid, if thou shalt propose unto thyself any of those things as either good, or evil; it must needs be that according as thou shalt either fall into that which thou dost think evil, or miss of that which thou dost think good, so wilt thou be ready both to complain of the Gods, and to hate those men, who either shall be so indeed, or shall by thee be suspected as the cause either of thy missing of the one, or falling into the other. And indeed we must needs commit many evils, if we incline to any of these things, more or less, with an opinion of any difference. But if we mind and fancy those things only, as good and bad, which wholly depend of our own wills, there is no more occasion why we should either murmur against the Gods, or be at enmity with any man.
pages.familiar: If you treat things outside your control as good or bad, then whenever you meet what you fear or miss what you want, you will complain about the gods and resent the people you blame or suspect. We are bound to do wrong when we attach moral value to such things. But if we call good and bad only what depends entirely on our own choices, we have no reason to complain against the gods or become enemies with anyone.
pages.abbreviated: If you call things outside your control good or bad, you will complain against the gods and resent people when events disappoint you. If good and bad concern only your choices, you have no reason for such complaints or hostility.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 37
pages.original: We all work to one effect, some willingly, and with a rational apprehension of what we do: others without any such knowledge. As I think Heraclitus in a place speaketh of them that sleep, that even they do work in their kind, and do confer to the general operations of the world. One man therefore doth co-operate after one sort, and another after another sort; but even he that doth murmur, and to his power doth resist and hinder; even he as much as any doth co-operate. For of such also did the world stand in need. Now do thou consider among which of these thou wilt rank thyself. For as for him who is the Administrator of all, he will make good use of thee whether thou wilt or no, and make thee (as a part and member of the whole) so to co-operate with him, that whatsoever thou doest, shall turn to the furtherance of his own counsels, and resolutions. But be not thou for shame such a part of the whole, as that vile and ridiculous verse (which Chrysippus in a place doth mention) is a part of the comedy.
pages.familiar: We all contribute to the world's activity. Some do so willingly and understand what they are doing; others do so without understanding. Even the person who complains and tries to resist still contributes, because the whole has a place for resistance as well. Decide which kind of person you will be. The power guiding everything will use you whether you agree or not, fitting your actions into the work of the whole. Do not make yourself a shameful and ridiculous part of it.
pages.abbreviated: Everyone contributes to the world's activity, willingly or unwillingly, since even resistance has a place in the whole. Choose to understand and cooperate with the guiding power rather than become a shameful part of its work.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 38
pages.original: Doth either the sun take upon him to do that which belongs to the rain? or his son Aesculapius that, which unto the earth doth properly belong? How is it with every one of the stars in particular? Though they all differ one from another, and have their several charges and functions by themselves, do they not all nevertheless concur and co-operate to one end?
pages.familiar: Does the sun try to do the work of rain, or the healer do the work that belongs to the earth? Each star has its own nature, task, and place. Yet although they differ, do they not all work together toward one end?
pages.abbreviated: Each part of nature has its own task and place, yet the sun, rain, healer, earth, and stars all cooperate toward one common end.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 39
pages.original: If so be that the Gods have deliberated in particular of those things that should happen unto me, I must stand to their deliberation, as discrete and wise. For that a God should be an imprudent God, is a thing hard even to conceive: and why should they resolve to do me hurt? for what profit either unto them or the universe (which they specially take care for) could arise from it? But if so be that they have not deliberated of me in particular, certainly they have of the whole in general, and those things which in consequence and coherence of this general deliberation happen unto me in particular, I am bound to embrace and accept of. But if so be that they have not deliberated at all (which indeed is very irreligious for any man to believe: for then let us neither sacrifice, nor pray, nor respect our oaths, neither let us any more use any of those things, which we persuaded of the presence and secret conversation of the Gods among us, daily use and practise:) but, I say, if so be that they have not indeed either in general, or particular deliberated of any of those things, that happen unto us in this world; yet God be thanked, that of those things that concern myself, it is lawful for me to deliberate myself, and all my deliberation is but concerning that which may be to me most profitable. Now that unto every one is most profitable, which is according to his own constitution and nature. And my nature is, to be rational in all my actions and as a good, and natural member of a city and commonwealth, towards my fellow members ever to be sociably and kindly disposed and affected. My city and country as I am Antoninus, is Rome; as a man, the whole world. Those things therefore that are expedient and profitable to those cities, are the only things that are good and expedient for me.
pages.familiar: If the gods have specifically ordered what happens to me, I should accept their decision as wise. It is difficult to imagine a god acting foolishly, and there is no reason they would choose to harm me. If they have not planned my events individually, they have at least ordered the whole, and I should accept what follows from that larger order. If nothing has been planned at all—which would make prayer, sacrifice, promises, and reverence meaningless—then I can still decide for myself what is most beneficial. What benefits me is what fits my nature. My nature is to act reasonably and to live kindly and cooperatively with others. As Antoninus, my city is Rome; as a human being, my city is the whole world. What serves those communities is good and beneficial for me.
pages.abbreviated: Whether events are individually ordered by the gods or follow a larger order, accept what happens as part of that order; if nothing is planned, choose what benefits your nature. Your nature is rational, kind, and cooperative, and what serves Rome and humanity serves you.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 40
pages.original: Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the whole. And thus much to content us might suffice, that it is expedient for the whole in general. But yet this also shalt thou generally perceive, if thou dost diligently take heed, that whatsoever doth happen to any one man or men.... And now I am content that the word expedient, should more generally be understood of those things which we otherwise call middle things, or things indifferent; as health, wealth, and the like.
pages.familiar: Whatever happens to one person contributes in some way to the whole. That alone should be enough to satisfy us. But if you look carefully, you will also see that what happens to one person or group can benefit others. Here, benefit should be understood broadly: health, money, and similar things are neither good nor bad in themselves, but circumstances that may serve the whole.
pages.abbreviated: Whatever happens to one person contributes to the whole, and may also benefit others in a broad sense. Health, money, and similar things are not good or bad in themselves, but circumstances that can serve the whole.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 41
pages.original: As the ordinary shows of the theatre and of other such places, when thou art presented with them, affect thee; as the same things still seen, and in the same fashion, make the sight ingrateful and tedious; so must all the things that we see all our life long affect us. For all things, above and below, are still the same, and from the same causes. When then will there be an end?
pages.familiar: The same performances grow dull when we see them again and again. Life is much the same: the things we witness every day repeat themselves, driven by the same causes. How long will this continue?
pages.abbreviated: Repeated performances become dull, and daily life likewise repeats the same events through the same causes. How long will this continue?

pages.label: Book VI · Section 42
pages.original: Let the several deaths of men of all sorts, and of all sorts of professions, and of all sort of nations, be a perpetual object of thy thoughts,... so that thou mayst even come down to Philistio, Phœbus, and Origanion. Pass now to other generations. Thither shall we after many changes, where so many brave orators are; where so many grave philosophers; Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates. Where so many heroes of the old times; and then so many brave captains of the latter times; and so many kings. After all these, where Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes; where so many other sharp, generous, industrious, subtile, peremptory dispositions; and among others, even they, that have been the greatest scoffers and deriders of the frailty and brevity of this our human life; as Menippus, and others, as many as there have been such as he. Of all these consider, that they long since are all dead, and gone. And what do they suffer by it! Nay they that have not so much as a name remaining, what are they the worse for it? One thing there is, and that only, which is worth our while in this world, and ought by us much to be esteemed; and that is, according to truth and righteousness, meekly and lovingly to converse with false, and unrighteous men.
pages.familiar: Keep in mind the deaths of people from every class, profession, and nation. Think of the famous speakers, serious philosophers, ancient heroes, later commanders, and kings. Think of brilliant, generous, hardworking, clever people—and even those who mocked how brief and fragile life is. All of them died long ago. What harm has death done to them? What difference does it make that some have been forgotten entirely? There is only one thing worth valuing here: living truthfully and justly, while treating dishonest and unjust people with gentleness and love.
pages.abbreviated: People of every class, nation, talent, and reputation have died, and death has not harmed them or made their obscurity significant. What matters is living truthfully and justly while treating dishonest and unjust people gently and lovingly.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 43
pages.original: When thou wilt comfort and cheer thyself, call to mind the several gifts and virtues of them, whom thou dost daily converse with; as for example, the industry of the one; the modesty of another; the liberality of a third; of another some other thing. For nothing can so much rejoice thee, as the resemblances and parallels of several virtues, visible and eminent in the dispositions of those who live with thee; especially when, all at once, as near as may be, they represent themselves unto thee. And therefore thou must have them always in a readiness.
pages.familiar: When you need comfort or encouragement, remember the particular gifts and virtues of the people around you: one person's diligence, another's humility, another's generosity, and someone else's different strength. Nothing lifts the spirit more than noticing many virtues clearly present in the people you live among. Keep these examples ready in your mind.
pages.abbreviated: When you need encouragement, remember the distinct virtues of people around you, such as diligence, humility, generosity, and other strengths. Keep these examples clearly present in your mind.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 44
pages.original: Dost thou grieve that thou dost weigh but so many pounds, and not three hundred rather? Just as much reason hast thou to grieve that thou must live but so many years, and not longer. For as for bulk and substance thou dost content thyself with that proportion of it that is allotted unto thee, so shouldst thou for time.
pages.familiar: Would you be upset that you weigh only a certain amount instead of three hundred pounds? Then you have just as much reason to be upset that you will live only a certain number of years instead of longer. You accept the share of physical size given to you; accept your share of time in the same way.
pages.abbreviated: You accept having only a certain physical size, so accept having only a certain amount of time. Your allotted years are no more a reason for distress than your allotted weight.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 45
pages.original: Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much against it. But if any shall by force withstand thee, and hinder thee in it, convert thy virtuous inclination from one object unto another, from justice to contented equanimity, and cheerful patience: so that what in the one is thy hindrance, thou mayst make use of it for the exercise of another virtue: and remember that it was with due exception, and reservation, that thou didst at first incline and desire. For thou didst not set thy mind upon things impossible. Upon what then? that all thy desires might ever be moderated with this due kind of reservation. And this thou hast, and mayst always obtain, whether the thing desired be in thy power or no. And what do I care for more, if that for which I was born and brought forth into the world (to rule all my desires with reason and discretion) may be?
pages.familiar: Do everything you reasonably can to persuade people. But if reason and justice require it, act even when they strongly oppose you. If someone uses force to stop you, turn your good intention toward another virtue: from justice to calm acceptance and cheerful patience. Let the obstacle become practice for that virtue. Remember that your original desire always carried a reservation: you wanted the right outcome, but never claimed that everything must go your way. You were not promised the impossible. Your real aim was to keep every desire measured by sound judgment. That is always within your power. What more do you need, if you can fulfill the purpose for which you were born—to govern your desires with reason and discretion?
pages.abbreviated: Persuade people when you can, but act according to reason and justice even when they resist; if blocked, turn your intention toward calm acceptance and cheerful patience. Your aim was never to control the outcome, but to govern your desires with sound judgment, which is always within your power.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 46
pages.original: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.
pages.familiar: The ambitious person makes someone else's actions, praise, and applause the source of happiness. The pleasure-seeker depends on personal feelings and sensations. The wise person finds happiness in acting well.
pages.abbreviated: The ambitious depend on others' actions and praise, and pleasure-seekers depend on their sensations. The wise find happiness in acting well.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 47
pages.original: It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
pages.familiar: You can completely refuse to form an opinion about what has happened, and by doing so keep grief and sorrow from taking over your mind. Events themselves do not have the power to force an interpretation upon you.
pages.abbreviated: You can refuse to form an opinion about an event and thereby prevent grief from taking over. Events cannot force their interpretation upon your mind.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 48
pages.original: Use thyself when any man speaks unto thee, so to hearken unto him, as that in the interim thou give not way to any other thoughts; that so thou mayst (as far as is possible) seem fixed and fastened to his very soul, whosoever he be that speaks unto thee.
pages.familiar: When someone speaks to you, practice listening without letting your mind wander to other thoughts. Give the speaker your full attention, as though you were trying to understand the deepest part of who they are, whoever they may be.
pages.abbreviated: Listen to whoever speaks with complete attention, without letting your mind wander, as though you were trying to understand the deepest part of that person.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 49
pages.original: That which is not good for the bee-hive, cannot be good for the bee.
pages.familiar: What harms the whole community cannot truly benefit any individual within it.
pages.abbreviated: What harms the community cannot truly benefit any individual within it.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 50
pages.original: Will either passengers, or patients, find fault and complain, either the one if they be well carried, or the others if well cured? Do they take care for any more than this; the one, that their shipmaster may bring them safe to land, and the other, that their physician may effect their recovery?
pages.familiar: Do passengers complain when they are carried safely, or patients when they are properly cured? Each cares about the essential result: passengers want to reach land safely, and patients want to recover. That is enough.
pages.abbreviated: Passengers care that they reach land safely, and patients that they recover; if those essential results occur, the rest is unimportant.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 51
pages.original: How many of them who came into the world at the same time when I did, are already gone out of it?
pages.familiar: How many people who entered the world when I did have already left it?
pages.abbreviated: Many people who entered the world at the same time as I did have already died.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 52
pages.original: To them that are sick of the jaundice, honey seems bitter; and to them that are bitten by a mad dog, the water terrible; and to children, a little ball seems a fine thing. And why then should I be angry? or do I think that error and false opinion is less powerful to make men transgress, than either choler, being immoderate and excessive, to cause the jaundice; or poison, to cause rage?
pages.familiar: Honey tastes bitter to someone with jaundice; water terrifies someone bitten by a rabid dog; and a small ball seems enormously important to a child. So why should I be angry? Do I really think false beliefs make people go wrong less powerfully than sickness or poison can distort them? The person is mistaken, and that mistake has taken hold of them.
pages.abbreviated: Illness and false beliefs distort perception, making bitterness seem sweet, water frightening, or trivial things important. People go wrong because mistaken beliefs have taken hold of them, so anger is misplaced.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 53
pages.original: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.
pages.familiar: No one can stop you from living according to your nature. Nothing can happen to you except what the nature of the whole requires.
pages.abbreviated: Nothing can prevent you from living according to your nature, and nothing can happen except what the nature of the whole requires.

pages.label: Book VI · Section 54
pages.original: What manner of men they be whom they seek to please, and what to get, and by what actions: how soon time will cover and bury all things, and how many it hath already buried!
pages.familiar: What kind of people are they trying to please, what are they trying to gain, and by what actions? Soon time will cover and bury everything—and how much has it already buried.
pages.abbreviated: Consider whom people seek to please, what they seek to gain, and what they do to pursue it. Time will soon bury everything, as it has already buried so much.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 1
pages.original: What is wickedness? It is that which many time and often thou hast already seen and known in the world. And so oft as anything doth happen that might otherwise trouble thee, let this memento presently come to thy mind, that it is that which thou hast already often Seen and known. Generally, above and below, thou shalt find but the same things. The very same things whereof ancient stories, middle age stories, and fresh stories are full whereof towns are full, and houses full. There is nothing that is new. All things that are, are both usual and of little continuance.
pages.familiar: What is wickedness? It is what you have already seen and recognized in the world many times. Whenever something happens that might trouble you, remind yourself at once: I have seen this before. Everywhere, above and below, you find the same things. Ancient histories, recent histories, towns, and households are all full of them. Nothing is new. Everything is familiar, and nothing lasts long.
pages.abbreviated: Wickedness is not new: whatever troubles you has appeared repeatedly throughout history, in places, households, and societies. Everything is familiar and nothing lasts long.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 2
pages.original: What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only, which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be right.
pages.familiar: Why worry that your principles will become lifeless and lose their power to help you live well, as long as you keep alive the thoughts and clear views that support them—and that you can renew whenever you choose? Whatever has happened, I can understand it rightly and truthfully. If I can, why am I troubled? What lies beyond my understanding has no power over what truly belongs to me. Keep this firmly in mind, and you will be steady.
pages.abbreviated: Your principles remain useful as long as you keep alive and renew the clear thoughts that support them. Whatever happens can be understood rightly; what you cannot understand does not control what is truly yours, so remember this and remain steady.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 3
pages.original: That which most men would think themselves most happy for, and would prefer before all things, if the Gods would grant it unto them after their deaths, thou mayst whilst thou livest grant unto thyself; to live again. See the things of the world again, as thou hast already seen them. For what is it else to live again? Public shows and solemnities with much pomp and vanity, stage plays, flocks and herds; conflicts and contentions: a bone thrown to a company of hungry curs; a bait for greedy fishes; the painfulness, and continual burden-bearing of wretched ants, the running to and fro of terrified mice: little puppets drawn up and down with wires and nerves: these be the objects of the world among all these thou must stand steadfast, meekly affected, and free from all manner of indignation; with this right ratiocination and apprehension; that as the worth is of those things which a man doth affect, so is in very deed every man's worth more or less.
pages.familiar: What most people would consider the greatest happiness, something they would choose above everything if the gods offered it after death, you can give yourself while alive: the chance to live again. Look at the world once more as you have already seen it. What is it, after all? Public spectacles and grand ceremonies full of vanity; plays; flocks and herds; quarrels and competitions; a bone tossed to hungry dogs; bait for greedy fish; ants struggling under their endless loads; frightened mice running back and forth; little puppets pulled by strings. These are the world's attractions. Amid them, stand firm, gentle, and free of resentment. Understand that a person's worth is measured by the value of what they care about.
pages.abbreviated: You can give yourself in life the renewed perspective others might hope to receive after death by seeing the world's spectacles, conflicts, and attractions for what they are. Stand among them calmly and without resentment, knowing that a person's worth is measured by what they value.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 4
pages.original: Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done, purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise. And as in matter of purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and relation of every one; so of words must we be as ready, to consider of every one what is the true meaning, and signification of it according to truth and nature, however it be taken in common use.
pages.familiar: Understand spoken words one at a time, each in its own right; and understand actions the same way, purpose by purpose. With every action, immediately see its proper use and what it serves. With every word, be equally ready to ask what it truly means according to reality and nature, whatever meaning people commonly give it.
pages.abbreviated: Understand each word and action separately, recognizing its precise meaning, purpose, and use. Judge words by what they mean according to reality and nature, not merely by common usage.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 5
pages.original: Is my reason, and understanding sufficient for this, or no? If it be sufficient, without any private applause, or public ostentation as of an instrument, which by nature I am provided of, I will make use of it for the work in hand, as of an instrument, which by nature I am provided of. if it be not, and that otherwise it belong not unto me particularly as a private duty, I will either give it over, and leave it to some other that can better effect it: or I will endeavour it; but with the help of some other, who with the joint help of my reason, is able to bring somewhat to pass, that will now be seasonable and useful for the common good. For whatsoever I do either by myself, or with some other, the only thing that I must intend, is, that it be good and expedient for the public. For as for praise, consider how many who once were much commended, are now already quite forgotten, yea they that commended them, how even they themselves are long since dead and gone. Be not therefore ashamed, whensoever thou must use the help of others. For whatsoever it be that lieth upon thee to effect, thou must propose it unto thyself, as the scaling of walls is unto a soldier. And what if thou through either lameness or some other impediment art not able to reach unto the top of the battlements alone, which with the help of another thou mayst; wilt thou therefore give it over, or go about it with less courage and alacrity, because thou canst not effect it all alone?
pages.familiar: Is my reason and understanding enough for this task? If they are, I will use them quietly, without seeking private approval or public display, as tools nature has given me. If they are not enough, and the task is not specifically my personal duty, I will leave it to someone better suited—or attempt it with another person's help, so that together we can accomplish what is useful and timely for the common good. Whether I act alone or with others, my only aim must be what benefits the public. As for praise, remember how many once-famous people are already forgotten—and how long ago the people who praised them died. Do not be embarrassed to ask for help. Whatever you must accomplish, think of it as a soldier scaling a wall. If an injury or some other obstacle keeps you from reaching the top alone, but another person can help you, will you abandon the task or approach it with less courage simply because you cannot do it by yourself?
pages.abbreviated: Use your abilities quietly for the common good; if they are insufficient or the task is not yours alone, seek better-suited help rather than abandoning it. Aim only at public benefit, disregard praise as temporary, and approach necessary assistance as courageously as a soldier helping to scale a wall.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 6
pages.original: Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both tolerable and acceptable unto thee. All things are linked and knitted together, and the knot is sacred, neither is there anything in the world, that is not kind and natural in regard of any other thing, or, that hath not some kind of reference and natural correspondence with whatsoever is in the world besides. For all things are ranked together, and by that decency of its due place and order that each particular doth observe, they all concur together to the making of one and the same κόσμος or world: as if you said, a comely piece, or an orderly composition. For all things throughout, there is but one and the same order; and through all things, one and the same God, the same substance and the same law. There is one common reason, and one common truth, that belongs unto all reasonable creatures, for neither is there save one perfection of all creatures that are of the same kind, and partakers of the same reason.
pages.familiar: Do not let future events trouble you. If they must happen, then when the time comes you will meet them with the same reason that makes the present bearable and acceptable. Everything is connected, held together by a sacred bond. Nothing in the world is unrelated to anything else; everything has some natural connection and correspondence with everything around it. All things belong to one order, and by each occupying its proper place, they work together to form one world—an orderly, beautiful whole. Throughout everything there is one order, one God, one substance, and one law. There is one reason and one truth shared by all rational beings, and one perfection belonging to creatures that share the same nature and reason.
pages.abbreviated: Do not fear future events, because when they arrive you will face them with the same reason that makes the present bearable. Everything is naturally connected within one orderly whole, governed by one shared order, God, substance, law, reason, truth, and perfection.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 7
pages.original: Whatsoever is material, doth soon vanish away into the common substance of the whole; and whatsoever is formal, or, whatsoever doth animate that which is material, is soon resumed into the common reason of the whole; and the fame and memory of anything, is soon swallowed up by the general age and duration of the whole.
pages.familiar: Everything physical soon dissolves back into the shared substance of the whole. Whatever gives life and form to it soon returns to the shared reason of the whole. And the fame and memory of everything are soon swallowed by the vast passage of time.
pages.abbreviated: Physical things soon dissolve back into the universe's shared substance, their life and form return to its shared reason, and their fame and memory disappear into time.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 8
pages.original: To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according to nature, and according to reason.
pages.familiar: For a reasonable being, the same action is both natural and rational.
pages.abbreviated: For a rational being, acting naturally and acting rationally are the same thing.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 9
pages.original: Straight of itself, not made straight.
pages.familiar: Straight by its own nature, not forced into straightness.
pages.abbreviated: What is naturally straight is straight by its own nature, not because it was forced into straightness.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 10
pages.original: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common operation. And this thou shalt apprehend the better, if thou shalt use thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and body of reasonable substances. But if thou shalt say I am μέρος, or a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart. The joy that thou takest in the exercise of bounty, is not yet grounded upon a due ratiocination and right apprehension of the nature of things. Thou dost exercise it as yet upon this ground barely, as a thing convenient and fitting; not, as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others.
pages.familiar: Just as the limbs of one body are joined together, reasonable beings are parts of one larger body, spread out but made to work toward a common purpose. You will understand this better if you often tell yourself, “I am a member of the whole community of rational beings.” If you say only, “I am a part,” you have not yet learned to love people from the heart. Your pleasure in helping others is not yet based on a true understanding of how things are. You do it because it seems proper and appropriate, not because you see that doing good for others is also doing good for yourself.
pages.abbreviated: Rational beings are parts of one larger community, like limbs of one body, and should work toward a common purpose. Merely calling yourself a part is not enough; you must understand that helping others is also helping yourself, and love them from that understanding.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 11
pages.original: Of things that are external, happen what will to that which can suffer by external accidents. Those things that suffer let them complain themselves, if they will; as for me, as long as I conceive no such thing, that that which is happened is evil, I have no hurt; and it is in my power not to conceive any such thing.
pages.familiar: When something external happens, let whatever is harmed by it complain if it wishes. As for me, as long as I do not judge what happened to be evil, I am not harmed. And it is within my power not to make that judgment.
pages.abbreviated: When something external happens, let the part affected complain if it wishes. You are not harmed unless you judge the event to be evil, and you can choose not to make that judgment.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 12
pages.original: Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, thou must be good; not for any man's sake, but for thine own nature's sake; as if either gold, or the emerald, or purple, should ever be saying to themselves, Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, I must still be an emerald, and I must keep my colour.
pages.familiar: Whatever anyone does or says, you must remain good—not for anyone else’s sake, but because that is your nature. Gold, emeralds, and purple cloth might as well say to themselves, “Whatever anyone does or says, I will remain gold, remain an emerald, and keep my color.”
pages.abbreviated: Remain good regardless of what anyone does or says because goodness is your nature, just as gold remains gold and an emerald remains an emerald regardless of what happens around them.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 13
pages.original: This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power. But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear. For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it. But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing. Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.
pages.familiar: This can always be my comfort and safety: my ruling mind will not create trouble for itself on its own. It will not frighten itself or drive itself into desperate desire. If someone else can force it to fear or grieve, they are free to use that power. But unless my own false judgment persuades me to feel that way, there is no fear. As for the body, why should I make its pain my mind’s pain? If the body can fear or complain, let it. But the soul—the part that can truly experience fear or grief—admits them only according to its own ideas and judgments. I can make sure it accepts none of these. The mind is sufficient to itself. If it does not make itself dependent on something else, nothing else can trouble or obstruct it.
pages.abbreviated: Your ruling mind need not frighten or distress itself; others can affect it only if your own false judgment allows fear or grief. The body's pain need not become the mind's pain, because a self-sufficient mind cannot be troubled or obstructed unless it makes itself dependent on something else.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 14
pages.original: What is εὐδαιμονία, or happiness: but ἀγαθὸς δαίμων, or, a good dæmon, or spirit? What then dost thou do here, O opinion? By the Gods I adjure thee, that thou get thee gone, as thou earnest: for I need thee not. Thou earnest indeed unto me according to thy ancient wonted manner. It is that, that all men have ever been subject unto. That thou camest therefore I am not angry with thee, only begone, now that I have found thee what thou art.
pages.familiar: What is happiness but having a good spirit within you? So what are you doing here, opinion? I call on you to leave, just as you came. I do not need you. You came to me in your usual old way, as you have come to everyone. I am not angry that you arrived. Now that I know what you are, simply go.
pages.abbreviated: Happiness is having a good spirit within, so dismiss opinions that arrive and stir you up. Once you recognize what they are, let them leave without anger or dependence.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 15
pages.original: Is any man so foolish as to fear change, to which all things that once were not owe their being? And what is it, that is more pleasing and more familiar to the nature of the universe? How couldst thou thyself use thy ordinary hot baths, should not the wood that heateth them first be changed? How couldst thou receive any nourishment from those things that thou hast eaten, if they should not be changed? Can anything else almost (that is useful and profitable) be brought to pass without change? How then dost not thou perceive, that for thee also, by death, to come to change, is a thing of the very same nature, and as necessary for the nature of the universe?
pages.familiar: Is anyone foolish enough to fear change, when everything that now exists came into being through change? What could be more natural and familiar to the universe? You could not enjoy a hot bath unless the wood that heats it changed into fire. You could not be nourished by what you eat unless it changed within you. Almost nothing useful can happen without change. So why do you not see that your own death and transformation are just as natural, and just as necessary to the universe?
pages.abbreviated: Everything comes into being through change, and nearly every useful process depends on transformation. Therefore your own death and transformation are natural and necessary parts of the universe.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 16
pages.original: Through the substance of the universe, as through a torrent pass all particular bodies, being all of the same nature, and all joint workers with the universe itself as in one of our bodies so many members among themselves. How many such as Chrysippus, how many such as Socrates, how many such as Epictetus, hath the age of the world long since swallowed up and devoured? Let this, be it either men or businesses, that thou hast occasion to think of, to the end that thy thoughts be not distracted and thy mind too earnestly set upon anything, upon every such occasion presently come to thy mind. Of all my thoughts and cares, one only thing shall be the object, that I myself do nothing which to the proper constitution of man, (either in regard of the thing itself, or in regard of the manner, or of the time of doing,) is contrary. The time when thou shalt have forgotten all things, is at hand. And that time also is at hand, when thou thyself shalt be forgotten by all. Whilst thou art, apply thyself to that especially which unto man as he is a mart, is most proper and agreeable, and that is, for a man even to love them that transgress against him. This shall be, if at the same time that any such thing doth happen, thou call to mind, that they are thy kinsmen; that it is through ignorance and against their wills that they sin; and that within a very short while after, both thou and he shall be no more. But above all things, that he hath not done thee any hurt; for that by him thy mind and understanding is not made worse or more vile than it was before.
pages.familiar: All individual bodies pass through the substance of the universe like a current, sharing its nature and working with it as the limbs of one body work together. How many people like Chrysippus, Socrates, and Epictetus has the passing world already swallowed? Let this come to mind whenever a person or a task threatens to scatter your thoughts or take hold of your mind too tightly. Keep one concern above all others: that you do nothing contrary to human nature—in the thing itself, in the way you do it, or in its proper time. The time when you will have forgotten everything is near, and so is the time when everyone will have forgotten you. While you are alive, devote yourself especially to what is most proper to a human being: loving even those who wrong you. Remember that they are your relatives, that they act wrongly through ignorance and against their better will, and that soon both of you will be gone. Above all, remember that they have not truly harmed you, because they have not made your mind or understanding worse than it was before.
pages.abbreviated: All bodies flow through and cooperate with the universe, and even the greatest people have been consumed by time, so keep your thoughts from being scattered by people or tasks. Above all, act in accordance with human nature, love those who wrong you because they are mistaken relatives, and remember that they have not truly harmed you unless they worsened your mind.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 17
pages.original: The nature of the universe, of the common substance of all things as it were of so much wax hath now perchance formed a horse; and then, destroying that figure, hath new tempered and fashioned the matter of it into the form and substance of a tree: then that again into the form and substance of a man: and then that again into some other. Now every one of these doth subsist but for a very little while. As for dissolution, if it be no grievous thing to the chest or trunk, to be joined together; why should it be more grievous to be put asunder?
pages.familiar: The universe keeps reshaping the same shared substance. It may form a horse, then break that shape down and make a tree, then a person, then something else. Each form lasts only briefly. If it is no hardship for parts to come together, why should it be a hardship for them to separate?
pages.abbreviated: The universe continually reshapes the same substance into different forms, each lasting only briefly. If forming parts together is not a hardship, separating them should not be one either.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 18
pages.original: An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death. But were it so, that all anger and passion were so thoroughly quenched in thee, that it were altogether impossible to kindle it any more, yet herein must not thou rest satisfied, but further endeavour by good consequence of true ratiocination, perfectly to conceive and understand, that all anger and passion is against reason. For if thou shalt not be sensible of thine innocence; if that also shall be gone from thee, the comfort of a good conscience, that thou doest all things according to reason: what shouldest thou live any longer for? All things that now thou seest, are but for a moment. That nature, by which all things in the world are administered, will soon bring change and alteration upon them, and then of their substances make other things like unto them: and then soon after others again of the matter and substance of these: that so by these means, the world may still appear fresh and new.
pages.familiar: An angry face is unnatural, and often looks like the face of someone near death. Even if you have completely extinguished your anger, do not stop there. Use clear reasoning to understand that anger and passion go against reason. If you cannot recognize your own innocence, or take comfort in a clear conscience and rational conduct, what are you living for? Everything you see lasts only a moment. Nature will soon change it, turn its substance into something else, and then transform that into something else again, keeping the world fresh and new.
pages.abbreviated: Anger is unnatural and opposed to reason, so extinguishing it is not enough; understand why it must be rejected and rely on innocence, clear conscience, and rational conduct. Everything changes briefly into something else, keeping the world fresh.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 19
pages.original: Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be evil, when he did trespass. For this when thou knowest, thou wilt pity him thou wilt have no occasion either to wonder, or to be angry. For either thou thyself dust yet live in that error and ignorance, as that thou dust suppose either that very thing that he doth, or some other like worldly thing, to be good; and so thou art bound to pardon him if he have done that which thou in the like case wouldst have done thyself. Or if so be that thou dost not any more suppose the same things to be good or evil, that he doth; how canst thou but be gentle unto him that is in an error?
pages.familiar: Whenever someone wrongs another person, first ask what that person believed was good or bad when they acted. Once you understand that, you will feel pity rather than surprise or anger. Perhaps you still make the same mistake, believing that worldly things are good, and would have acted the same way yourself. Then you must forgive them. Or perhaps you no longer share their ideas about good and evil. How could you not be gentle with someone who is mistaken?
pages.abbreviated: When someone does wrong, first understand what they believed was good or bad. If you might have made the same mistake, forgive them; if you know better, be gentle with someone whose judgment is mistaken.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 20
pages.original: Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou wouldst want them, if they were not present. But take heed withal, lest that whilst thou dust settle thy contentment in things present, thou grow in time so to overprize them, as that the want of them (whensoever it shall so fall out) should be a trouble and a vexation unto thee. Wind up thyself into thyself. Such is the nature of thy reasonable commanding part, as that if it exercise justice, and have by that means tranquillity within itself, it doth rest fully satisfied with itself without any other thing.
pages.familiar: Do not imagine future events as though they were happening now. From the things present, choose a few you benefit from most and consider how deeply you would miss them if they were gone. But be careful not to value them so highly that losing them would later distress you. Return into yourself. Your rational ruling part can be fully satisfied when it acts justly and remains peaceful within, needing nothing else.
pages.abbreviated: Do not treat imagined future events as present realities, and value present benefits without making their loss unbearable. Return to yourself, where the rational mind can be satisfied by acting justly and remaining peaceful without needing anything else.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 21
pages.original: Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the last hour. That which thy neighbour hath committed, where the guilt of it lieth, there let it rest. Examine in order whatsoever is spoken. Let thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes. Rejoice thyself with true simplicity, and modesty; and that all middle things between virtue and vice are indifferent unto thee. Finally, love mankind; obey God.
pages.familiar: Strip away assumptions. Restrain unreasonable desires and passions. Stay within the present moment. Examine carefully whatever has happened to you or someone else. Separate each present thing into its form and its material. Remember that your last hour may be near. Let your neighbor's wrongdoing remain where its guilt belongs. Examine each statement in order, tracing both its causes and its effects. Take joy in genuine simplicity and modesty. Treat everything between virtue and vice as indifferent. Finally, love humanity and obey the divine order.
pages.abbreviated: Remove assumptions, control irrational desires, stay present, and examine events, statements, causes, effects, and the distinction between form and material.
