Remember death, leave others' guilt with them, value simplicity and modesty, treat what lies between virtue and vice as indifferent, love humanity, and follow the divine order.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 22
pages.original: All things (saith he) are by certain order and appointment. And what if the elements only. It will suffice to remember, that all things in general are by certain order and appointment: or if it be but few. And as concerning death, that either dispersion, or the atoms, or annihilation, or extinction, or translation will ensue. And as concerning pain, that that which is intolerable is soon ended by death; and that which holds long must needs be tolerable; and that the mind in the meantime (which is all in all) may by way of interclusion, or interception, by stopping all manner of commerce and sympathy with the body, still retain its own tranquillity. Thy understanding is not made worse by it. As for those parts that suffer, let them, if they can, declare their grief themselves. As for praise and commendation, view their mind and understanding, what estate they are in; what kind of things they fly, and what things they seek after: and that as in the seaside, whatsoever was before to be seen, is by the continual succession of new heaps of sand cast up one upon another, soon hid and covered; so in this life, all former things by those which immediately succeed.
pages.familiar: Everything happens according to an order. Even if you cannot explain the whole universe, it is enough to remember that things unfold according to some order. At death there may be separation, dissolution, extinction, or transformation. Pain that cannot be endured soon ends in death; pain that lasts must be bearable. Meanwhile, the mind, which matters most, can stop sharing the body's distress and remain calm. Pain does not make your understanding worse. Let the suffering parts of the body speak for themselves. As for praise, examine the minds of those offering it: what they avoid and what they pursue. Just as waves of sand quickly cover what was once visible on a shore, new events quickly bury everything that came before.
pages.abbreviated: Everything follows an order even when you cannot explain the whole universe, and death may mean separation, dissolution, extinction, or transformation. Unbearable pain soon ends, lasting pain is bearable, and the mind can remain calm without sharing the body's distress; meanwhile, praise and past events quickly disappear beneath new events.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 23
pages.original: Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest thou) seem any great matter unto him? It is not possible, answered he. Then neither will such a one account death a grievous thing? By no means.'
pages.familiar: Someone whose mind is truly great, and who has trained himself to consider all times and all things together, cannot think this brief human life is a very big deal. And such a person cannot regard death as something terrible.
pages.abbreviated: Someone who considers all times and things together sees that a brief human life is insignificant. Such a person therefore does not regard death as terrible.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 24
pages.original: Out of Antisthenes. 'It is a princely thing to do well, and to be ill-spoken of. It is a shameful thing that the face should be subject unto the mind, to be put into what shape it will, and to be dressed by it as it will; and that the mind should not bestow so much care upon herself, as to fashion herself, and to dress herself as best becometh her.'
pages.familiar: It is a royal thing to do what is right while being spoken of badly. It is shameful for the face to let the mind shape and decorate it however it wants, while the mind gives so little care to shaping and tending itself as it should.
pages.abbreviated: It is noble to do what is right despite being spoken of badly. It is shameful to let the face be shaped by the mind's whims while neglecting to shape and care for the mind itself.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 25
pages.original: Out of several poets and comics. 'It will but little avail thee, to turn thine anger and indignation upon the things themselves that have fallen across unto thee. For as for them, they are not sensible of it, &c. Thou shalt but make thyself a laughing-stock; both unto the Gods and men, &c. Our life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn; one is yet standing and another is down, &c. But if so be that I and my children be neglected by the gods, there is some reason even for that, &c. As long as right and equity is of my side, &c. Not to lament with them, not to tremble, &c.'
pages.familiar: It will do you little good to direct your anger at the things that have happened to you. They cannot feel your anger. You will only make yourself ridiculous to gods and people. Our lives are cut down like ripe grain: one stalk remains standing while another falls. If the gods neglect me and my children, there may still be a reason for it. As long as justice and fairness are on my side, I have no cause to complain, tremble, or mourn with those who do.
pages.abbreviated: Anger at events is useless because they cannot feel it and only make you look ridiculous. Life and death come according to a larger order, so if justice and fairness are on your side, you have no reason to complain, tremble, or mourn.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 26
pages.original: Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c. For thus in very truth stands the case, O ye men of Athens. What place or station soever a man either hath chosen to himself, judging it best for himself; or is by lawful authority put and settled in, therein do I think (all appearance of danger notwithstanding) that he should continue, as one who feareth neither death, nor anything else, so much as he feareth to commit anything that is vicious and shameful, &c. But, O noble sir, consider I pray, whether true generosity and true happiness, do not consist in somewhat else rather, than in the preservation either of our, or other men's lives. For it is not the part of a man that is a man indeed, to desire to live long or to make much of his life whilst he liveth: but rather (he that is such) will in these things wholly refer himself unto the Gods, and believing that which every woman can tell him, that no man can escape death; the only thing that he takes thought and care for is this, that what time he liveth, he may live as well and as virtuously as he can possibly, &c. To look about, and with the eyes to follow the course of the stars and planets as though thou wouldst run with them; and to mind perpetually the several changes of the elements one into another. For such fancies and imaginations, help much to purge away the dross and filth of this our earthly life,' &c. That also is a fine passage of Plato's, where he speaketh of worldly things in these words: 'Thou must also as from some higher place look down, as it were, upon the things of this world, as flocks, armies, husbandmen's labours, marriages, divorces, generations, deaths: the tumults of courts and places of judicatures; desert places; the several nations of barbarians, public festivals, mournings, fairs, markets.' How all things upon earth are pell-mell; and how miraculously things contrary one to another, concur to the beauty and perfection of this universe.
pages.familiar: A just answer would be this: You are mistaken if you think a worthwhile person should treat life or death as the greatest danger. His real concern should be whether his actions are just or unjust, worthy or shameful. Wherever a person has rightly chosen to stand, or has been lawfully placed, he should remain there despite apparent danger, fearing wrongdoing more than death or anything else. True generosity and happiness consist in more than preserving our own lives or anyone else's. A truly human person does not cling to living long or make life precious merely because it is life. He leaves its length to the gods, knowing that no one escapes death, and cares only to live as well and virtuously as possible. Look up at the stars and the constant transformations of the elements; such thoughts help clear away the dirt of earthly life. From a higher viewpoint, look down on everything below: herds, armies, farm work, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, courts, wilderness, foreign peoples, celebrations, grief, fairs, and markets. Everything is mixed together, yet opposing things somehow combine to create the beauty and perfection of the whole universe.
pages.abbreviated: A worthwhile person should fear injustice and shame, not life or death, and should remain where duty and law place him despite apparent danger. True generosity and happiness mean living virtuously without clinging to length of life, while viewing the world's constant changes and mixtures from above as parts of one beautiful and perfect whole.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 27
pages.original: To look back upon things of former ages, as upon the manifold changes and conversions of several monarchies and commonwealths. We may also foresee things future, for they shall all be of the same kind; neither is it possible that they should leave the tune, or break the concert that is now begun, as it were, by these things that are now done and brought to pass in the world. It comes all to one therefore, whether a man be a spectator of the things of this life but forty years, or whether he see them ten thousand years together: for what shall he see more? 'And as for those parts that came from the earth, they shall return unto the earth again; and those that came from heaven, they also shall return unto those heavenly places.' Whether it be a mere dissolution and unbinding of the manifold intricacies and entanglements of the confused atoms; or some such dispersion of the simple and incorruptible elements... 'With meats and drinks and divers charms, they seek to divert the channel, that they might not die. Yet must we needs endure that blast of wind that cometh from above, though we toil and labour never so much.'
pages.familiar: Look back at history: kingdoms rise, change, and disappear. The future will bring more of the same. The world will keep unfolding in its established rhythm, so whether you watch it for forty years or ten thousand, you will see essentially the same patterns. What comes from the earth returns to the earth, and what comes from the heavens returns there. Whether everything is simply breaking apart into its basic elements or being dispersed in some other way, we still have to accept the force of nature's wind, no matter how hard we struggle to avoid it.
pages.abbreviated: History repeats its patterns of rise, change, and disappearance, whether observed for decades or millennia. Whatever the universe’s exact process, we must accept nature’s force rather than struggle against it.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 28
pages.original: He hath a stronger body, and is a better wrestler than I. What then? Is he more bountiful? is he more modest? Doth he bear all adverse chances with more equanimity: or with his neighbour's offences with more meekness and gentleness than I?
pages.familiar: He has a stronger body and is a better athlete than I am. So what? Is he more generous? More modest? Does he meet bad luck more calmly, or respond to other people's offenses with more patience and kindness?
pages.abbreviated: Physical strength and athletic ability matter less than generosity, modesty, calmness under misfortune, and patience with others’ offenses.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 29
pages.original: Where the matter may be effected agreeably to that reason, which both unto the Gods and men is common, there can be no just cause of grief or sorrow. For where the fruit and benefit of an action well begun and prosecuted according to the proper constitution of man may be reaped and obtained, or is sure and certain, it is against reason that any damage should there be suspected. In all places, and at all times, it is in thy power religiously to embrace whatsoever by God's appointment is happened unto thee, and justly to converse with those men, whom thou hast to do with, and accurately to examine every fancy that presents itself, that nothing may slip and steal in, before thou hast rightly apprehended the true nature of it.
pages.familiar: When you act in a way that agrees with the reason shared by human beings and the universe, there is no good reason for grief. If you begin and carry out an action in the way human nature requires, its proper benefit is already within reach, so there is no sense in expecting harm. Wherever you are and whatever happens, you can accept it with reverence and deal fairly with the people around you. Examine every impression that enters your mind, so nothing slips past before you understand what it really is.
pages.abbreviated: When you act according to shared human and universal reason, the action’s proper benefit is already present, so grief and fear of harm are misplaced. Accept circumstances reverently, treat others fairly, and examine every impression before accepting it.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 30
pages.original: Look not about upon other men's minds and understandings; but look right on forwards whither nature, both that of the universe, in those things that happen unto thee; and thine in particular, in those things that are done by thee: doth lead, and direct thee. Now every one is bound to do that, which is consequent and agreeable to that end which by his true natural constitution he was ordained unto. As for all other things, they are ordained for the use of reasonable creatures: as in all things we see that that which is worse and inferior, is made for that which is better. Reasonable creatures, they are ordained one for another. That therefore which is chief in every man's constitution, is, that he intend the common good. The second is, that he yield not to any lusts and motions of the flesh. For it is the part and privilege of the reasonable and intellective faculty, that she can so bound herself, as that neither the sensitive, nor the appetitive faculties, may not anyways prevail upon her. For both these are brutish. And therefore over both she challengeth mastery, and cannot anyways endure, if in her right temper, to be subject unto either. And this indeed most justly. For by nature she was ordained to command all in the body. The third thing proper to man by his constitution, is, to avoid all rashness and precipitancy; and not to be subject to error. To these things then, let the mind apply herself and go straight on, without any distraction about other things, and she hath her end, and by consequent her happiness.
pages.familiar: Do not keep measuring yourself against other people's minds. Look straight ahead to where nature leads: the nature of the universe in what happens to you, and your own nature in what you choose to do. Everyone is meant to act according to their true purpose. For human beings, that purpose is first to serve the common good. Second, do not let bodily urges rule you; reason is meant to govern them. Third, avoid haste and carelessness, and do not surrender to error. Let your mind stay focused on these things without being pulled in every direction. Then you will be doing what you were made to do, and that is where happiness lies.
pages.abbreviated: Do not compare yourself with others; follow universal nature in what happens and human nature in what you choose. Serve the common good, govern bodily urges with reason, avoid haste and error, and remain focused on these duties, for fulfilling them is happiness.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 31
pages.original: As one who had lived, and were now to die by right, whatsoever is yet remaining, bestow that wholly as a gracious overplus upon a virtuous life. Love and affect that only, whatsoever it be that happeneth, and is by the fates appointed unto thee. For what can be more reasonable? And as anything doth happen unto thee by way of cross, or calamity, call to mind presently and set before thine eyes, the examples of some other men, to whom the self-same thing did once happen likewise. Well, what did they? They grieved; they wondered; they complained. And where are they now? All dead and gone. Wilt thou also be like one of them? Or rather leaving to men of the world (whose life both in regard of themselves, and them that they converse with, is nothing but mere mutability; or men of as fickle minds, as fickle bodies; ever changing and soon changed themselves) let it be thine only care and study, how to make a right use of all such accidents. For there is good use to be made of them, and they will prove fit matter for thee to work upon, if it shall be both thy care and thy desire, that whatsoever thou doest, thou thyself mayst like and approve thyself for it. And both these, see, that thou remember well, according as the diversity of the matter of the action that thou art about shall require. Look within; within is the fountain of all good. Such a fountain, where springing waters can never fail, so thou dig still deeper and deeper.
pages.familiar: Live as someone who has already lived enough and is now ready to die, and treat whatever time remains as a gift to spend on a virtuous life. Love whatever happens to you, because it is the material life has given you to work with. When misfortune comes, remember others who faced the same thing. They suffered, were shocked, and complained. Where are they now? Dead and gone. Do not become trapped in the same turmoil. Instead, focus on using every event well. Any circumstance can become useful material if your aim is to act in a way you yourself can respect. Remember this, and apply it according to the situation. Look within yourself; that is where all good begins. It is a spring that will never run dry if you keep digging deeper.
pages.abbreviated: Treat the remaining time of life as a gift for virtuous action and love circumstances as the material available to you. Rather than sharing the turmoil of those who suffered before you, use every event well and draw good from the inexhaustible source within yourself.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 32
pages.original: Thou must use thyself also to keep thy body fixed and steady; free from all loose fluctuant either motion, or posture. And as upon thy face and looks, thy mind hath easily power over them to keep them to that which is grave and decent; so let it challenge the same power over the whole body also. But so observe all things in this kind, as that it be without any manner of affectation.
pages.familiar: Train yourself to keep your body steady and composed, without restless movements or careless posture. If your mind can keep your face and expression serious and decent, it should have the same authority over your whole body. Just make sure your composure is natural, never theatrical.
pages.abbreviated: Train your body to remain steady, composed, and properly controlled, as your mind controls your expression. Keep this composure natural rather than theatrical.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 33
pages.original: The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's, than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing may cast him down.
pages.familiar: The art of living well is more like wrestling than dancing. A dancer moves through planned steps; a wrestler must be ready for whatever comes. Both require preparation, but the wrestler's practice teaches you to meet anything without being knocked down.
pages.abbreviated: Living well is like wrestling rather than dancing: it requires preparation, but also readiness for whatever happens. Practice should teach you to meet events without being knocked down.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 34
pages.original: Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire. For then neither wilt thou see cause to complain of them that offend against their wills; or find any want of their applause, if once thou dost but penetrate into the true force and ground both of their opinions, and of their desires. 'No soul (saith he) is willingly bereft of the truth,' and by consequent, neither of justice, or temperance, or kindness, and mildness; nor of anything that is of the same kind. It is most needful that thou shouldst always remember this. For so shalt thou be far more gentle and moderate towards all men.
pages.familiar: Keep considering what kind of people they are whose approval you want, and what condition their minds are in. Then you will neither resent people who hurt you unintentionally nor feel deprived when they withhold their praise. No one willingly gives up truth, justice, self-control, kindness, or gentleness. Remember that, and you will treat everyone with greater patience and moderation.
pages.abbreviated: Consider the character and mental condition of those whose approval you seek. Then you will neither resent unintended harm nor feel deprived by withheld praise, and you will treat everyone with more patience and moderation.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 35
pages.original: What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind, that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all, can be made worse. For neither in regard of the substance of it, nor in regard of the end of it (which is, to intend the common good) can it alter and corrupt it. This also of Epicurus mayst thou in most pains find some help of, that it is 'neither intolerable, nor eternal;' so thou keep thyself to the true bounds and limits of reason and give not way to opinion. This also thou must consider, that many things there be, which oftentimes unsensibly trouble and vex thee, as not armed against them with patience, because they go not ordinarily under the name of pains, which in very deed are of the same nature as pain; as to slumber unquietly, to suffer heat, to want appetite: when therefore any of these things make thee discontented, check thyself with these words: Now hath pain given thee the foil; thy courage hath failed thee.
pages.familiar: Whatever pain you are in, remember at once that it is nothing shameful and cannot damage the part of you that governs everything: your understanding. It cannot corrupt that part either by what it is or by its outcome, since your purpose remains the common good. You may also find help in the thought that pain is neither unbearable nor endless, as long as you stay within reason and do not make it worse with your judgments. Remember, too, that many things quietly upset us even though we do not call them pain: restless sleep, excessive heat, or a lack of appetite. When one of these makes you miserable, tell yourself: Pain has beaten you this time; your courage gave way.
pages.abbreviated: Pain is not shameful and cannot corrupt the governing mind or prevent its commitment to the common good; it is also neither unbearable nor endless unless judgment worsens it. Even ordinary discomforts can defeat courage, so acknowledge when your own resilience has failed.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 36
pages.original: Take heed lest at any time thou stand so affected, though towards unnatural evil men, as ordinary men are commonly one towards another.
pages.familiar: Be careful that, even when dealing with truly unnatural and vicious people, you do not become like ordinary people are with one another.
pages.abbreviated: Even when dealing with genuinely vicious and unnatural people, do not become like ordinary people in their treatment of one another.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 37
pages.original: How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so extraordinary a disposition? For that he died more gloriously, that he disputed with the Sophists more subtilty; that he watched in the frost more assiduously; that being commanded to fetch innocent Salaminius, he refused to do it more generously; all this will not serve. Nor that he walked in the streets, with much gravity and majesty, as was objected unto him by his adversaries: which nevertheless a man may well doubt of, whether it were so or no, or, which above all the rest, if so be that it were true, a man would well consider of, whether commendable, or dis-commendable. The thing therefore that we must inquire into, is this; what manner of soul Socrates had: whether his disposition was such; as that all that he stood upon, and sought after in this world, was barely this, that he might ever carry himself justly towards men, and holily towards the Gods. Neither vexing himself to no purpose at the wickedness of others, nor yet ever condescending to any man's evil fact, or evil intentions, through either fear, or engagement of friendship. Whether of those things that happened unto him by God's appointment, he neither did wonder at any when it did happen, or thought it intolerable in the trial of it. And lastly, whether he never did suffer his mind to sympathise with the senses, and affections of the body. For we must not think that Nature hath so mixed and tempered it with the body, as that she hath not power to circumscribe herself, and by herself to intend her own ends and occasions.
pages.familiar: How do we know that Socrates was truly exceptional, with such an extraordinary character? Was it because he died more honorably, argued more cleverly with the Sophists, endured the cold more patiently, or bravely refused to arrest an innocent man when ordered to do so? None of that proves it. Nor does the grave, dignified way his enemies said he walked through the streets—if that was even true, and if it was, whether it deserves praise or blame. What we should ask is this: what kind of soul did Socrates have? Was everything he pursued in life simply to act justly toward people and reverently toward the gods? Did he avoid pointless anger at other people's wrongdoing, while never excusing anyone's evil actions or intentions out of fear or friendship? Did he accept whatever happened by divine order without being surprised when it arrived or finding it unbearable while enduring it? And did he keep his mind from being dragged along by the body's sensations and passions? Nature could not have joined the mind to the body so completely that the mind has no power to set its own limits and pursue its own purposes.
pages.abbreviated: Socrates’ greatness is not proved by his death, clever arguments, endurance, or outward dignity, but by the character of his soul. Ask whether he pursued justice and reverence, rejected anger without excusing evil, accepted what happened without surprise or resistance, and kept his mind independent of bodily passions.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 38
pages.original: For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very divine man, and yet be altogether unknown. This thou must ever be mindful of, as of this also, that a man's true happiness doth consist in very few things. And that although thou dost despair, that thou shalt ever be a good either logician, or naturalist, yet thou art never the further off by it from being either liberal, or modest, or charitable, or obedient unto God.
pages.familiar: A person can be deeply admirable, almost godlike, and still remain completely unknown. Remember this too: real happiness depends on very few things. Even if you give up hope of ever becoming an expert logician or scientist, you are no further from being generous, modest, compassionate, or obedient to God.
pages.abbreviated: A person can be deeply admirable without anyone knowing it. Happiness requires little, and lacking expertise in logic or science does not prevent generosity, modesty, compassion, or obedience to God.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 39
pages.original: Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy pampered mass of flesh. For what in either of these or the like cases should hinder the mind to retain her own rest and tranquillity, consisting both in the right judgment of those things that happen unto her, and in the ready use of all present matters and occasions? So that her judgment may say, to that which is befallen her by way of cross: this thou art in very deed, and according to thy true nature: notwithstanding that in the judgment of opinion thou dust appear otherwise: and her discretion to the present object; thou art that, which I sought for. For whatsoever it be, that is now present, shall ever be embraced by me as a fit and seasonable object, both for my reasonable faculty, and for my sociable, or charitable inclination to work upon. And that which is principal in this matter, is that it may be referred either unto the praise of God, or to the good of men. For either unto God or man, whatsoever it is that doth happen in the world hath in the ordinary course of nature its proper reference; neither is there anything, that in regard of nature is either new, or reluctant and intractable, but all things both usual and easy.
pages.familiar: You can live out your time freely, cheerfully, and without being forced by anything, even if people condemn you loudly and wild animals tear apart your body. What could prevent your mind from keeping its calm in either case? Its peace comes from judging events correctly and making good use of whatever is in front of it. When something painful happens, judgment can say: this is truly what you are, according to your nature, even if public opinion makes you look different. And practical wisdom can say to the present moment: you are exactly what I needed. Whatever is happening now, I can accept as the right material and the right opportunity for reason and for concern for others. Most importantly, it can be directed either toward honoring God or benefiting people. Everything that happens in the world naturally relates to one of those ends. Nothing is unnatural, unprecedented, or impossible to work with; everything is familiar and workable.
pages.abbreviated: Even condemnation, violence, or death cannot prevent a calm mind that judges events correctly and uses them well. Every present circumstance is workable material for reason, concern for others, honoring God, or benefiting people; nothing that happens is truly foreign or impossible to use.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 40
pages.original: Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day: never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
pages.familiar: A person has reached a mature way of living when each day is spent as though it were the last: never overheated and ruled by passion, but never numb or senseless either, and free from every kind of pretense.
pages.abbreviated: Maturity means living each day as though it were the last: neither ruled by passion nor numb and senseless, and free from pretense.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 41
pages.original: Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou that art one of those sinners thyself? A very ridiculous thing it is, that any man should dispense with vice and wickedness in himself, which is in his power to restrain; and should go about to suppress it in others, which is altogether impossible.
pages.familiar: The immortal gods have endured age after age of sinners without becoming angry, and they still care for them and provide what they need. Yet you, who will live only a moment—and are a sinner yourself—become furious as though you could tolerate them no longer? It is absurd to excuse in yourself a vice you could restrain, then try to eliminate it in others when that is completely beyond your power.
pages.abbreviated: The gods patiently care for sinners across the ages, while you, who live briefly and sin yourself, become furious with others. It is absurd to excuse a vice in yourself that you could restrain while trying to eliminate it in others, where you have no power.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 42
pages.original: What object soever, our reasonable and sociable faculty doth meet with, that affords nothing either for the satisfaction of reason, or for the practice of charity, she worthily doth think unworthy of herself.
pages.familiar: Whenever our rational and social nature meets something that offers nothing for clear thinking or for helping others, it rightly considers that thing beneath its attention.
pages.abbreviated: When something contributes neither to clear reasoning nor to helping others, our rational and social nature rightly regards it as beneath attention.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 43
pages.original: When thou hast done well, and another is benefited by thy action, must thou like a very fool look for a third thing besides, as that it may appear unto others also that thou hast done well, or that thou mayest in time, receive one good turn for another? No man useth to be weary of that which is beneficial unto him. But every action according to nature, is beneficial. Be not weary then of doing that which is beneficial unto thee, whilst it is so unto others.
pages.familiar: When you have done something good and someone has benefited, why act like a fool and look for a third reward—public recognition that you did well, or the promise of receiving a favor in return? No one grows tired of what genuinely benefits them. Every action that follows nature is beneficial. So do not grow tired of doing what benefits you while it benefits others too.
pages.abbreviated: After doing good and benefiting someone, do not seek the extra reward of recognition or repayment. Actions that follow nature benefit both you and others, so continue doing them without growing tired.

pages.label: Book VII · Section 44
pages.original: The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon the creation of the world. Now since that time, whatsoever it is, that is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and first deliberation: or if so be that this ruling rational part of the world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of his particular care and providence. This often thought upon, will much conduce to thy tranquillity.
pages.familiar: Before the universe was created, its nature must have determined what it would do; everything that has happened since has followed from that first decision. And if the rational power governing the world takes particular care of individual things, surely its special concern is for its rational and most important creatures. Reflecting on this often can bring you peace.
pages.abbreviated: The universe’s original nature determined its course, and its rational governing power continues to care especially for rational creatures. Frequent reflection on this can bring peace.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 1
pages.original: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life. For both unto others, and to thyself especially, it is well known, that thou hast done many things contrary to that perfection of life. Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and credit of a philosopher. And to it also is thy calling and profession repugnant. If therefore thou dost truly understand, what it is that is of moment indeed; as for thy fame and credit, take no thought or care for that: let it suffice thee if all the rest of thy life, be it more or less, thou shalt live as thy nature requireth, or according to the true and natural end of thy making. Take pains therefore to know what it is that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee. Thou hast already had sufficient experience, that of those many things that hitherto thou hast erred and wandered about, thou couldst not find happiness in any of them. Not in syllogisms, and logical subtilties, not in wealth, not in honour and reputation, not in pleasure. In none of all these. Wherein then is it to be found? In the practice of those things, which the nature of man, as he is a man, doth require. How then shall he do those things? if his dogmata, or moral tenets and opinions (from which all motions and actions do proceed), be right and true. Which be those dogmata? Those that concern that which is good or evil, as that there is nothing truly good and beneficial unto man, but that which makes him just, temperate, courageous, liberal; and that there is nothing truly evil and hurtful unto man, but that which causeth the contrary effects.
pages.familiar: This can also protect you from vanity: remember that you are not in a position to claim the praise given to someone who has lived as a philosopher all his life, or at least since youth. You and everyone else know that you have often lived contrary to that ideal. Your course has become confused, and recovering the name and reputation of a philosopher will be difficult. Your profession makes the claim even harder. If you understand what truly matters, then stop worrying about fame and reputation. Let it be enough that, for whatever time remains, you live as your nature requires and fulfill the purpose for which you were made. Work to discover what that is, and let nothing else distract you. You have already learned that happiness was not found in the things you chased before—not in logical puzzles, wealth, honor, reputation, or pleasure. Where is it found, then? In doing what human nature requires. And how can you do that? By holding true moral beliefs, because every action begins there. These beliefs concern good and evil: nothing is truly good for a person except what makes them just, self-controlled, brave, and generous; and nothing is truly harmful except what produces the opposite qualities.
pages.abbreviated: Do not claim the reputation of a lifelong philosopher when you know you have often lived against that ideal; let go of fame and live according to human nature for the time remaining. Happiness lies in actions grounded in true moral beliefs: justice, self-control, courage, and generosity are good, while their opposites are harmful.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 2
pages.original: Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself; How will this when it is done agree with me? Shall I have no occasion to repent of it? Yet a very little while and I am dead and gone; and all things are at end. What then do I care for more than this, that my present action whatsoever it be, may be the proper action of one that is reasonable; whose end is, the common good; who in all things is ruled and governed by the same law of right and reason, by which God Himself is.
pages.familiar: Before every action, ask yourself: how will I feel about this once it is done? Will I have reason to regret it? Soon enough I will be dead, and everything will be over. What matters then except that whatever I am doing now should be the fitting action of a reasonable person—someone whose purpose is the common good, and who is guided in everything by the same law of justice and reason that governs God?
pages.abbreviated: Before acting, ask whether you will regret it after death, and choose what a reasonable person devoted to the common good and guided by justice and reason would do.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 3
pages.original: Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so far did their slavery extend.
pages.familiar: Alexander, Gaius, Pompey—what were they to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? Those philosophers understood the true nature of things, their causes, and their subjects, and so they had power over themselves. The others were slaves only to the extent that they were mistaken.
pages.abbreviated: Great rulers had no power over philosophers who understood reality, its causes, and their own subjects. They were slaves only insofar as they were mistaken.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 4
pages.original: What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang thyself. First; let it not trouble thee. For all things both good and evil: come to pass according to the nature and general condition of the universe, and within a very little while, all things will be at an end; no man will be remembered: as now of Africanus (for example) and Augustus it is already come to pass. Then secondly; fix thy mind upon the thing itself; look into it, and remembering thyself, that thou art bound nevertheless to be a good man, and what it is that thy nature requireth of thee as thou art a man, be not diverted from what thou art about, and speak that which seemeth unto thee most just: only speak it kindly, modestly, and without hypocrisy.
pages.familiar: They have acted this way before, and they will keep doing so, even if you destroy yourself over it. First, do not let it trouble you. Good and bad events arise from the nature and order of the universe, and soon everything will be over. No one is remembered forever; even Africanus and Augustus are already fading from memory. Second, focus on what actually happened. Remember that you are still bound to be a good person, and ask what your human nature requires of you. Do not abandon your task. Say what seems most just to you—but say it kindly, modestly, and honestly.
pages.abbreviated: People will repeat their behavior, and destroying yourself over it will not change them; events arise from the universe and soon pass, while even famous people fade from memory. Focus on what happened, remain good, and state what seems just kindly, modestly, and honestly.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 5
pages.original: That which the nature of the universe doth busy herself about, is; that which is here, to transfer it thither, to change it, and thence again to take it away, and to carry it to another place. So that thou needest not fear any new thing. For all things are usual and ordinary; and all things are disposed by equality.
pages.familiar: The universe is always changing what is here: moving it somewhere else, transforming it, then taking it away and carrying it elsewhere. So do not fear something entirely new. Everything follows familiar patterns, and everything is arranged with balance.
pages.abbreviated: The universe continually transforms, relocates, and removes things, but nothing is wholly new because everything follows familiar and balanced patterns.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 6
pages.original: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain. Secondly, when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only, and that it desireth nothing, and flieth from nothing, bet what is in its own power to compass or avoid. And lastly, when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature. For it is part of it; even as the nature of any one leaf, is part of the common nature of all plants and trees. But that the nature of a leaf, is part of a nature both unreasonable and unsensible, and which in its proper end may be hindered; or, which is servile and slavish: whereas the nature of man is part of a common nature which cannot be hindered, and which is both reasonable and just. From whence also it is, that according to the worth of everything, she doth make such equal distribution of all things, as of duration, substance form, operation, and of events and accidents. But herein consider not whether thou shalt find this equality in everything absolutely and by itself; but whether in all the particulars of some one thing taken together, and compared with all the particulars of some other thing, and them together likewise.
pages.familiar: Every living thing is fulfilled when it follows its own proper course. A rational person is fulfilled by refusing to accept as true anything false or uncertain; by directing every choice and action toward the common good; by desiring and avoiding only what lies within their power; and by willingly accepting whatever the nature of the whole assigns to them. We are part of that whole, just as a leaf is part of the nature of every plant and tree. But a leaf belongs to a nature that is mindless and can be hindered; human beings belong to a nature that is rational, just, and not ultimately defeated. That is why the whole distributes time, matter, form, activity, and circumstances in proportion. Do not ask whether this balance appears in every single thing by itself. Look instead at the complete pattern of one life compared with the complete pattern of another.
pages.abbreviated: A rational person is fulfilled by rejecting false or uncertain beliefs, directing action toward the common good, wanting or avoiding only what lies within their power, and accepting what the whole assigns. Humans are rational, just parts of a larger whole, so judge life’s balance by complete lives and patterns rather than isolated events.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 7
pages.original: Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful; but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?
pages.familiar: You have no time or opportunity to read? Then you still have time to practice: not to harm yourself, to resist being ruled by physical pleasures and pains, to rise above the need for praise, and not only to avoid anger toward people who are thoughtless or ungrateful, but to keep caring about them and their well-being.
pages.abbreviated: Even without time to read, you can practice not harming yourself, resisting bodily pleasures and pains, rising above the need for praise, and caring for thoughtless or ungrateful people rather than becoming angry with them.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 8
pages.original: Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life, either in public before others, or in private by thyself.
pages.familiar: From now on, stop complaining about the difficulties of life among powerful and demanding people—whether you complain publicly or only to yourself.
pages.abbreviated: Stop complaining, privately or publicly, about the difficulties of living among powerful and demanding people.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 9
pages.original: Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure: no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
pages.familiar: Regret is blaming yourself inwardly for neglecting or failing to do something useful. Whatever is good is useful, and an honest, virtuous person should value it accordingly. But no honest, virtuous person has ever regretted giving up a bodily pleasure. Bodily pleasure, then, is neither truly good nor truly useful.
pages.abbreviated: Regret concerns failing to do something useful, and whatever is good is useful. Since no virtuous person regrets giving up bodily pleasure, such pleasure is neither truly good nor useful.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 10
pages.original: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.
pages.familiar: What is this thing, in itself and apart from your reaction to it? What is it made of? What is its material and its use? What gives it its form and brings it about? What purpose does it serve in the world, and how long will it last? Examine everything that comes before you this way.
pages.abbreviated: Examine each thing itself: its material, purpose, form, causes, role in the world, and duration, apart from your reaction to it.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 11
pages.original: When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep, admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?
pages.familiar: When you struggle to get out of bed, remind yourself that acting for the common good is what your own nature—and human nature—requires. Sleeping is something animals do too. What could be more natural, more fitting, or more satisfying than doing what your nature calls you to do?
pages.abbreviated: Getting up to serve the common good fulfills both your individual and human nature. Sleeping is natural to animals, but acting according to your nature is more fitting and satisfying.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 12
pages.original: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.
pages.familiar: Whenever an impression or thought presents itself, examine it if you can. Ask what it really is, what qualities it has, and reason it through with yourself.
pages.abbreviated: When a thought or impression appears, examine what it really is, what qualities it has, and whether reason supports it.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 13
pages.original: At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself: This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil? as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour, and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus. Now if it be no wonder that a man should have such and such opinions, how can it be a wonder that he should do such and such things? I will remember then, that he cannot but do as he doth, holding those opinions that he doth. Remember, that as it is a shame for any man to wonder that a fig tree should bear figs, so also to wonder that the world should bear anything, whatsoever it is which in the ordinary course of nature it may bear. To a physician also and to a pilot it is a shame either for the one to wonder, that such and such a one should have an ague; or for the other, that the winds should prove Contrary.
pages.familiar: When you first meet someone, remind yourself: What does this person believe is good or bad? What do they think about pain and pleasure, honor and disgrace, life and death? If their beliefs make their views understandable, why be surprised when they act according to them? Remember that they cannot help acting from the beliefs they hold. It would be as foolish to wonder that a fig tree bears figs as to wonder that the world produces whatever naturally follows from it. A doctor should not be surprised that someone has a fever, nor a pilot that the wind turns against them.
pages.abbreviated: People act according to their beliefs about good and bad, pleasure and pain, honor and disgrace, and life and death. Once you understand those beliefs, their actions should not surprise you, just as natural results do not surprise a doctor, pilot, or gardener.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 14
pages.original: Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun. merit, and of thine own understanding.
pages.familiar: Remember that changing your mind when needed, and following someone who can correct you, is just as honorable as discovering the right and fair course on your own. You are responsible only for what lies within your own judgment, understanding, and ability to decide.
pages.abbreviated: Changing your mind and accepting correction is as honorable as discovering the right course yourself. You are responsible only for what lies within your judgment and ability to decide.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 15
pages.original: If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.
pages.familiar: If this were your own action and within your power, would you do it? If it was not, whom are you blaming—the atoms or the gods? Either way, you are thinking irrationally. Blame no one. If you can fix what is wrong, fix it. If you cannot, what purpose does complaining serve? Nothing should be done without a clear purpose.
pages.abbreviated: Blame neither atoms nor gods for what is outside your control. Fix what you can, and if you cannot, stop complaining; every action should have a clear purpose.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 16
pages.original: Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why shouldest thou?
pages.familiar: Whatever dies and falls, wherever and however it dies, does not leave the world. It remains here, changing form, and eventually returns to the elements from which it came. Those are the same elements that make you. When they change, they do not complain. Why should you?
pages.abbreviated: What dies remains in the world by changing form and returning to its elements, the same elements that make you. Since those elements do not complain when they change, neither should you.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 17
pages.original: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.
pages.familiar: Everything exists for some purpose—a horse, a vine, the sun itself. The sun could say, “I was made for something,” and every god has its own proper work. What, then, were you made for? To amuse yourself and chase pleasure? Even ordinary judgment and reason cannot accept that.
pages.abbreviated: Everything has a purpose, including you. Mere amusement and pleasure cannot be your purpose, since even ordinary reason rejects that.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 18
pages.original: Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
pages.familiar: Nature fulfills its purpose not only in the beginning and continuation of everything, but also in its ending and completion.
pages.abbreviated: Nature fulfills its purpose not only by creating and sustaining things, but also by bringing them to their proper ending.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 19
pages.original: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground? So for the bubble; if it continue, what it the better? and if it dissolve, what is it the worse And so is it of a candle too. And so must thou reason with thyself, both in matter of fame, and in matter of death. For as for the body itself, (the subject of death) wouldest thou know the vileness of it? Turn it about that thou mayest behold it the worst sides upwards as well, as in its more ordinary pleasant shape; how doth it look, when it is old and withered? when sick and pained? when in the act of lust, and fornication? And as for fame. This life is short. Both he that praiseth, and he that is praised; he that remembers, and he that is remembered, will soon be dust and ashes. Besides, it is but in one corner of this part of the world that thou art praised; and yet in this corner, thou hast not the joint praises of all men; no nor scarce of any one constantly. And yet the whole earth itself, what is it but as one point, in regard of the whole world?
pages.familiar: Think of a ball thrown into the air. Is it better when it rises, worse when it falls, or harmed when it hits the ground? What does a bubble gain by lasting, or lose by bursting? The same is true of a candle. Think this way about both reputation and death. As for the body itself, the thing that dies, look at it from every angle, including its least appealing ones: old and withered, sick and hurting, or caught up in lust. This life is short. The person who praises and the person praised, the one who remembers and the one remembered, will all soon be dust. And your reputation reaches only one small corner of the world, where you are not even praised by everyone, or perhaps by anyone for long. The whole earth itself is only a point compared with the universe.
pages.abbreviated: Rise, fall, bursting, and death do not make a ball, bubble, candle, or person better or worse; they are simply part of its course. Reputation is brief and limited, the body is vulnerable and unattractive in many ways, and everyone and everything soon becomes dust within the vast universe.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 20
pages.original: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.
pages.familiar: Whatever you are considering, examine the thing itself, the belief you hold about it, what it does, or what it truly means.
pages.abbreviated: Examine whatever you consider directly, including your belief about it, its effects, and its true meaning.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 21
pages.original: Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be so to-day.
pages.familiar: These things happened to you for good reason. Why are you not correcting yourself? But you would rather promise to become good tomorrow than become good today.
pages.abbreviated: What happens may give you reason to correct yourself, yet you keep promising to become good tomorrow instead of doing so today.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 22
pages.original: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
pages.familiar: Will I do it? I will, if the purpose of my action is to help people. Has some difficulty or misfortune come to me? I accept it, remembering the gods and their providence—the source from which everything comes and on which everything depends.
pages.abbreviated: Act when your purpose is to help people, and accept difficulty or misfortune by remembering divine providence as the source and support of everything.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 23
pages.original: By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body: all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life; and every worldly object.
pages.familiar: Judge everything else by one clear example: what is bathing, which takes up so much of our time? Oil, sweat, dirt, and the sticky waste left by ointments, all mixed together—something low and disgusting. Much of life, and nearly everything the world prizes, is like that.
pages.abbreviated: Bathing reveals that even attractive or prized things may consist of something low and disgusting. Much of life, especially what the world values, is like this.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 24
pages.original: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself. So Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself. So Antoninus Pius, Faustina his wife; then Antoninus himself. This is the course of the world. First Celer, Adrianus; then Adrianus himself. And those austere ones; those that foretold other men's deaths; those that were so proud and stately, where are they now? Those austere ones I mean, such as were Charax, and Demetrius the Platonic, and Eudaemon, and others like unto those. They were all but for one day; all dead and gone long since. Some of them no sooner dead, than forgotten. Others soon turned into fables. Of others, even that which was fabulous, is now long since forgotten. This thereafter thou must remember, that whatsoever thou art compounded of, shall soon be dispersed, and that thy life and breath, or thy soul, shall either be no more or shall ranslated (sp.), and appointed to some certain place and station.
pages.familiar: Lucilla buried Verus, and later others buried Lucilla. Secunda buried Maximus, and then Secunda was buried. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, and then Epitynchanus himself. Antoninus Pius buried Faustina, and then Antoninus died. This is how the world goes. The proud, severe, impressive people who once predicted others’ deaths are gone too. They lived for a day, then died. Some were forgotten almost immediately; others became stories, and even those stories eventually disappeared. Remember this: whatever you are made of will soon scatter, and your life or spirit will either end or move on to another place and condition.
pages.abbreviated: People repeatedly bury one another, regardless of their status, wealth, or reputation. Whatever you are made of will soon scatter, and your life or spirit will either end or move into another condition.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 25
pages.original: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the universe; both it, and things that are done in it. In which kind of contemplation three several relations are to be observed The first, to the apparent secondary cause. The Second to the first original cause, God, from whom originally proceeds whatsoever doth happen in the world. The third and last, to them that we live and converse with: what use may be made of it, to their use and benefit.
pages.familiar: A person’s real joy is doing what belongs properly to a human being. That means, first, treating others of our kind with goodwill; resisting the pull of mere pleasure and appetite; seeing through attractive but misleading impressions; and understanding the nature of the universe and everything happening within it. In that understanding, keep three relationships in view: the immediate causes of events, the first source from which everything comes, and the people around you—especially how what happens can be used for their benefit.
pages.abbreviated: Human joy comes from acting humanely: treating others well, resisting pleasure and appetite, seeing through misleading appearances, and understanding the universe, its causes, its source, and how events can benefit those around you.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 26
pages.original: If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil. For all judgment and deliberation; all prosecution, or aversation is from within, whither the sense of evil (except it be let in by opinion) cannot penetrate.
pages.familiar: If pain is an evil, it must be an evil either for the body or for the soul. It cannot be evil for the body by itself, since the body has no judgment of its own. And the soul can preserve its peace and refuse to call pain evil. Every judgment, choice, pursuit, and rejection comes from within. Pain cannot enter that inner judgment unless we let our opinion turn it into harm.
pages.abbreviated: Pain is not evil to the body by itself, because the body cannot judge, and the soul can remain peaceful. Pain harms the inner life only when your judgment chooses to regard it as harmful.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 27
pages.original: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
pages.familiar: Clear away every useless thought and keep telling yourself: if I choose, I can keep wickedness, lust, anxiety, and confusion out of my mind. I can look at everything as it really is and respond to each thing according to its true value. Remember that this power was given to you by nature.
pages.abbreviated: You can keep wickedness, lust, anxiety, and confusion out of your mind, see things as they are, and respond according to their true value. Nature gave you this power.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 28
pages.original: Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking, concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth prescribe.
pages.familiar: Whether you are speaking to a crowd or to one person, let your words be serious and restrained. But do not make a public display of using the precise language reserved for discussing what is truly good, truly honorable, and the emptiness of worldly ambition. Reason may call for truth, but wisdom also calls for modesty.
pages.abbreviated: Speak seriously and with restraint, whether to crowds or individuals. Truth may require precise language about genuine goodness and honor, but wisdom also requires modesty.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 29
pages.original: Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together. Proceed now on to the rest that have been since that of Augustus. Hath death dwelt with them otherwise, though so many and so stately whilst they lived, than it doth use to deal with any one particular man? Consider now the death of a whole kindred and family, as of that of the Pompeys, as that also that useth to be written upon some monuments, HE WAS THE LAST OF HIS OWN KINDRED. O what care did his predecessors take, that they might leave a successor, yet behold at last one or other must of necessity be THE LAST. Here again therefore consider the death of a whole kindred.
pages.familiar: Look at the court of Augustus: his wife, daughter, nephews, sons-in-law, sister, Agrippa, his relatives, servants, friends, and the people who performed sacrifices and divinations. Death took the whole court. Consider everyone who came after Augustus. Though they lived with such wealth and status, did death treat them any differently from one ordinary person? Consider the death of an entire family, like the Pompeys, or the inscription sometimes placed on a tomb: “The last of his family.” His ancestors worked so hard to leave descendants, yet eventually someone must be the last. So consider again the death of an entire family line.
pages.abbreviated: Death took Augustus’s entire court and treated the wealthy and powerful no differently from ordinary people. Entire families and lineages eventually disappear, and someone is always the last.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 30
pages.original: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be, instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.
pages.familiar: Reduce your whole life to the scale of one action. If, in each action, you do what is right to the best of your ability, let that be enough. What can stop you from acting rightly, calmly, and with reverence? Something external may block the particular thing you intended to do. Even then, you can accept the obstacle peacefully and turn your mind toward what is possible. Another action can take the place of the first, and it can fit just as well within this focused way of living.
pages.abbreviated: Focus on doing each action rightly, calmly, and reverently. If an external obstacle prevents your intended action, accept it peacefully and replace it with another possible action that fits the same way of living.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 31
pages.original: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.
pages.familiar: Accept temporary blessings without showing off when they come, and you will be able to let them go easily when they are taken away.
pages.abbreviated: Receive temporary blessings without pride, so you can release them easily when they are taken away.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 32
pages.original: If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body, such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men: or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art, thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a part, as he was before.
pages.familiar: If you saw a hand, foot, or head lying apart from the body, cut off from the rest, you would understand it as a picture of someone who separates himself from what happens, violates the natural bonds between people, or acts without compassion. Whoever you are, you become like that when you cast yourself out of the unity of nature. You were born as a part of the whole, but you have cut yourself away. Still, there is reason for joy: you can be joined again. No other separated part has been given that possibility. This is the greatness of goodness: humanity was made so that we did not need to divide ourselves from the whole, and even after we have cut ourselves off, we can choose to return, grow together again, and take our place among the whole as before.
pages.abbreviated: Separating yourself from nature and other people through selfishness or lack of compassion makes you like a severed body part. Yet humans can rejoin the whole through goodness, because they can choose to return to unity.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 33
pages.original: As almost all her other faculties and properties the nature of the universe hath imparted unto every reasonable creature, so this in particular we have received from her, that as whatsoever doth oppose itself unto her, and doth withstand her in her purposes and intentions, she doth, though against its will and intention, bring it about to herself, to serve herself of it in the execution of her own destinated ends; and so by this though not intended co-operation of it with herself makes it part of herself whether it will or no. So may every reasonable creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed unto itself as its natural end and happiness.
pages.familiar: Just as the nature of the universe has given every rational creature its other abilities, it has also given us the power to turn resistance to our advantage. Whatever stands against nature’s purposes is drawn into its larger work and made to serve it, whether willingly or not. In the same way, whatever obstacles you meet in this mortal life can become the very material you use to move toward the end and happiness proper to your nature.
pages.abbreviated: Nature has given rational beings the ability to turn resistance into useful material. Obstacles in mortal life can therefore serve our natural purpose and happiness.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 34
pages.original: Let not the general representation unto thyself of the wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee. Let not thy mind wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other. But as everything in particular doth happen, put this question unto thyself, and say: What is it that in this present matter, seems unto thee so intolerable? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess it. Then upon this presently call to mind, that neither that which is future, nor that which is past can hurt thee; but that only which is present. (And that also is much lessened, if thou dost lightly circumscribe it:) and then check thy mind if for so little a while, (a mere instant), it cannot hold out with patience.
pages.familiar: Do not trouble yourself by imagining all the misery of mortal life at once. Do not let your mind roam about collecting every difficulty and disaster to which human beings are exposed. When something happens, ask yourself: What exactly seems so unbearable about this? You will be embarrassed to say. Then remember that neither the future nor the past can harm you; only the present can. And even that is greatly reduced when you limit it to its immediate boundaries. Tell yourself that your mind can surely endure this brief moment with patience.
pages.abbreviated: Do not imagine every human misery at once; examine only what is unbearable about the present event. The past and future cannot harm you, and the brief present can be endured when kept within its limits.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 35
pages.original: What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus? O foolery! For what if they did, would their masters be sensible of It? or if sensible, would they be glad of it? or if glad, were these immortal? Was not it appointed unto them also (both men and women,) to become old in time, and then to die? And these once dead, what would become of these former? And when all is done, what is all this for, but for a mere bag of blood and corruption?
pages.familiar: Are Panthea or Pergamus still waiting beside their masters’ tombs? Are Chabrias or Diotimus still beside Hadrian’s? Foolishness. Even if they had remained there, would their masters know it? If they knew, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would those servants live forever? They too were destined to grow old and die. And after they died, what would become of the whole devotion? In the end, what is all this attachment to but a body made of blood and decay?
pages.abbreviated: Devotion to the dead cannot preserve them, please them, or prevent the devoted from aging and dying. In the end, such attachment is attachment to a temporary body of blood and decay.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 36
pages.original: If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and best discretion, saith he.
pages.familiar: If you are sharp-sighted, be sharp-sighted in your judgment and discernment.
pages.abbreviated: Use clear vision for sound judgment and discernment.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 37
