pages.original: In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.
pages.familiar: In the whole human constitution, I see no virtue opposed to justice that could resist it. But I do see one that can resist pleasure and indulgence: self-control.
pages.abbreviated: Justice has no opposing virtue strong enough to resist it, but self-control can resist pleasure and indulgence.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 38
pages.original: If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
pages.familiar: If you can withdraw your judgment about what merely seems harmful or offensive, you are as safe as anyone can be. You may ask, “Safe? Who am I?” Your reason. “But I am not just reason.” Very well. Even so, do not let your reason or understanding admit grief. And if there is some other part of you that suffers, let it recognize its own suffering, if it can.
pages.abbreviated: If you suspend judgment about what seems harmful or offensive, you are as safe as possible. Do not let reason admit grief; if another part of you suffers, let it recognize its own suffering.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 39
pages.original: That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise, whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.
pages.familiar: Whatever obstructs the senses is an evil to our sensitive nature. Whatever obstructs desire and purposeful action is an evil to that same nature. In the same way, whatever obstructs growth is an evil to the living body, and whatever obstructs the mind and understanding is the proper evil of our rational nature. Apply this to yourself. Do pain or pleasure seize you? Let the senses deal with that. Have you encountered an obstacle in what you intended to do? If you acted without allowing for obstacles, then your rational part has truly been struck. But if you had already accepted that anything might happen, you are neither harmed nor truly prevented. No one can hinder what belongs to the mind. Not fire, iron, a tyrant’s power, a slanderous tongue, or anything else can penetrate it.
pages.abbreviated: What obstructs each faculty is its corresponding evil: pain affects the senses, frustrated plans affect reason, and impeded understanding harms the rational nature. But anticipated obstacles do not truly harm or prevent the mind, which nothing can penetrate.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 40
pages.original: If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.
pages.familiar: Once something is rounded and solid, there is no reason to fear that it will change.
pages.abbreviated: What has become rounded and solid has no reason to fear being changed.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 41
pages.original: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according to to true worth of the thing itself.
pages.familiar: Why should I make myself miserable when I have never willingly made anyone else miserable? One person rejoices in one thing, another in something else. As for me, this is my joy: that my understanding remains sound and clear, hostile toward no one and refusing none of the things that belong to human life; that I can look upon everything in the world gently and kindly, accept what comes, and treat each thing according to its true worth.
pages.abbreviated: You need not make yourself miserable when you have not willingly harmed anyone. Your proper joy is keeping your understanding clear and kind, accepting what comes, and judging everything according to its true worth.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 42
pages.original: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning thee, what is it to thee?
pages.familiar: Give this present moment to yourself. Those who chase fame after death forget that the people who come later will be just like the people they find so difficult to tolerate now. They too will be mortal. And in itself, what difference does it make to you if countless people, speaking with countless voices, make a certain sound or hold a certain opinion about you?
pages.abbreviated: Give your attention to the present instead of chasing posthumous fame. Future people will be mortal and difficult like those alive now, and their many opinions ultimately make no difference to you.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 43
pages.original: Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.
pages.familiar: Take me wherever you want; I am not shaken by it. Wherever I am, the spirit within me can remain favorable and content, as long as I keep living and acting in ways that fit my nature.
pages.abbreviated: Take me wherever you wish; I remain unshaken because the spirit within me can stay content wherever I live and act according to my nature.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 44
pages.original: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
pages.familiar: Is this really so important that my soul should suffer for it and become worse—humiliated, disturbed, confused, or afraid? What could possibly deserve that much power over you?
pages.abbreviated: Ask whether the matter is important enough to make your soul worse through humiliation, confusion, disturbance, or fear. Nothing should be granted that much power over you.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 45
pages.original: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable. If therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt. But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee. Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men, thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.
pages.familiar: Nothing can happen to you that is not part of being human. An ox, a vine, and a stone each meet things that belong to their own nature. If nothing can happen to anything except what is ordinary and natural to it, why are you upset? The shared nature of things would not bring you something unbearable. If something outside you causes your grief, remember that it is not the event itself but your judgment about it. You can let go of that judgment whenever you choose. If the problem is within your character, cannot you correct your values and beliefs? If you are troubled because you are not doing what seems right and just, why not choose to do it instead of suffering over it? Perhaps something beyond your control prevents you. Then do not blame yourself for what you cannot accomplish. “But my life is not worth living unless I can accomplish it.” If that is true, then leave this life with kindness and love toward everyone. Even when others stand in your way, you are doing your best when you die still wishing them well.
pages.abbreviated: Nothing happens to you except what belongs to human nature, so events themselves are not unbearable; your judgment makes them painful and can be released. Correct flawed values, do what is just when you can, and if prevented from doing so, do not blame yourself; even death should be met while wishing others well.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 46
pages.original: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy. How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this, hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.
pages.familiar: Remember that your mind becomes unconquerable when it gathers itself and wants nothing except to remain free from force. Even if it resists something unreasonable, it cannot be overcome. How much stronger is it when reason helps it judge clearly? So let your main refuge and defense be a mind free from passion. No one has a stronger, safer fortress. Anyone who does not see this lacks understanding. Anyone who sees it but does not retreat there is choosing misery.
pages.abbreviated: The mind is unconquerable when it wants only freedom from compulsion, and reason makes that refuge stronger. A passion-free mind is the safest fortress; failing to see or use it is a choice of misery.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 47
pages.original: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in the world.
pages.familiar: Hold to the first plain facts as they appear, and do not add your own story. Someone says that a person has spoken badly of you. Fine—that is what was reported. But that you have been harmed was not reported; that is your opinion added on top. You see that your child is sick. You see the sickness, but you do not yet see that the child is in danger of dying. Keep to the first impressions things give you, without adding fears and conclusions from within. Or add only what someone understands about the true nature of everything that happens.
pages.abbreviated: Hold to the plain facts without adding interpretations. Reported insults and visible sickness are not yet proof of harm or death; add only conclusions grounded in an understanding of nature.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 48
pages.original: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame them for it. And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.
pages.familiar: Is the cucumber bitter? Set it aside. Are there brambles in the way? Go around them. That is enough. Do not immediately ask, “Why does the world contain things like this?” Someone who understands nature would laugh at that question, just as a carpenter or shoemaker would laugh if you criticized the scraps in their workshop. They keep those scraps there for a time not because they have nowhere else to put them, but because they are part of the work. The universe has no outside place to discard anything. Its skill is that, within its own limits, it can transform what seems damaged, old, or useless into something new. It needs to seek neither fresh material nor a place to dump what has decayed, because it is sufficient in place, material, and craft.
pages.abbreviated: When something is unpleasant or obstructive, set it aside or go around it without questioning why nature contains it. Like a workshop using scraps, the universe transforms damaged or useless things within its own sufficient material and order.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 49
pages.original: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
pages.familiar: Do not be careless, lazy, loose, or self-indulgent in your actions. Do not be argumentative or difficult with people. Do not let your imagination wander aimlessly. Do not shrink your spirit in shame, or fling it outward in anger. And never let yourself become without a worthwhile task.
pages.abbreviated: Do not act carelessly, lazily, self-indulgently, argumentatively, or aimlessly. Do not contract in shame or lash out in anger, and never remain without a worthwhile task.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 50
pages.original: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure, prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared. She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity, and true simplicity and modesty.
pages.familiar: “They are killing me, cutting me, and covering me with curses.” So what? Can your mind not remain pure, wise, self-controlled, and just? A spring of clear, sweet water remains clear even when someone curses beside it. Even if mud or filth is thrown in, it quickly disperses and the water clears again. It cannot be permanently stained or infected. What must you do to have such an overflowing spring within you instead of a stagnant well? Through constant effort, cultivate real freedom joined with kindness, and genuine simplicity and modesty.
pages.abbreviated: Even amid violence and curses, the mind can remain pure, wise, self-controlled, and just, like clear water that quickly clears after contamination. Cultivate this inner spring through persistent freedom, kindness, simplicity, and modesty.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 51
pages.original: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world. Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything that he doth?
pages.familiar: Anyone who does not understand the world does not understand where they themselves stand. Anyone who does not know what the world is for cannot understand its nature or qualities. And anyone ignorant of those things cannot know what they were made for. What should we think of someone who treats public noise and applause as supremely important, even though the people making it do not understand where they are or who they are? Do you really want praise from someone who may curse himself three times in an hour? Do you want to please someone who cannot please himself? Can a person who regrets nearly everything he does truly be content?
pages.abbreviated: Anyone who does not understand the world cannot understand their place, nature, or purpose within it. Public praise is therefore a poor goal, especially when it comes from people who do not understand themselves, cannot be content, and regret their actions.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 52
pages.original: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should) everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the air doth, if a man can but suck it in.
pages.familiar: Do not merely share the air around you; share a common mind with the rational order that surrounds and moves through everything. That order is present everywhere by its own nature, just as air is, if you know how to draw it in. Let your mind breathe in harmony with it.
pages.abbreviated: Do not merely share the world's air; let your mind share the rational order present throughout it. Breathe mentally in harmony with that order.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 53
pages.original: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it. Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will, whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent. For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction. For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy: which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.
pages.familiar: Wickedness as a whole does not harm the world. A particular person's wickedness harms no one else; it harms only the person who does wrong. That person can be freed from it whenever they sincerely choose to be. My neighbor's will—whoever they are, and whatever they do—is completely separate from my own. We were made for one another, but each mind has its own proper authority. Otherwise another person's wickedness could become my evil, and the universe would have given someone else the power to make me unhappy. Nothing can do that except my own wickedness.
pages.abbreviated: Another person's wickedness harms that person, not you, because each mind has its own authority. You were made for others, but only your own wickedness can become your evil or make you unhappy.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 54
pages.original: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension. What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them; neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
pages.familiar: The sun seems to pour itself everywhere, but really it spreads outward without being emptied. Its rays extend in straight lines. You can see this when sunlight enters a dark room through a narrow opening: the beam travels directly, and when it meets something solid, it is broken by that obstacle without sliding away or falling. The mind should spread in the same way—not spill out helplessly, but extend itself. Whatever obstacles it meets, it should not attack them violently or collapse before them. It should remain steady and give light wherever light is accepted. If something refuses that light, the loss belongs to it.
pages.abbreviated: Like sunlight extending steadily without spilling or collapsing when blocked, the mind should spread toward its purpose without attacking obstacles or yielding to them. It should give light wherever it is received; refusal harms only the one who refuses it.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 55
pages.original: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
pages.familiar: Someone who fears death fears either having no awareness at all or having awareness unlike the awareness they have now. But they should take comfort: if there is no awareness, there is no awareness of suffering; and if there is awareness, then there is another kind of life, so death is not truly an end.
pages.abbreviated: Fear of death concerns either total loss of awareness or a different kind of awareness. The first contains no awareness of suffering, and the second is another form of life, so neither makes death a true end.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 56
pages.original: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.
pages.familiar: We were all made for one another. So either teach people to do better, or be patient with them.
pages.abbreviated: Because people were made for one another, either teach them to improve or patiently endure them.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 57
pages.original: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
pages.familiar: The mind does not move like an arrow. When it is alert and careful, looking closely in several directions, it can still be said to move straight toward its purpose—just as much as when it rushes ahead without considering anything.
pages.abbreviated: The mind can move directly toward its purpose while carefully considering several directions. Alert, deliberate movement is no less straight than rushing ahead without reflection.

pages.label: Book VIII · Section 58
pages.original: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
pages.familiar: Look deeply into the understanding of everyone you deal with. At the same time, make your own understanding open and clear enough for others to see into.
pages.abbreviated: Understand deeply the people you deal with, while keeping your own understanding open and clear enough for them to see.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 1
pages.original: He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe, having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that they should do one another good; more or less according to the several persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities. For the nature of the universe, is the nature the common parent of all, and therefore piously to be observed of all things that are, and that which now is, to whatsoever first was, and gave it its being, hath relation of blood and kindred. She is also called truth and is the first cause of all truths. He therefore that willingly and wittingly doth lie, is impious in that he doth receive, and so commit injustice: but he that against his will, in that he disagreeth from the nature of the universe, and in that striving with the nature of the world he doth in his particular, violate the general order of the world. For he doth no better than strive and war against it, who contrary to his own nature applieth himself to that which is contrary to truth. For nature had before furnished him with instincts and opportunities sufficient for the attainment of it; which he having hitherto neglected, is not now able to discern that which is false from that which is true. He also that pursues after pleasures, as that which is truly good and flies from pains, as that which is truly evil: is impious. For such a one must of necessity oftentimes accuse that common nature, as distributing many things both unto the evil, and unto the good, not according to the deserts of either: as unto the bad oftentimes pleasures, and the causes of pleasures; so unto the good, pains, and the occasions of pains. Again, he that feareth pains and crosses in this world, feareth some of those things which some time or other must needs happen in the world. And that we have already showed to be impious. And he that pursueth after pleasures, will not spare, to compass his desires, to do that which is unjust, and that is manifestly impious. Now those things which unto nature are equally indifferent (for she had not created both, both pain and pleasure, if both had not been unto her equally indifferent): they that will live according to nature, must in those things (as being of the same mind and disposition that she is) be as equally indifferent. Whosoever therefore in either matter of pleasure and pain; death and life; honour and dishonour, (which things nature in the administration of the world, indifferently doth make use of), is not as indifferent, it is apparent that he is impious. When I say that common nature doth indifferently make use of them, my meaning is, that they happen indifferently in the ordinary course of things, which by a necessary consequence, whether as principal or accessory, come to pass in the world, according to that first and ancient deliberation of Providence, by which she from some certain beginning, did resolve upon the creation of such a world, conceiving then in her womb as it were some certain rational generative seeds and faculties of things future, whether subjects, changes, successions; both such and such, and just so many.
pages.familiar: Anyone who acts unjustly is also acting against the sacred order of life. The nature of the universe made rational beings for one another, so that they could help one another according to their abilities and circumstances—not harm one another. Anyone who violates that purpose shows disrespect toward the oldest and most honored source of all things. The universe is the common parent of everything, and everything is related to what first brought it into being. It is also truth, and the source of every truth. So the person who knowingly lies acts against that order by accepting falsehood and committing injustice. The person who lies unwillingly is still out of harmony with the nature of the universe, struggling against the world's order in their own small part of it. Anyone who turns away from truth for something contrary to their own nature is fighting against the whole. Nature has already given them instincts and opportunities enough to recognize truth; they have neglected them, and now cannot tell what is false from what is true. The person who treats pleasure as the true good and pain as the true evil also acts against nature. They will often accuse the universe of distributing pleasure to bad people and pain to good people without regard to merit. Anyone who fears pain and hardship fears things that must sometimes occur in the world, and that too is a failure to accept nature. Anyone who chases pleasure will eventually do something unjust to get it, which is plainly a violation of the common order. Pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and disgrace are all things nature uses alike in carrying out the course of the world. Someone who wants to live according to nature must therefore meet them with the same calm indifference. Nature did not create both pleasure and pain unless both were equally acceptable within the whole. They occur as part of the ordinary chain of events, arising from the ancient order that brought this world into being, along with all its beings, changes, and successive generations.
pages.abbreviated: Injustice, falsehood, rejecting truth, fearing pain, and pursuing pleasure as the true good all oppose the universe's order, which made rational beings to help one another. Pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and disgrace are all natural parts of that order and should therefore be met with equal calm.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 2
pages.original: It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood, dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are men or reasonable.
pages.familiar: It would be happier and more peaceful to leave this world after living free from falsehood, deceit, indulgence, and pride. But if that has not been possible, there is still comfort in leaving gladly, tired of and disgusted with those habits, rather than wanting to remain alive and continue in them. Experience has taught you to avoid a plague. But corruption of the mind is a far worse plague than any sickness in the surrounding air. That disease harms living creatures; corruption harms human beings in what makes them human—their reason.
pages.abbreviated: It is best to leave life free from falsehood, deceit, indulgence, and pride; if that was not possible, it is still better to leave gladly and disgusted with those habits than to continue in them. Mental corruption is worse than physical disease because it damages what makes humans human: reason.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 3
pages.original: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed. For what thou dost conceive of these, of a boy to become a young man, to wax old, to grow, to ripen, to get teeth, or a beard, or grey hairs to beget, to bear, or to be delivered; or what other action soever it be, that is natural unto man according to the several seasons of his life; such a thing is it also to be dissolved. It is therefore the part of a wise man, in matter of death, not in any wise to carry himself either violently, or proudly but patiently to wait for it, as one of nature's operations: that with the same mind as now thou dost expect when that which yet is but an embryo in thy wife's belly shall come forth, thou mayst expect also when thy soul shall fall off from that outward coat or skin: wherein as a child in the belly it lieth involved and shut up. But thou desirest a more popular, and though not so direct and philosophical, yet a very powerful and penetrative recipe against the fear of death, nothing can make they more willing to part with thy life, than if thou shalt consider, both what the subjects themselves are that thou shalt part with, and what manner of disposition thou shalt no more have to do with. True it is, that, offended with them thou must not be by no means, but take care of them, and meekly bear with them However, this thou mayst remember, that whensoever it happens that thou depart, it shall not be from men that held the same opinions that thou dost. For that indeed, (if it were so) is the only thing that might make thee averse from death, and willing to continue here, if it were thy hap to live with men that had obtained the same belief that thou hast. But now, what a toil it is for thee to live with men of different opinions, thou seest: so that thou hast rather occasion to say, Hasten, I thee pray, O Death; lest I also in time forget myself.
pages.familiar: Do not meet death with contempt. Meet it calmly, even willingly, as one of the things nature has appointed. Becoming a young person, growing old, maturing, growing teeth or a beard or gray hair, conceiving a child, carrying it, and giving birth—all are natural processes belonging to different stages of human life. Dissolving is another such process. A wise person therefore does not face death violently or proudly, but waits for it patiently as one of nature's workings. Just as you wait for the child growing in your partner's womb to emerge from its enclosed beginning, you can wait for the soul to leave the outer covering in which it is now wrapped. If you want a simpler but powerful remedy for fear of death, consider both the people and things you will leave behind and the disposition you will no longer have to endure. You must not resent these people; care for them and bear with them gently. Still, remember that when you die, you will not be leaving people who share your deepest convictions. If they did, perhaps you would be reluctant to leave and willing to stay. But you already know how exhausting it can be to live among people who see things differently. You may even find yourself saying, “Please come soon, Death, before I forget who I am.”
pages.abbreviated: Meet death calmly and willingly as a natural process, like birth or aging. Care for the people you leave, but remember that living among those who do not share your deepest convictions can be exhausting, so death need not be feared as a loss.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 4
pages.original: He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes unjust.
pages.familiar: When someone does wrong, they harm themselves. The unjust person hurts themselves by becoming worse than they were before. And injustice can come not only from doing something wrong, but also from failing to do what should have been done.
pages.abbreviated: Wrongdoing harms the wrongdoer by making them worse, and injustice comes both from doing what is wrong and from failing to do what should be done.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 5
pages.original: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
pages.familiar: If I understand the situation correctly, act with kindness, and accept willingly whatever comes from God, that is enough.
pages.abbreviated: If you understand the situation, act kindly, and willingly accept what comes from God, that is enough.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 6
pages.original: To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to keep the mind free to herself.
pages.familiar: Clear away appearances, think carefully, quiet your cravings, and keep your mind free and self-possessed.
pages.abbreviated: Strip away appearances, reason carefully, quiet your cravings, and keep your mind free and self-possessed.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 7
pages.original: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing, naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder. Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones, and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable, yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets, though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold, what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a man that naturally can live by himself alone.
pages.familiar: Among all living creatures, there is one nature without reason, and one rational nature shared among all who can reason. Just as there is one earth beneath us, one light by which we see, and one air we breathe, everything that shares a nature is naturally drawn toward what it belongs to. Earth sinks toward the common earth. Water runs together. Air gathers with air. Without some force holding them apart, they do not remain separate. Fire rises toward fire and readily joins it; anything dry enough to offer no resistance catches flame. A rational being, sharing in the highest common nature, longs even more strongly to join what is like itself. This is why animals, though without reason, quickly gather into herds, flocks, nests, and families, showing affection for one another. Plants and stones have less need for union, but animals have a more developed nature and therefore a stronger impulse toward it. Among human beings, that impulse has produced communities, friendships, families, public gatherings, agreements, and even truces during war. The stars and planets, though far apart, move in a kind of harmony with one another. Unity is so natural to what is excellent that it can create sympathy across great distances. And yet human beings, the only creatures capable of reason, are now the ones who have forgotten their natural bond. Among creatures of the same kind, we alone resist coming together. We run from nature, but nature still catches and holds us. Watch closely and you will admit it: you are more likely to find earth where there is no earth than to find a human being who can truly live entirely alone.
pages.abbreviated: Everything sharing a nature is drawn toward union, and this impulse produces herds, families, communities, friendships, agreements, and wider harmony. Humans, despite having reason and the strongest basis for unity, resist their natural bond, though no person can truly live entirely alone.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 8
pages.original: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits. All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it begets in others, and so doth multiply.
pages.familiar: A person, God, and the world each bear their own kind of fruit, and everything has its season. We usually use the word for vines and similar plants, but the principle applies everywhere. Reason produces both shared fruits, useful to other people, and private fruits, enjoyed by the person who possesses it. Reason naturally spreads outward: whatever it becomes within one person, it can awaken in others, multiplying itself.
pages.abbreviated: Everything produces its kind of fruit in its proper season; reason produces benefits for both its possessor and others. Whatever reason develops in one person can awaken and multiply in others.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 9
pages.original: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee. The Gods themselves are good unto such; yea and in some things, (as in matter of health, of wealth, of honour,) are content often to further their endeavours: so good and gracious are they. And mightest thou not be so too? or, tell me, what doth hinder thee?
pages.familiar: Teach them to do better if you can. If you cannot, remember that patience with them is precisely what gentleness and goodness have given you. The gods themselves are kind to such people; they often help them pursue health, wealth, or honor. They are generous even when people do not deserve it. Can you not be generous too? What, exactly, is stopping you?
pages.abbreviated: Teach people to improve if you can; otherwise be patient with them, since gentleness and goodness enable patience. The gods show generosity even to undeserving people, so you should ask what prevents you from doing the same.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 10
pages.original: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
pages.familiar: Do not work as though misery were your assigned role, or as though you were seeking pity or admiration. Let your only concern be to act or hold back, always and in every situation, as kindness and our shared human life require.
pages.abbreviated: Do not act as though misery were your role or seek pity or admiration; in every situation, simply act or refrain as kindness and shared human life require.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 11
pages.original: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
pages.familiar: Today I escaped all my trouble. No—I threw all my trouble out. That is the better way to put it, because whatever was troubling you was not somewhere outside you, waiting for you to escape it. It was inside your own judgments. You must cast it out from there before you can be truly and steadily at peace.
pages.abbreviated: Trouble is not something outside you that you escape; it comes from your own judgments. Cast those judgments out to gain lasting peace.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 12
pages.original: All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary; for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are they now also, and no otherwise.
pages.familiar: All these things are ordinary when you have seen enough of life, brief because they last only a day, and low and dirty in their substance. They were the same in the time of those now buried, and they are no different today.
pages.abbreviated: After enough experience, worldly things appear ordinary, brief, and low in substance; they were the same for those now buried and are no different today.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 13
pages.original: The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors, neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on them? The understanding.
pages.familiar: The things that affect us stand outside us. They know nothing about themselves and cannot tell anyone what they are. So what passes judgment on them? The understanding.
pages.abbreviated: External things cannot understand or describe themselves, so judgment of them belongs to the understanding.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 14
pages.original: As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action.
pages.familiar: Virtue and wrongdoing are not found in what you feel, but in what you do. In the same way, the true good or harm of a rational and caring person lies not in emotion, but in conduct and action.
pages.abbreviated: Virtue and wrongdoing lie in conduct, not feelings; likewise, the true good or harm of a rational, caring person is found in actions rather than emotions.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 15
pages.original: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
pages.familiar: When a stone is thrown upward, coming back down does not harm it; rising brought it no lasting benefit either.
pages.abbreviated: A stone gains no lasting benefit from rising and suffers no harm from falling back down.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 16
pages.original: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.
pages.familiar: Examine the minds and understanding of the people whose judgment you fear. See what kind of people they are, and what they themselves think of their own lives.
pages.abbreviated: Examine the minds, understanding, character, and self-judgments of those whose opinions you fear.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 17
pages.original: All things that are in the world, are always in the estate of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
pages.familiar: Everything in the world is always changing. You are changing too, and part of you is continually wearing away. The whole world is the same.
pages.abbreviated: Everything is continually changing, including you, as parts of you wear away; the whole world changes in the same way.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 18
pages.original: it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
pages.familiar: That is not your sin; it belongs to someone else. Why let it trouble you? Let the person who committed it deal with it.
pages.abbreviated: If someone else committed the wrong, it is not your sin, so do not let it trouble you; let them deal with it.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 19
pages.original: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it. In all this there is no hurt. Apply this now to a man's age, as first, a child; then a youth, then a young man, then an old man; every change from one age to another is a kind of death And all this while here no matter of grief yet. Pass now unto that life first, that which thou livedst under thy grandfather, then under thy mother, then under thy father. And thus when through the whole course of thy life hitherto thou hast found and observed many alterations, many changes, many kinds of endings and cessations, put this question to thyself What matter of grief or sorrow dost thou find in any of these? Or what doest thou suffer through any of these? If in none of these, then neither in the ending and consummation of thy whole life, which is also but a cessation and change.
pages.familiar: An action comes to an end, a purpose is fulfilled, and an opinion can finally disappear. None of this is harmful. Think of your life in stages: a child, then a youth, then a young adult, then an old person. Each change is a kind of death, yet none of these changes has caused you grief. Now think of the life you lived with your grandfather, then with your mother, then with your father. Look back over your whole life and notice all its changes, endings, and departures. What real sorrow did any of them bring you? If none, then do not fear the ending of your whole life. It too is only an ending and a change.
pages.abbreviated: Actions, purposes, opinions, life stages, and relationships all end and change without necessarily causing real harm or grief. Since earlier endings brought no essential sorrow, do not fear the ending of your whole life.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 20
pages.original: As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy refuge be with all speed. To thine own, that it resolve upon nothing against justice. To that of the universe, that thou mayest remember, part of whom thou art. Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to mind, that he is thy kinsman.
pages.familiar: Whenever you need help, turn quickly to the right place: your own judgment, the order of the whole, or the person you are dealing with. Turn to your own judgment so you do not decide anything unjustly. Turn to the whole so you remember that you are one part of it. Turn to the other person so you can ask whether they acted from ignorance or understanding. And remember that they are your relative, too.
pages.abbreviated: When you need help, turn to your own judgment to avoid injustice, to the whole to remember your place within it, or to the other person to understand whether they acted knowingly or ignorantly, remembering that they are your relative.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 21
pages.original: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself.
pages.familiar: Just as you were made to help complete a shared human community, every action you take should help build a genuinely cooperative life. Any action that has no connection, direct or indirect, to the common good is unruly and out of place. It is like one citizen breaking away from the agreement and unity that hold the people together.
pages.abbreviated: Because you were made to help complete human community, every action should contribute directly or indirectly to cooperative common life; actions unrelated to the common good break away from social unity.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 22
pages.original: Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that common dirge song.
pages.familiar: The anger of children is just noise. Miserable people carry around dead bodies, trying to delay their inevitable fall, like mourners in an old funeral song.
pages.abbreviated: Children's anger is mere noise, while miserable people cling to dead bodies and try to delay what must inevitably fall.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 23
pages.original: Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
pages.familiar: Look at the quality of the cause that produced the effect. Examine it by itself, stripped of all material circumstances. Then consider how long a cause of that kind can possibly last.
pages.abbreviated: Examine the quality of the cause that produced an effect apart from material circumstances, then consider how long such a cause could last.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 24
pages.original: Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural constitution.
pages.familiar: You have already suffered countless troubles because you were not satisfied with one simple source of happiness: letting your mind work according to its own nature.
pages.abbreviated: You have suffered countless troubles because you failed to rely on the one simple source of happiness: letting your mind function according to its own nature.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 25
pages.original: When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee, get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them, and behold what manner of men they be. Thou shalt see, that there is no such occasion why it should trouble thee, what such as they are think of thee. Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends. And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
pages.familiar: When people accuse you falsely, insult you, or treat you badly, look closely at their minds and understandings. See what kind of people they are, and you will realize that their opinions do not deserve to trouble you. Still, you must love them, because by nature they are your fellow human beings. Even the gods, when people ask them for important things, are willing to help them in many different ways, through dreams, signs, and answers. So you can help such people too, without being ruled by their judgment.
pages.abbreviated: Examine the minds of those who mistreat you and see that their opinions need not trouble you. Still love and help them as fellow human beings, without being ruled by their judgment.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 26
pages.original: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same. And either of everything in particular before it come to pass, the mind of the universe doth consider with itself and deliberate: and if so, then submit for shame unto the determination of such an excellent understanding: or once for all it did resolve upon all things in general; and since that whatsoever happens, happens by a necessary consequence, and all things indivisibly in a manner and inseparably hold one of another. In sum, either there is a God, and then all is well; or if all things go by chance and fortune, yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern thee properly; and then art thou well.
pages.familiar: The ordinary things of the world keep returning through every age, always much the same. Either the universe considers each event beforehand, and you should accept the decision of such an excellent intelligence; or it settled everything once and for all, and each event follows necessarily from everything connected before it. In the end, either there is a God, and everything is ordered well, or things happen by chance. Even then, you can use your own judgment in the matters that belong to you—and that is enough to live well.
pages.abbreviated: Whether events are planned by providence or follow necessarily from prior causes, the universe is either well ordered or events are random. In either case, use your own judgment in what is yours to govern, and that is enough for a good life.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 27
pages.original: Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself shall have her change. And then the course will be, from one period of eternity unto another, and so a perpetual eternity. Now can any man that shall consider with himself in his mind the several rollings or successions of so many changes and alterations, and the swiftness of all these rulings; can he otherwise but contemn in his heart and despise all worldly things? The cause of the universe is as it were a strong torrent, it carrieth all away.
pages.familiar: Before long, the earth will cover us all, and then the earth itself will change. The process will continue from one age of eternity into another, forever. Anyone who considers how many changes and reversals have already passed, how quickly everything moves, and how many more will come, cannot help but hold worldly things in contempt. The force that drives the universe is like a powerful current, sweeping everything along.
pages.abbreviated: Everything is swept through endless cycles of change, and human lives and worldly things soon disappear. Seeing this vast, rapid succession should make you hold worldly concerns in contempt.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 28
pages.original: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves? O man! what ado doest thou keep? Do what thy nature doth now require. Resolve upon it, if thou mayest: and take no thought, whether anybody shall know it or no. Yea, but sayest thou, I must not expect a Plato's commonwealth. If they profit though never so little, I must be content; and think much even of that little progress. Doth then any of them forsake their former false opinions that I should think they profit? For without a change of opinions, alas! what is all that ostentation, but mere wretchedness of slavish minds, that groan privately, and yet would make a show of obedience to reason, and truth? Go too now and tell me of Alexander and Philippus, and Demetrius Phalereus. Whether they understood what the common nature requireth, and could rule themselves or no, they know best themselves. But if they kept a life, and swaggered; I (God be thanked) am not bound to imitate them. The effect of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty. Persuade me not to ostentation and vainglory.
pages.familiar: Look at these people who call themselves practical politicians and true philosophers, who make a show of seriousness and claim to love virtue and honesty. What are they really? Often miserable, shallow, and contemptible. Enough. Do what your nature requires now, if you can, and do not worry whether anyone notices. You say, “I cannot expect to create Plato’s ideal society.” Fine. If people improve even a little, be satisfied with that small progress. But have they actually abandoned their false beliefs? Without a change in their thinking, what is all their display but the misery of people who privately resist reason and truth while pretending to obey them? Do not distract me with stories about Alexander, Philip, or Demetrius. They alone knew whether they understood human nature and could govern themselves. If they lived arrogantly and extravagantly, I am not required to imitate them. True philosophy produces plainness and modesty, not performance and vanity.
pages.abbreviated: People who publicly perform seriousness and virtue are often shallow and miserable. Do what your nature requires, accept even small improvements, and remember that without changed thinking, displays of virtue are false; true philosophy produces simplicity and modesty, not vanity.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 29
pages.original: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last. Their lives also, who were long ago, and theirs who shall be hereafter, and the present estate and life of those many nations of barbarians that are now in the world, thou must likewise consider in thy mind. And how many there be, who never so much as heard of thy name, how many that will soon forget it; how many who but even now did commend thee, within a very little while perchance will speak ill of thee. So that neither fame, nor honour, nor anything else that this world doth afford, is worth the while. The sum then of all; whatsoever doth happen unto thee, whereof God is the cause, to accept it contentedly: whatsoever thou doest, whereof thou thyself art the cause, to do it justly: which will be, if both in thy resolution and in thy action thou have no further end, than to do good unto others, as being that, which by thy natural constitution, as a man, thou art bound unto.
pages.familiar: Imagine looking down from a high place and seeing flocks, sacrifices, ships crossing the sea—some in storms, some in calm—along with things just beginning and things nearing their end. Consider the relationships among everything existing together, the lives of people long dead and people not yet born, and the many nations now living far from you. Think of how many people have never heard your name, how many will soon forget it, and how some who praise you today may criticize you before long. Fame, honor, and everything else the world offers are not worth much. Accept peacefully whatever happens to you through the order of the universe. Do whatever you do justly, with no goal beyond helping others. That is what your nature as a human being requires.
pages.abbreviated: From a broad view, lives, nations, fame, honor, and worldly events quickly pass, and people soon forget or reverse their opinions of you. Accept what happens through the universe's order and act justly for the benefit of others, as human nature requires.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 30
pages.original: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.
pages.familiar: Many things that trouble and confine you can be removed, because they depend entirely on your judgments and assumptions. Let those go, and you will have plenty of room to live freely.
pages.abbreviated: Many troubles and restrictions exist only because of your judgments and assumptions. Release those judgments, and you will have room to live freely.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 31
pages.original: To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object. How short the time is from the generation of anything, unto the dissolution of the same; but how immense and infinite both that which was before the generation, and that which after the generation of it shall be. All things that thou seest, will soon be perished, and they that see their corruptions, will soon vanish away themselves. He that dieth a hundred years old, and he that dieth young, shall come all to one.
pages.familiar: Hold the whole world in your mind, along with the entire course of this present age. Notice how quickly every particular thing changes. The time between something coming into existence and falling apart is short, while the time before it existed and the time after it is vast beyond measure. Everything you see will soon be gone, and those who watch it disappear will soon be gone too. Someone who dies at a hundred and someone who dies young ultimately arrive at the same place.
pages.abbreviated: Everything changes and disappears quickly, while the time before and after it is vast. Those who see things vanish also soon vanish, so dying young or after a hundred years ultimately leads to the same place.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 32
pages.original: What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
pages.familiar: Consider the minds of the people around you, what they devote themselves to, what they love, and what they hate. Imagine their inner lives laid open for everyone to see. When they think they have seriously harmed someone by speaking badly of them, or done them a great favor by praising them, how full they are of vanity and mistaken judgment.
pages.abbreviated: People are vain and mistaken about the importance of their praise and blame, imagining that words have seriously harmed or greatly benefited others. Examining their inner lives reveals how little basis these judgments have.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 33
pages.original: Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is well done. For that was the estate of worldly things from the beginning, and so shall it ever be. Or wouldest thou rather say, that all things in the world have gone ill from the beginning for so many ages, and shall ever go ill? And then among so many deities, could no divine power be found all this while, that could rectify the things of the world? Or is the world, to incessant woes and miseries, for ever condemned?
pages.familiar: What we call loss and decay is really change. Change is what the nature of the universe continually brings about, and within that nature, whatever happens is done properly. This has always been the condition of the world and will always be so. Would you rather claim that everything has gone wrong for countless ages and will continue to go wrong forever? Among all the divine powers, could none have corrected the world by now? Or is the universe condemned to endless suffering? No. Change is not proof that the whole order of things is failing.
pages.abbreviated: What we call loss and decay is the change continually produced by the universe's nature, within which events occur properly. Change does not show that the world has been failing throughout the ages or will fail forever.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 34
pages.original: How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted. And again those other things that are so much prized and admired, as marble stones, what are they, but as it were the kernels of the earth? gold and silver, what are they, but as the more gross faeces of the earth? Thy most royal apparel, for matter, it is but as it were the hair of a silly sheep, and for colour, the very blood of a shell-fish; of this nature are all other things. Thy life itself, is some such thing too; a mere exhalation of blood: and it also, apt to be changed into some other common thing.
pages.familiar: How lowly and perishable ordinary things are: water and dust, then bones formed from them, and all the unpleasant material that makes up our bodies—so easily infected and corrupted. The things people admire so much are no better. Marble is only a hardened part of the earth; gold and silver are merely its heavier waste. Your finest clothing is, in substance, sheep’s hair, and its color comes from a shellfish. Everything else is made of the same sort of material. Your life is much the same: a brief breath of blood, ready to change into something else.
pages.abbreviated: Bodies and admired possessions are all lowly, perishable materials: bodies are made of vulnerable matter, and marble, metals, clothing, and other luxuries come from the earth or animals. Life itself is only a brief breath of blood, ready to change into something else.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 35
pages.original: Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and dissembling never be at an end? What then is it, that troubleth thee? Doth any new thing happen unto thee? What doest thou so wonder at? At the cause, or the matter? Behold either by itself, is either of that weight and moment indeed? And besides these, there is not anything. But thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself of it with more goodness and simplicity.
pages.familiar: Will this irritability, grumbling, complaining, and hiding what you really think never end? What exactly is troubling you? Has anything truly new happened? What are you so surprised by—the cause or the event itself? Look at either one alone: is either really so important? Beyond these things, there is nothing more. And it is time you fulfilled your duty toward the divine with greater goodness and simplicity.
pages.abbreviated: Stop endlessly grumbling and hiding your thoughts: neither the causes nor the events troubling you are truly new or important. Fulfill your duty toward the divine with greater goodness and simplicity.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 36
pages.original: It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together or but for three years.
pages.familiar: Seeing these things for a hundred years is no different from seeing them for three.
pages.abbreviated: Seeing the world for a hundred years is ultimately no different from seeing it for three, because both periods are brief against the whole.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 37
pages.original: If he have sinned, his is the harm, not mine. But perchance he hath not.
pages.familiar: If he has done wrong, the harm is his, not mine. But perhaps he has not even done wrong.
pages.abbreviated: If someone has done wrong, the harm belongs to them, not you. But first consider that they may not have done wrong at all.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 38
pages.original: Either all things by the providence of reason happen unto every particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the whole; or if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things, and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
pages.familiar: Either everything happens through reason and providence, with each person part of one greater whole. In that case, it is unreasonable for one part to complain about what benefits the whole. Or, as Epicurus believed, everything comes from atoms, life is only a random mixture, and death is simply dispersal. In either case, why trouble yourself?
pages.abbreviated: If providence governs all things, each person is part of a greater whole and should not resent what benefits it. If everything is instead a random mixture of atoms, death is only dispersal; either way, there is no reason to trouble yourself.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 39
pages.original: Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as well as the body?
pages.familiar: Do you say to the rational part of yourself, “You are dead; decay has taken hold of you”? Does it then also produce waste? Does it graze and feed like an ox or sheep? Must it be mortal simply because the body is?
pages.abbreviated: The rational part of you is not shown to be mortal merely because the body decays. Ask whether it itself undergoes bodily processes such as feeding and producing waste before assuming it shares the body's fate.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 40
pages.original: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind. If they can do nothing, why doest thou pray? If they can, why wouldst not thou rather pray, that they will grant unto thee, that thou mayst neither fear, nor lust after any of those worldly things which cause these distractions and distempers of it? Why not rather, that thou mayst not at either their absence or presence, be grieved and discontented: than either that thou mayst obtain them, or that thou mayst avoid them? For certainly it must needs be, that if the Gods can help us in anything, they may in this kind also. But thou wilt say perchance, 'In those things the Gods have given me my liberty: and it is in mine own power to do what I will.' But if thou mayst use this liberty, rather to set thy mind at true liberty, than wilfully with baseness and servility of mind to affect those things, which either to compass or to avoid is not in thy power, wert not thou better? And as for the Gods, who hath told thee, that they may not help us up even in those things that they have put in our own power? whether it be so or no, thou shalt soon perceive, if thou wilt but try thyself and pray. One prayeth that he may compass his desire, to lie with such or such a one, pray thou that thou mayst not lust to lie with her. Another how he may be rid of such a one; pray thou that thou mayst so patiently bear with him, as that thou have no such need to be rid of him. Another, that he may not lose his child. Pray thou that thou mayst not fear to lose him. To this end and purpose, let all thy prayer be, and see what will be the event.
pages.familiar: Either the divine can do nothing for us, or it can calm and settle every disturbance in the mind. If it can do nothing, why pray? If it can help, why not ask instead for freedom from fear and craving for the worldly things that disturb you? Why not ask to remain steady whether those things are present or absent, rather than asking only to gain them or escape them? Surely if the divine can help us at all, it can help in this way too. You may say, “I have been given freedom in these matters; I can choose what I do.” But if you can use that freedom to set your mind truly free, rather than enslaving yourself to things whose arrival or absence you cannot control, would that not be better? And who says the divine cannot help even with what lies within your power? Try it and pray, and you will soon see. One person prays to satisfy a desire for someone; pray that you will not be ruled by that desire.
