Another prays to be rid of someone difficult; pray that you can bear with them patiently and no longer need them gone. Another fears losing a child; pray that you will not be ruled by fear of loss. Let this be the purpose of your prayers, and see what follows.
pages.abbreviated: If the divine cannot help, prayer is pointless; if it can, ask for freedom from fear, craving, and dependence on worldly outcomes rather than merely for those outcomes. Pray to remain steady, endure difficult people, and avoid being ruled by desire or fear, then see what follows.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 41
pages.original: 'In my sickness' (saith Epicurus of himself:) 'my discourses were not concerning the nature of my disease, neither was that, to them that came to visit me, the subject of my talk; but in the consideration and contemplation of that, which was of especial weight and moment, was all my time bestowed and spent, and among others in this very thing, how my mind, by a natural and unavoidable sympathy partaking in some sort with the present indisposition of my body, might nevertheless keep herself free from trouble, and in present possession of her own proper happiness. Neither did I leave the ordering of my body to the physicians altogether to do with me what they would, as though I expected any great matter from them, or as though I thought it a matter of such great consequence, by their means to recover my health: for my present estate, methought, liked me very well, and gave me good content.' Whether therefore in sickness (if thou chance to sicken) or in what other kind of extremity soever, endeavour thou also to be in thy mind so affected, as he doth report of himself: not to depart from thy philosophy for anything that can befall thee, nor to give ear to the discourses of silly people, and mere naturalists.
pages.familiar: Epicurus said that when he was sick, he did not spend his conversations describing the illness or making it the subject of every visit. He spent his time considering what mattered most, including how his mind, naturally affected by his body's condition, could still remain free from distress and keep its own proper happiness. Nor did he leave his body entirely to the doctors, as if his recovery depended on them or were the most important thing. He was content with his present condition. So when you are sick, or facing any other hardship, try to keep the same attitude: do not abandon your philosophy because of what happens, and do not let foolish talk or narrow-minded explanations take over your mind.
pages.abbreviated: When illness came, Epicurus focused on preserving his mind's freedom and happiness rather than constantly discussing the illness or treating recovery as everything. In hardship, remain content with the present and do not abandon philosophy for foolish talk or narrow explanations.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 42
pages.original: It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
pages.familiar: In every trade and profession, people focus on the work immediately before them and on the tool they use to do it.
pages.abbreviated: In every trade or profession, people concentrate on the work immediately before them and the tool used to perform it.

pages.label: Book IX · Section 43
pages.original: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What? Is it then possible, that there should not be any impudent men in the world! Certainly it is not possible.' Desire not then that which is impossible. For this one, (thou must think) whosoever he be, is one of those impudent ones, that the world cannot be without. So of the subtile and crafty, so of the perfidious, so of every one that offendeth, must thou ever be ready to reason with thyself. For whilst in general thou dost thus reason with thyself, that the kind of them must needs be in the world, thou wilt be the better able to use meekness towards every particular. This also thou shalt find of very good use, upon every such occasion, presently to consider with thyself, what proper virtue nature hath furnished man with, against such a vice, or to encounter with a disposition vicious in this kind. As for example, against the unthankful, it hath given goodness and meekness, as an antidote, and so against another vicious in another kind some other peculiar faculty. And generally, is it not in thy power to instruct him better, that is in an error? For whosoever sinneth, doth in that decline from his purposed end, and is certainly deceived, And again, what art thou the worse for his sin? For thou shalt not find that any one of these, against whom thou art incensed, hath in very deed done anything whereby thy mind (the only true subject of thy hurt and evil) can be made worse than it was. And what a matter of either grief or wonder is this, if he that is unlearned, do the deeds of one that is unlearned? Should not thou rather blame thyself, who, when upon very good grounds of reason, thou mightst have thought it very probable, that such a thing would by such a one be committed, didst not only not foresee it, but moreover dost wonder at it, that such a thing should be. But then especially, when thou dost find fault with either an unthankful, or a false man, must thou reflect upon thyself. For without all question, thou thyself art much in fault, if either of one that were of such a disposition, thou didst expect that he should be true unto thee: or when unto any thou didst a good turn, thou didst not there bound thy thoughts, as one that had obtained his end; nor didst not think that from the action itself thou hadst received a full reward of the good that thou hadst done. For what wouldst thou have more? Unto him that is a man, thou hast done a good turn: doth not that suffice thee? What thy nature required, that hast thou done. Must thou be rewarded for it? As if either the eye for that it seeth, or the feet that they go, should require satisfaction. For as these being by nature appointed for such an use, can challenge no more, than that they may work according to their natural constitution: so man being born to do good unto others whensoever he doth a real good unto any by helping them out of error; or though but in middle things, as in matter of wealth, life, preferment, and the like, doth help to further their desires he doth that for which he was made, and therefore can require no more.
pages.familiar: Whenever someone's shamelessness angers you, ask yourself at once: “Is it possible for there to be no shameless people in the world?” Of course not. So do not demand what is impossible. This person is simply one of the shameless people the world must contain. Think the same way about the cunning, the dishonest, the treacherous, and everyone else who offends you. When you remember that such people must exist in general, you will deal more calmly with each individual. It also helps to ask what virtue nature has given you to oppose that particular fault: kindness and patience toward the ungrateful, for example, and some other strength for some other vice. And is it not within your power to teach someone who is mistaken? Anyone who does wrong has missed the goal and been misled. Besides, how has their wrongdoing truly harmed you? You will not find that they have made your mind—the only place where real harm can occur—worse than it was. How surprising is it that an ignorant person acts ignorantly? You should blame yourself instead for failing to expect it when reason gave you good grounds to do so. Especially when you accuse someone of ingratitude or dishonesty, examine yourself. You are partly at fault if you expected loyalty from someone known to be unreliable, or if you did a favor while expecting repayment instead of seeing the act itself as its complete reward. What more do you need? You have done a good turn for another person. Is that not enough? You have done what your nature required. Must you be paid for it? That would be like an eye demanding payment for seeing or a foot for walking. Nature gave them those functions, and they need only perform them. Human beings were made to help one another. When you help someone out of error, or help them with ordinary matters such as money, health, or advancement, you are doing what you were made to do. You can ask for nothing more.
pages.abbreviated: Since shameless, dishonest, and difficult people must exist, do not demand otherwise; meet each fault with the virtue suited to it and teach mistakes patiently when possible. Their wrongdoing need not harm your mind, and you are partly responsible if you expected loyalty or repayment from the unreliable; helping others is simply what human nature requires, so the good act itself is enough.

pages.label: Book X · Section 1
pages.original: O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple, single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed. Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full, and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything, either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity, nor the favour either of the weather or of men. When thou shalt have content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things; all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of them he may beget others again like unto them. Such one day shall be thy disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
pages.familiar: My soul, I trust the day will come when you are good, simple, sincere, and open—more transparent than the body that surrounds you. One day you will understand the happiness of those whose lives are shaped by love and whose attachments to worldly things have died. You will be complete and need nothing outside yourself, seeking pleasure from nothing this world can offer—needing neither more time, a special place, favorable weather, nor anyone's approval. You will be content with the present, and everything present will deepen that contentment. You will believe that you have everything you need, that everything serves your good, and that all unfolds through divine providence. You will trust the future as well, seeing that it will contribute in some way to the preservation of the perfect life, goodness, and beauty of the whole—the source that creates everything, holds everything within itself, and gathers back what has fallen apart so that it may create new things like them. One day you will live in such a way that, toward both the divine and other people, you neither complain about what they do nor do anything yourself for which you could rightly be condemned.
pages.abbreviated: The soul should become sincere, loving, self-sufficient, content with the present, and free from dependence on worldly pleasures or approval. It should trust providence and the future's contribution to the whole, complain about neither gods nor people, and do nothing deserving condemnation.

pages.label: Book X · Section 2
pages.original: As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature, doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.
pages.familiar: As someone guided by nature, first ask what your nature as a living creature requires. If it will not harm you, accept it and do it. Then ask whether it will harm you as a rational being. Whatever is reasonable is also social. Follow these rules, and do not trouble yourself with useless things.
pages.abbreviated: Ask first what your nature as a living creature requires and accept it if it causes no harm, then ask whether it is compatible with your rational and social nature. Follow these rules and ignore useless concerns.

pages.label: Book X · Section 3
pages.original: Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural constitution either able, or not able to bear. If thou beest able, be not offended, but bear it according to thy natural constitution, or as nature hath enabled thee. If thou beest not able, be not offended. For it will soon make an end of thee, and itself, (whatsoever it be) at the same time end with thee. But remember, that whatsoever by the strength of opinion, grounded upon a certain apprehension of both true profit and duty, thou canst conceive tolerable; that thou art able to bear that by thy natural constitution.
pages.familiar: Whatever happens to you, your nature has either given you the strength to bear it or it has not. If you can bear it, do so without resentment, according to the strength you have. If you cannot, do not resent that either; it will soon end, and you with it. But remember that anything your judgment recognizes as worthwhile and your duty makes necessary, you are capable of enduring.
pages.abbreviated: Whatever happens is either within your strength to bear or not, so endure it without resentment if you can, and do not resent your inability if you cannot, since it will soon end. Anything your judgment values and duty requires is something you can endure.

pages.label: Book X · Section 4
pages.original: Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
pages.familiar: Teach the person who wrongs you, with kindness and patience, and show them their mistake. If you cannot do that, blame yourself—or better, do not blame yourself at all, if you have not failed in your willingness or your effort.
pages.abbreviated: Teach someone who wrongs you with kindness and patience when possible. If you cannot, blame yourself only if you failed in willingness or effort—and otherwise do not blame yourself.

pages.label: Book X · Section 5
pages.original: Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all time was appointed unto thee. For by the same coherence of causes, by which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
pages.familiar: Whatever happens to you was appointed by the same chain of causes that brought you into being. The events that meet you were woven into the same order that shaped you from the beginning.
pages.abbreviated: Whatever happens to you belongs to the same chain of causes that brought you into existence. Your circumstances were woven into the order that shaped you from the beginning.

pages.label: Book X · Section 6
pages.original: Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred. For of these, if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is, that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that should tend to her own hurt and prejudice. As then I bear in mind that I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto, as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.
pages.familiar: Either everything comes from blind atoms, or there is an ordering nature. Begin with this: you are a part of a universe governed by nature. You are also related to all other human beings because they share your kind of nature. If you remember that you are a part of the whole, you will not resent what falls to your individual share. What benefits the whole cannot truly harm one of its parts. Nature does not create and preserve anything that is contrary to its own good. So accept what happens as part of the universe, and be careful never to harm the human community. Let the common good guide every decision, and prevent whatever works against it. Then you will live as happily as a citizen who works for the good of the city and is glad to belong to it.
pages.abbreviated: Whether the universe comes from atoms or an ordering nature, you are part of it and connected to all human beings. Accept your share as part of the whole, protect the human community, let the common good guide your choices, and avoid what harms it; then you will live happily as a good citizen.

pages.label: Book X · Section 7
pages.original: All parts of the world, (all things I mean that are contained within the whole world), must of necessity at some time or other come to corruption. Alteration I should say, to speak truly and properly; but that I may be the better understood, I am content at this time to use that more common word. Now say I, if so be that this be both hurtful unto them, and yet unavoidable, would not, thinkest thou, the whole itself be in a sweet case, all the parts of it being subject to alteration, yea and by their making itself fitted for corruption, as consisting of things different and contrary? And did nature then either of herself thus project and purpose the affliction and misery of her parts, and therefore of purpose so made them, not only that haply they might, but of necessity that they should fall into evil; or did not she know what she did, when she made them? For either of these two to say, is equally absurd. But to let pass nature in general, and to reason of things particular according to their own particular natures; how absurd and ridiculous is it, first to say that all parts of the whole are, by their proper natural constitution, subject to alteration; and then when any such thing doth happen, as when one doth fall sick and dieth, to take on and wonder as though some strange thing had happened? Though this besides might move not so grievously to take on when any such thing doth happen, that whatsoever is dissolved, it is dissolved into those things, whereof it was compounded. For every dissolution is either a mere dispersion, of the elements into those elements again whereof everything did consist, or a change, of that which is more solid into earth; and of that which is pure and subtile or spiritual, into air. So that by this means nothing is lost, but all resumed again into those rational generative seeds of the universe; and this universe, either after a certain period of time to lie consumed by fire, or by continual changes to be renewed, and so for ever to endure. Now that solid and spiritual that we speak of, thou must not conceive it to be that very same, which at first was, when thou wert born. For alas! all this that now thou art in either kind, either for matter of substance, or of life, hath but two or three days ago partly from meats eaten, and partly from air breathed in, received all its influx, being the same then in no other respect, than a running river, maintained by the perpetual influx and new supply of waters, is the same. That therefore which thou hast since received, not that which came from thy mother, is that which comes to change and corruption. But suppose that that for the general substance, and more solid part of it, should still cleave unto thee never so close, yet what is that to the proper qualities and affections of it, by which persons are distinguished, which certainly are quite different?
pages.familiar: Everything in the world must eventually change. If change were harmful and unavoidable, would the whole universe have been made so poorly that all its parts were destined to suffer? Did nature intend misery for everything it created, or did it simply not know what it was doing? Both ideas are absurd. It is just as foolish to say that everything naturally changes and then act shocked when someone becomes sick or dies. Whatever comes apart returns to what it was made from: elements are dispersed, and solid matter becomes earth while the finer parts become air. Nothing is truly lost; everything is taken back into the universe and made available for new forms. Even the material and life you possess now are not the same as what you were born with. Most of them arrived only recently through food and breath, like a river that remains itself only through the constant arrival of new water. So what changes is not some permanent possession, but the temporary substance and qualities by which people are distinguished.
pages.abbreviated: Everything changes by nature, and nothing is truly lost: what comes apart returns to the elements and becomes available for new forms. Even your present body and life are temporary substances continually replaced by food and breath, not permanent possessions.

pages.label: Book X · Section 8
pages.original: Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest, true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and lose thy right to these appellations. Or if thou do, return unto them again with all possible speed. And remember, that the word ἔμφρων notes unto thee an intent and intelligent consideration of every object that presents itself unto thee, without distraction. And the word σύμφρων, a ready and contented acceptation of whatsoever by the appointment of the common nature, happens unto thee. And the word ὑπέρφρων, a super-extension, or a transcendent, and outreaching disposition of thy mind, whereby it passeth by all bodily pains and pleasures, honour and credit, death and whatsoever is of the same nature, as matters of absolute indifferency, and in no wise to be stood upon by a wise man. These then if inviolably thou shalt observe, and shalt not be ambitious to be so called by others, both thou thyself shalt become a new man, and thou shalt begin a new life. For to continue such as hitherto thou hast been, to undergo those distractions and distempers as thou must needs for such a life as hitherto thou hast lived, is the part of one that is very foolish, and is overfond of his life. Whom a man might compare to one of those half-eaten wretches, matched in the amphitheatre with wild beasts; who as full as they are all the body over with wounds and blood, desire for a great favour, that they may be reserved till the next day, then also, and in the same estate to be exposed to the same nails and teeth as before. Away therefore, ship thyself; and from the troubles and distractions of thy former life convey thyself as it were unto these few names; and if thou canst abide in them, or be constant in the practice and possession of them, continue there as glad and joyful as one that were translated unto some such place of bliss and happiness as that which by Hesiod and Plato is called the Islands of the Blessed, by others called the Elysian Fields. And whensoever thou findest thyself; that thou art in danger of a relapse, and that thou art not able to master and overcome those difficulties and temptations that present themselves in thy present station: get thee into any private corner, where thou mayst be better able. Or if that will not serve forsake even thy life rather. But so that it be not in passion but in a plain voluntary modest way: this being the only commendable action of thy whole life that thus thou art departed, or this having been the main work and business of thy whole life, that thou mightest thus depart. Now for the better remembrance of those names that we have spoken of, thou shalt find it a very good help, to remember the Gods as often as may be: and that, the thing which they require at our hands of as many of us, as are by nature reasonable creation is not that with fair words, and outward show of piety and devotion we should flatter them, but that we should become like unto them: and that as all other natural creatures, the fig tree for example; the dog the bee: both do, all of them, and apply themselves unto that which by their natural constitution, is proper unto them; so man likewise should do that, which by his nature, as he is a man, belongs unto him.
pages.familiar: You have taken the names good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, cooperative, and above worldly concerns. Be careful not to act against them and misuse those names. If you do, return to them quickly. To be clear-minded is to consider each thing attentively, without distraction. To be cooperative is to accept willingly whatever the nature of the whole brings you. To rise above worldly concerns is to pass beyond bodily pain and pleasure, reputation, honor, death, and everything of that kind, treating them as things a wise person need not cling to. Hold firmly to these qualities, and you will become a different person and begin a different life. Continuing in your old distractions is foolish, like a wounded captive in an arena begging to be kept alive until tomorrow only to face the same claws and teeth again. Leave that life behind and take refuge in these qualities. Stay with them gladly, as if you had reached a place of perfect happiness. If your current circumstances threaten to overwhelm you, withdraw to a quiet place where you can regain control. If even that is not enough, leave life calmly and voluntarily, never in anger. Remember the gods, not to flatter them with words or outward devotion, but to become like them. Just as every creature does what its nature calls it to do, human beings should do what belongs to human nature.
pages.abbreviated: Live consistently with clarity, cooperation with nature, and freedom from attachment to bodily and worldly concerns; if you lapse, return to these qualities quickly. Leave behind your old distractions, accept circumstances willingly, and act according to human nature, becoming like the gods rather than merely praising them.

pages.label: Book X · Section 9
pages.original: Toys and fooleries at home, wars abroad: sometimes terror, sometimes torpor, or stupid sloth: this is thy daily slavery. By little and little, if thou doest not better look to it, those sacred dogmata will be blotted out of thy mind. How many things be there, which when as a mere naturalist, thou hast barely considered of according to their nature, thou doest let pass without any further use? Whereas thou shouldst in all things so join action and contemplation, that thou mightest both at the same time attend all present occasions, to perform everything duly and carefully and yet so intend the contemplative part too, that no part of that delight and pleasure, which the contemplative knowledge of everything according to its true nature doth of itself afford, might be lost. Or, that the true and contemnplative knowledge of everything according to its own nature, might of itself, (action being subject to many lets and impediments) afford unto thee sufficient pleasure and happiness. Not apparent indeed, but not concealed. And when shalt thou attain to the happiness of true simplicity, and unaffected gravity? When shalt thou rejoice in the certain knowledge of every particular object according to its true nature: as what the matter and substance of it is; what use it is for in the world: how long it can subsist: what things it doth consist of: who they be that are capable of it, and who they that can give it, and take it away?
pages.familiar: Small distractions at home, conflict in the world; sometimes fear, sometimes numbness and lazy dullness—this is your daily bondage. If you do not pay attention, these guiding principles will slowly disappear from your mind. You often consider things merely as a naturalist would, understanding what they are but gaining no practical use from that understanding. Instead, join thought and action. Handle every present responsibility carefully, while keeping your attention on the deeper nature of things so that you do not lose the satisfaction that understanding can give. Even when action is blocked by circumstances, clear understanding can still provide enough happiness. When will you achieve true simplicity and unforced seriousness? When will you take joy in knowing each thing as it really is: what it is made of, what purpose it serves, how long it lasts, what it contains, and who can possess, provide, or take it away?
pages.abbreviated: Distraction, conflict, fear, and dullness can make you forget your guiding principles. Unite understanding with action by handling present duties carefully while contemplating what things are, do, contain, and how long they last; even blocked action can leave understanding as a source of happiness.

pages.label: Book X · Section 10
pages.original: As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud, and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or northern nations lately defeated. For these also, these famous soldiers and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what do they for the most part but hunt after prey?
pages.familiar: A spider is not especially proud after catching the fly it was hunting. The person who catches a hare or fish, or brings down a boar or bear, may feel proud of the feat. So may soldiers boast of their victories over northern peoples. But look closely at their minds and opinions: what are these celebrated warriors doing, for the most part, except hunting for prey?
pages.abbreviated: People boast about hunting animals or defeating enemies, but their celebrated achievements are essentially just forms of hunting prey, much like a spider catching a fly.

pages.label: Book X · Section 11
pages.original: To find out, and set to thyself some certain way and method of contemplation, whereby thou mayest clearly discern and represent unto thyself, the mutual change of all things, the one into the other. Bear it in thy mind evermore, and see that thou be throughly well exercised in this particular. For there is not anything more effectual to beget true magnanimity.
pages.familiar: Find a definite method of contemplation that lets you clearly see how all things continually change into one another. Keep this process constantly in mind and practice seeing it clearly. Nothing is more effective at creating true greatness of spirit.
pages.abbreviated: Develop a clear way of contemplating how everything continually changes into something else, and keep practicing it. Nothing does more to create genuine greatness of spirit.

pages.label: Book X · Section 12
pages.original: He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell, and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things that should happen unto him. And contenting himself with these two things, to do all things justly, and whatsoever God doth send to like well of it: what others shall either say or think of him, or shall do against him, he doth not so much as trouble his thoughts with it. To go on straight, whither right and reason directed him, and by so doing to follow God, was the only thing that he did mind, that, his only business and occupation.
pages.familiar: He has escaped the bonds of the body and knows that soon he must leave the world and everything in it behind. So he gives himself entirely to two things: acting justly, and accepting willingly whatever the nature of things brings. What others say, think, or do against him does not disturb him. His only concern is to follow the straight path that reason shows him, and in doing so to live in harmony with God.
pages.abbreviated: Knowing that he will soon leave the body and the world, a person should devote himself to acting justly and willingly accepting whatever nature brings. Others' opinions and actions should not disturb him; he should follow reason's straight path and live in harmony with God.

pages.label: Book X · Section 13
pages.original: What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy mind at all? What now is to be done, if thou mayest search and inquiry into that, what needs thou care for more? And if thou art well able to perceive it alone, let no man divert thee from it. But if alone thou doest not so well perceive it, suspend thine action, and take advice from the best. And if there be anything else that doth hinder thee, go on with prudence and discretion, according to the present occasion and opportunity, still proposing that unto thyself, which thou doest conceive most right and just. For to hit that aright, and to speed in the prosecution of it, must needs be happiness, since it is that only which we can truly and properly be said to miss of, or miscarry in.
pages.familiar: What good is suspicion? Why let guesses about the future trouble your mind? Look carefully into what needs to be done now. If the answer is clear, do it, and do not let anyone pull you away from it. If you cannot see clearly on your own, pause and seek advice from the wisest person you know. If something else stands in the way, proceed carefully, using the opportunity before you and aiming at what seems most right and just. That is where success truly matters: in choosing and pursuing the right course.
pages.abbreviated: Do not let suspicions about the future trouble you; determine what must be done now and do it when clear. If uncertain, seek wise advice, then proceed carefully toward the most right and just course, since success lies in choosing and pursuing it.

pages.label: Book X · Section 14
pages.original: What is that that is slow, and yet quick? merry, and yet grave? He that in all things doth follow reason for his guide.
pages.familiar: What is both slow and quick, cheerful and serious? A person who lets reason guide everything.
pages.abbreviated: A person guided by reason can be both deliberate and swift, cheerful and serious.

pages.label: Book X · Section 15
pages.original: In the morning as soon as thou art awaked, when thy judgment, before either thy affections, or external objects have wrought upon it, is yet most free and impartial: put this question to thyself, whether if that which is right and just be done, the doing of it by thyself, or by others when thou art not able thyself; be a thing material or no. For sure it is not. And as for these that keep such a life, and stand so much upon the praises, or dispraises of other men, hast thou forgotten what manner of men they be? that such and such upon their beds, and such at their board: what their ordinary actions are: what they pursue after, and what they fly from: what thefts and rapines they commit, if not with their hands and feet, yet with that more precious part of theirs, their minds: which (would it but admit of them) might enjoy faith, modesty, truth, justice, a good spirit.
pages.familiar: When you wake in the morning, before emotions and outside events cloud your judgment, ask yourself: if something right and just gets done, does it really matter whether I do it or someone else does it? Of course it does not. Have you forgotten what the people who live for praise and blame are like? Think of them in bed, at meals, and in their ordinary lives: what they chase, what they avoid, and the wrongs they commit—not always with their hands, but in their minds. Their minds could hold trust, humility, truth, justice, and a good spirit, if they would only make room for them.
pages.abbreviated: Before emotions and events cloud judgment, remember that justice matters whether you perform it or someone else does. Those who live for praise and blame fill their lives and minds with empty pursuits and wrongdoing, leaving no room for trust, humility, truth, justice, and a good spirit.

pages.label: Book X · Section 16
pages.original: Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but in mere love, and humble submission.
pages.familiar: Give whatever you choose to give, and take whatever you choose to take, says the person who is truly educated and humble to the one who gives and takes away. He does not say this stubbornly or defiantly, but with love and willing submission.
pages.abbreviated: The truly educated and humble person accepts whatever is given or taken away with love and willing submission, not stubborn defiance.

pages.label: Book X · Section 17
pages.original: So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here, or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for the place. Let them behold and see a man, that is a man indeed, living according to the true nature of man. If they cannot bear with me, let them kill me. For better were it to die, than so to live as they would have thee.
pages.familiar: Live as though the world and its prizes could not control you, like someone living alone on a remote hillside. Whether you are there or here makes little difference if the whole world is only one community. Let people see someone living as a human being is meant to live. If they cannot tolerate that, they may as well kill me. It is better to die than to live as they demand.
pages.abbreviated: Live as though worldly rewards cannot control you, showing people how a human being should live wherever you are. If they cannot tolerate that, death is preferable to living according to their demands.

pages.label: Book X · Section 18
pages.original: Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be such.
pages.familiar: Stop debating and describing what makes a good person. Become one in your actual life.
pages.abbreviated: Stop merely discussing what makes a good person and become one through your actual conduct.

pages.label: Book X · Section 19
pages.original: Ever to represent unto thyself; and to set before thee, both the general age and time of the world, and the whole substance of it. And how all things particular in respect of these are for their substance, as one of the least seeds that is: and for their duration, as the turning of the pestle in the mortar once about. Then to fix thy mind upon every particular object of the world, and to conceive it, (as it is indeed,) as already being in the state of dissolution, and of change; tending to some kind of either putrefaction or dispersion; or whatsoever else it is, that is the death as it were of everything in his own kind.
pages.familiar: Keep before your mind the whole span of history and the entire world. Compared with them, each individual thing is as small as a single seed, and lasts no longer than one turn of a pestle. Look at everything in the world this way: already breaking down and changing, moving toward decay, scattering, or whatever form its own kind of death takes.
pages.abbreviated: Compared with the whole span of history and the entire world, each thing is tiny and brief. See everything as already changing, breaking down, and moving toward its own form of death.

pages.label: Book X · Section 20
pages.original: Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives: as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust. Again, when they either are in their greatest exultation; and in the middle of all their pomp and glory; or being angry and displeased, in great state and majesty, as from an higher place, they chide and rebuke. How base and slavish, but a little while ago, they were fain to be, that they might come to this; and within a very little while what will be their estate, when death hath once seized upon them.
pages.familiar: Look at people through every part of their lives: while they eat, sleep, attend to bodily needs, and pursue desire; when they are celebrating at the height of their success; and when they are angry, commanding others with pride and authority. Not long ago they had to humble themselves to reach that position, and before long death will reduce them to another state entirely.
pages.abbreviated: Observe people through eating, sleeping, desire, success, anger, and authority: those now powerful once humbled themselves to rise, and death will soon reduce them to another state.

pages.label: Book X · Section 21
pages.original: That is best for every one, that the common nature of all doth send unto every one, and then is it best, when she doth send it.
pages.familiar: Whatever the nature shared by all things sends to each person is best for that person—and it is best precisely when it arrives.
pages.abbreviated: Whatever the shared nature of all things sends to each person is best for that person, especially at the moment it arrives.

pages.label: Book X · Section 22
pages.original: The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues a mutual kind of love between them. And so (say I) doth the world bear a certain affection of love to whatsoever shall come to pass With thine affections shall mine concur, O world. The same (and no other) shall the object of my longing be which is of thine. Now that the world doth love it is true indeed so is it as commonly said, and acknowledged ledged, when, according to the Greek phrase, imitated by the Latins, of things that used to be, we say commonly, that they love to be.
pages.familiar: The earth, as the poet says, often longs for rain. And the sky seems to long to fall upon the earth. This shows a kind of mutual love between them. In the same way, the world has an affection for everything that comes to pass. Let my desires agree with yours, world. Let me long for exactly what you bring about. That the world loves is true enough; we say that things “want” to be what they regularly become.
pages.abbreviated: The earth and sky seem drawn toward one another, showing the world's affection for what happens within it. Therefore, let your desires agree with the world's; things can be said to want what they regularly become.

pages.label: Book X · Section 23
pages.original: Either thou dost Continue in this kind of life and that is it, which so long thou hast been used unto and therefore tolerable: or thou doest retire, or leave the world, and that of thine own accord, and then thou hast thy mind: or thy life is cut off; and then mayst thou rejoice that thou hast ended thy charge. One of these must needs be. Be therefore of good comfort. XXIV Let it always appear and be manifest unto thee that solitariness, and desert places, by many philosophers so much esteemed of and affected, are of themselves but thus and thus; and that all things are them to them that live in towns, and converse with others as they are the same nature everywhere to be seen and observed: to them that have retired themselves to the top of mountains, and to desert havens, or what other desert and inhabited places soever. For anywhere it thou wilt mayest thou quickly find and apply that to thyself; which Plato saith of his philosopher, in a place: as private and retired, saith he, as if he were shut up and enclosed about in some shepherd's lodge, on the top of a hill. There by thyself to put these questions to thyself or to enter in these considerations: What is my chief and principal part, which hath power over the rest? What is now the present estate of it, as I use it; and what is it, that I employ it about? Is it now void of reason ir no? Is it free, and separated; or so affixed, so congealed and grown together as it were with the flesh, that it is swayed by the motions and inclinations of it?
pages.familiar: Either you continue living this life, the one you have followed for so long, and therefore can endure; or you withdraw from the world by your own choice, and then your mind is your own; or your life is cut short, and your work is finished. One of these must happen. So take courage. Solitude and remote places, so admired by many philosophers, are not special in themselves. Everything is the same for people living in cities and dealing with others. Nature is everywhere the same—even on mountaintops, in wilderness, or in deserted harbors. Wherever you are, you can quickly withdraw into yourself. Ask: What is the most important part of me, the part that governs the rest? What condition is it in now, and what am I using it for? Is it guided by reason? Is it free and independent, or has it become so entangled with the body that its impulses control it?
pages.abbreviated: You will either continue living, withdraw by choice, or die, so take courage. Solitude is not required for inner retreat: wherever you are, examine whether the ruling part of you is rational and free or controlled by bodily impulses.

pages.label: Book X · Section 25
pages.original: He that runs away from his master is a fugitive. But the law is every man's master. He therefore that forsakes the law, is a fugitive. So is he, whosoever he be, that is either sorry, angry, or afraid, or for anything that either hath been, is, or shall be by his appointment, who is the Lord and Governor of the universe. For he truly and properly is Νόμος, or the law, as the only νέμων, or distributor and dispenser of all things that happen unto any one in his lifetime--Whatsoever then is either sorry, angry, or afraid, is a fugitive.
pages.familiar: Someone who runs away from a master is a fugitive. But the law is everyone's master. So anyone who abandons the law is a fugitive. The same is true of anyone who feels sorrow, anger, or fear about something that has happened, is happening, or will happen according to the order of the universe. The ruler of the universe is truly the law—the one who assigns and distributes everything that happens in each person's life. Whoever is sorrowful, angry, or afraid is running from that law.
pages.abbreviated: The law governs everyone, so anyone who resists what happens according to the universe's order is like a fugitive from its master. Sorrow, anger, and fear over past, present, or future events are forms of fleeing that universal law.

pages.label: Book X · Section 26
pages.original: From man is the seed, that once cast into the womb man hath no more to do with it. Another cause succeedeth, and undertakes the work, and in time brings a child (that wonderful effect from such a beginning!) to perfection. Again, man lets food down through his throat; and that once down, he hath no more to do with it. Another cause succeedeth and distributeth this food into the senses, and the affections: into life, and into strength; and doth with it those other many and marvellous things, that belong unto man. These things therefore that are so secretly and invisibly wrought and brought to pass, thou must use to behold and contemplate; and not the things themselves only, but the power also by which they are effected; that thou mayst behold it, though not with the eyes of the body, yet as plainly and visibly as thou canst see and discern the outward efficient cause of the depression and elevation of anything.
pages.familiar: A man provides the seed, but once it enters the womb, he has no further part in the work. Another cause takes over and, in time, brings a child—this astonishing result—from such a beginning. Again, a person swallows food, and once it is down, he no longer directs it. Another cause distributes it through the senses, emotions, life, and strength, carrying out countless other marvels within him. Train yourself to observe these hidden and invisible processes—not only the results, but also the power that produces them. You cannot see that power with your bodily eyes, but you can understand it as clearly as you can see what pushes or lifts an object.
pages.abbreviated: After a man provides seed or swallows food, hidden causes take over and produce birth, nourishment, strength, emotion, and countless other processes. Train yourself to recognize not only their visible results but also the invisible power that produces them.

pages.label: Book X · Section 27
pages.original: Ever to mind and consider with thyself; how all things that now are, have been heretofore much after the same sort, and after the same fashion that now they are: and so to think of those things which shall be hereafter also. Moreover, whole dramata, and uniform scenes, or scenes that comprehend the lives and actions of men of one calling and profession, as many as either in thine own experience thou hast known, or by reading of ancient histories; (as the whole court of Adrianus, the whole court of Antoninus Pius, the whole court of Philippus, that of Alexander, that of Crœsus): to set them all before thine eyes. For thou shalt find that they are all but after one sort and fashion: only that the actors were others.
pages.familiar: Keep reminding yourself that everything happening now has happened before in much the same way, and will happen again in the future. Think of entire dramas and repeated scenes: the lives of people in the same professions, the households and courts you have known through experience or history—the courts of Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Philip, Alexander, and Croesus. Put them all before your eyes. You will find that they follow nearly the same pattern. Only the actors have changed.
pages.abbreviated: Everything happening now has happened before and will happen again in much the same pattern. The settings and actors change, but the dramas of households, courts, professions, and rulers repeat.

pages.label: Book X · Section 28
pages.original: As a pig that cries and flings when his throat is cut, fancy to thyself every one to be, that grieves for any worldly thing and takes on. Such a one is he also, who upon his bed alone, doth bewail the miseries of this our mortal life. And remember this, that Unto reasonable creatures only it is granted that they may willingly and freely submit unto Providence: but absolutely to submit, is a necessity imposed upon all creatures equally.
pages.familiar: Imagine that anyone who grieves over worldly troubles is like a pig squealing and struggling while its throat is cut. The person who lies alone in bed mourning the misery of human life is doing the same. Remember that only rational creatures can willingly and freely accept Providence; but every creature is compelled to submit to it, whether willingly or not.
pages.abbreviated: Grieving over worldly troubles is like an animal struggling while being killed. Rational creatures can freely accept Providence, but every creature must submit to it, willingly or unwillingly.

pages.label: Book X · Section 29
pages.original: Whatsoever it is that thou goest about, consider of it by thyself, and ask thyself, What? because I shall do this no more when I am dead, should therefore death seem grievous unto me?
pages.familiar: Whatever you are doing, ask yourself honestly: Because I will never do this again after I die, should that make death seem unbearable to me?
pages.abbreviated: Ask whether the fact that you will never perform what you are doing again after death truly makes death unbearable.

pages.label: Book X · Section 30
pages.original: When thou art offended with any man's transgression, presently reflect upon thyself; and consider what thou thyself art guilty of in the same kind. As that thou also perchance dost think it a happiness either to be rich, or to live in pleasure, or to be praised and commended, and so of the rest in particular. For this if thou shalt call to mind, thou shalt soon forget thine anger; especially when at the same time this also shall concur in thy thoughts, that he was constrained by his error and ignorance so to do: for how can he choose as long as he is of that opinion? Do thou therefore if thou canst, take away that from him, that forceth him to do as he doth.
pages.familiar: When someone offends you, immediately look at yourself and consider whether you are guilty of something similar. Perhaps you also think happiness means being wealthy, comfortable, admired, or praised. Remembering this will quickly lessen your anger. Also remember that the person acted from error and ignorance. How could they act differently while holding that belief? If you can, remove the mistaken belief that is driving them to act this way.
pages.abbreviated: When offended, examine whether you hold a similar belief, such as equating happiness with wealth or praise, and remember that the offender acted from error. Correcting the mistaken belief behind the action, if possible, will lessen your anger.

pages.label: Book X · Section 31
pages.original: When thou seest Satyro, think of Socraticus and Eutyches, or Hymen, and when Euphrates, think of Eutychio, and Sylvanus, when Alciphron, of Tropaeophorus, when Xenophon, of Crito, or Severus. And when thou doest look upon thyself, fancy unto thyself some one or other of the Cæsars; and so for every one, some one or other that hath been for estate and profession answerable unto him. Then let this come to thy mind at the same time; and where now are they all? Nowhere or anywhere? For so shalt thou at all time be able to perceive how all worldly things are but as the smoke, that vanisheth away: or, indeed, mere nothing. Especially when thou shalt call to mind this also, that whatsoever is once changed, shall never be again as long as the world endureth. And thou then, how long shalt thou endure? And why doth it not suffice thee, if virtuously, and as becometh thee, thou mayest pass that portion of time, how little soever it be, that is allotted unto thee?
pages.familiar: When you see Satyro, think of Socraticus and Eutyches, or Hymen. When you see Euphrates, think of Eutychio and Sylvanus; when Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus; when Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus. When you look at yourself, imagine one of the Caesars, someone comparable in position and profession. Then ask: Where are they all now? Gone, or somewhere beyond our sight? This will help you see that worldly things are smoke, quickly vanishing—or less than smoke, really nothing. Remember too that whatever changes will never return in exactly the same form for as long as the world lasts. How long will you last? Why is it not enough to spend your allotted time, however short, living virtuously and as you should?
pages.abbreviated: Use familiar people to remember comparable figures who are now gone, and see worldly things as vanishing smoke or less. Since nothing returns in exactly the same form, use your short allotted time to live virtuously.

pages.label: Book X · Section 32
pages.original: What a subject, and what a course of life is it, that thou doest so much desire to be rid of. For all these things, what are they, but fit objects for an understanding, that beholdeth everything according to its true nature, to exercise itself upon? Be patient, therefore, until that (as a strong stomach that turns all things into his own nature; and as a great fire that turneth in flame and light, whatsoever thou doest cast into it) thou have made these things also familiar, and as it were natural unto thee.
pages.familiar: What exactly are you so eager to escape, and what kind of life are you trying to get away from? All these things are fitting material for a mind that sees reality clearly and exercises itself upon whatever appears. So be patient until, like a strong stomach that turns everything into its own substance, or a great fire that transforms whatever is thrown into it into flame and light, you have made these experiences familiar—almost natural—to yourself.
pages.abbreviated: Do not ask what you are escaping; whatever happens is material for a clear and disciplined mind. Be patient until, like a strong stomach or transformative fire, you can turn every experience into something natural and your own.

pages.label: Book X · Section 33
pages.original: Let it not be in any man's power, to say truly of thee, that thou art not truly simple, or sincere and open, or not good. Let him be deceived whosoever he be that shall have any such opinion of thee. For all this doth depend of thee. For who is it that should hinder thee from being either truly simple or good? Do thou only resolve rather not to live, than not to be such. For indeed neither doth it stand with reason that he should live that is not such. What then is it that may upon this present occasion according to best reason and discretion, either be said or done? For whatsoever it be, it is in thy power either to do it, or to say it, and therefore seek not any pretences, as though thou wert hindered. Thou wilt never cease groaning and complaining, until such time as that, what pleasure is unto the voluptuous, be unto thee, to do in everything that presents itself, whatsoever may be done conformably and agreeably to the proper constitution of man, or, to man as he is a man. For thou must account that pleasure, whatsoever it be, that thou mayest do according to thine own nature. And to do this, every place will fit thee. Unto the _cylindrus_, or roller, it is not granted to move everywhere according to its own proper motion, as neither unto the water, nor unto the fire, nor unto any other thing, that either is merely natural, or natural and sensitive; but not rational for many things there be that can hinder their operations. But of the mind and understanding this is the proper privilege, that according to its own nature, and as it will itself, it can pass through every obstacle that it finds, and keep straight on forwards. Setting therefore before thine eyes this happiness and felicity of thy mind, whereby it is able to pass through all things, and is capable of all motions, whether as the fire, upwards; or as the stone downwards, or as the _cylindrus_ through that which is sloping: content thyself with it, and seek not after any other thing. For all other kind of hindrances that are not hindrances of thy mind either they are proper to the body, or merely proceed from the opinion, reason not making that resistance that it should, but basely, and cowardly suffering itself to be foiled; and of themselves can neither wound, nor do any hurt at all. Else must he of necessity, whosoever he be that meets with any of them, become worse than he was before. For so is it in all other subjects, that that is thought hurtful unto them, whereby they are made worse. But here contrariwise, man (if he make that good use of them that he should) is rather the better and the more praiseworthy for any of those kind of hindrances, than otherwise. But generally remember that nothing can hurt a natural citizen, that is not hurtful unto the city itself, nor anything hurt the city, that is not hurtful unto the law itself. But none of these casualties, or external hindrances, do hurt the law itself; or, are contrary to that course of justice and equity, by which public societies are maintained: neither therefore do they hurt either city or citizen.
pages.familiar: Do not let anyone be able to say truthfully that you are insincere, closed-off, or not a good person. If someone believes that about you, let them be mistaken; whether you are honest and good is in your own power. Decide that you would rather not live than live without those qualities, because a life without them is not worth choosing. At every moment, ask what reason and good judgment require you to say or do. Since that choice is yours, do not make excuses about what supposedly prevents you. You will stop complaining only when doing what fits human nature gives you the same satisfaction others find in pleasure. That kind of goodness can be practiced anywhere. A rolling cylinder, fire, or water cannot always follow its natural movement, because outside forces can block them. But the mind has a special freedom: it can move according to its nature and continue forward through every obstacle. Be content with this power of your mind. Other obstacles affect the body or arise from weak opinions; they cannot truly harm you unless your judgment gives way. In fact, when used properly, such obstacles can make you better and more worthy of respect. Remember also that nothing can harm a citizen unless it harms the community, and nothing harms the community unless it violates justice. External accidents and hindrances do not damage justice itself, so they do not truly damage either the community or the person who belongs to it.
pages.abbreviated: Make honesty, goodness, and sound judgment your constant choices, since these remain within your power and are worth more than life without them. External obstacles cannot truly harm you unless your judgment yields; rightly used, they can strengthen you, and they do not injure the community unless they violate justice.

pages.label: Book X · Section 34
pages.original: As he that is bitten by a mad dog, is afraid of everything almost that he seeth: so unto him, whom the dogmata have once bitten, or in whom true knowledge hath made an impression, everything almost that he sees or reads be it never so short or ordinary, doth afford a good memento; to put him out of all grief and fear, as that of the poet, 'The winds blow upon the trees, and their leaves fall upon the ground. Then do the trees begin to bud again, and by the spring-time they put forth new branches. So is the generation of men; some come into the world, and others go out of it.' Of these leaves then thy children are. And they also that applaud thee so gravely, or, that applaud thy speeches, with that their usual acclamation, ἀξιοπίστως, O wisely spoken I and speak well of thee, as on the other side, they that stick not to curse thee, they that privately and secretly dispraise and deride thee, they also are but leaves. And they also that shall follow, in whose memories the names of men famous after death, is preserved, they are but leaves neither. For even so is it of all these worldly things. Their spring comes, and they are put forth. Then blows the wind, and they go down. And then in lieu of them grow others out of the wood or common matter of all things, like unto them. But, to endure but for a while, is common unto all. Why then shouldest thou so earnestly either seek after these things, or fly from them, as though they should endure for ever? Yet a little while, and thine eyes will be closed up, and for him that carries thee to thy grave shall another mourn within a while after.
pages.familiar: Someone bitten by a rabid dog may fear almost everything he sees. In the same way, once a person has been marked by sound understanding, nearly anything he sees or reads—even something brief and ordinary—can remind him of what matters and ease his grief and fear. Think of the trees: the wind strips off their leaves, then spring brings new buds and branches. Human beings are the same. Your children are leaves; so are the people who praise your speeches, admire you, curse you, mock you, or remember your name after you are gone. All worldly things follow that pattern. Spring brings them forth, the wind carries them away, and others grow in their place from the same common material. Everything lasts only a little while. Why cling to these things or flee from them as though they could last forever? Before long your eyes will close, and soon after, someone else will mourn the person who carries you to your grave.
pages.abbreviated: Once sound understanding has marked you, ordinary sights and words can remind you that grief and fear pass, like leaves that fall and grow again. Children, praise, insults, and reputation are temporary, so do not cling to or flee from them as though they lasted forever.

pages.label: Book X · Section 35
pages.original: A good eye must be good to see whatsoever is to be seen, and not green things only. For that is proper to sore eyes. So must a good ear, and a good smell be ready for whatsoever is either to be heard, or smelt: and a good stomach as indifferent to all kinds of food, as a millstone is, to whatsoever she was made for to grind. As ready therefore must a sound understanding be for whatsoever shall happen. But he that saith, O that my children might live! and, O that all men might commend me for whatsoever I do! is an eye that seeks after green things; or as teeth, after that which is tender.
pages.familiar: A good eye should be ready to see whatever is there, not just pleasant green things; that preference belongs to an irritated eye. A good ear and a good sense of smell should be ready for whatever must be heard or smelled. A healthy stomach accepts all kinds of food, as a millstone accepts whatever it was made to grind. Your understanding should be just as ready for whatever happens. Someone who says, “I only hope my children live,” or, “I only hope everyone praises everything I do,” is like an eye searching for green or teeth searching for soft food. That is not strength; it is a demand for comfort.
pages.abbreviated: A healthy eye, ear, stomach, and understanding should receive whatever naturally comes to them, rather than demanding only pleasant experiences. Wanting only praise, comfort, or favorable outcomes is weakness, not strength.

pages.label: Book X · Section 36
pages.original: There is not any man that is so happy in his death, but that some of those that are by him when he dies, will be ready to rejoice at his supposed calamity. Is it one that was virtuous and wise indeed? will there not some one or other be found, who thus will say to himself; 'Well now at last shall I be at rest from this pedagogue. He did not indeed otherwise trouble us much: but I know well enough that in his heart, he did much condemn us.' Thus will they speak of the virtuous. But as for us, alas I how many things be there, for which there be many that glad would be to be rid of us. This therefore if thou shalt think of whensoever thou diest, thou shalt die the more willingly, when thou shalt think with thyself; I am now to depart from that world, wherein those that have been my nearest friends and acquaintances, they whom I have so much suffered for, so often prayed for, and for whom I have taken such care, even they would have me die, hoping that after my death they shall live happier, than they did before. What then should any man desire to continue here any longer? Nevertheless, whensoever thou diest, thou must not be less kind and loving unto them for it; but as before, see them, continue to be their friend, to wish them well, and meekly, and gently to carry thyself towards them, but yet so that on the other side, it make thee not the more unwilling to die. But as it fareth with them that die an easy quick death, whose soul is soon separated from their bodies, so must thy separation from them be. To these had nature joined and annexed me: now she parts us; I am ready to depart, as from friends and kinsmen, but yet without either reluctancy or compulsion. For this also is according to Nature.
pages.familiar: No one dies so happily that everyone nearby will grieve. Even if the dying person was wise and virtuous, someone may think, “At last I will be free of that moral instructor. He did not trouble us much, but I know he judged us in his heart.” If this can be said about the virtuous, how many people might be glad to be rid of us? Remember this when you die, and you may meet death more willingly: you are leaving a world in which even those closest to you—those you endured hardship for, prayed for, and cared for—might hope life becomes easier after you are gone. Why insist on staying? Still, do not become less kind to them. Continue to wish them well, remain their friend, and treat them gently. Just do not let love for them make you afraid to leave. When nature separates you from them, let it be like a peaceful, swift death: I was joined to these people by nature, and now nature is parting us. I am ready to go, as someone leaving friends and relatives, without resistance or force. This too is according to nature.
pages.abbreviated: Even the virtuous may be mourned by people who feel burdened by them, so remember that your departure may also ease those closest to you. Still remain kind, wish them well, and accept separation from them peacefully when nature requires it.

pages.label: Book X · Section 37
pages.original: Use thyself; as often, as thou seest any man do anything, presently (if it be possible) to say unto thyself, What is this man's end in this his action? But begin this course with thyself first of all, and diligently examine thyself concerning whatsoever thou doest.
pages.familiar: Whenever you see someone doing something, ask yourself, if you can, what outcome that person is pursuing. But begin with yourself. Examine carefully what you are trying to accomplish in everything you do.
pages.abbreviated: When observing someone's action, ask what result they seek, and begin by examining carefully what you yourself are trying to accomplish.

pages.label: Book X · Section 38
pages.original: Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that (to speak true) is man himself. As for thy body, which as a vessel, or a case, compasseth thee about, and the many and curious instruments that it hath annexed unto it, let them not trouble thy thoughts. For of themselves they are but as a carpenter's axe, but that they are born with us, and naturally sticking unto us. But otherwise, without the inward cause that hath power to move them, and to restrain them, those parts are of themselves of no more use unto us, than the shuttle is of itself to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the coachman.
pages.familiar: What sets a person in motion and pulls his feelings this way or that is not really something outside him. It is the hidden beliefs and judgments within him. Those beliefs are his voice, his life, and, in truth, the person himself. His body is only the case surrounding him, along with all its complicated parts. These are like tools a carpenter is born carrying: without the inner power that directs and restrains them, they are no more useful by themselves than a shuttle is to a weaver, a pen to a writer, or a whip to a driver.
pages.abbreviated: A person's hidden beliefs and judgments—not external things—direct feelings and actions and constitute the person himself. The body is only a set of tools, useless without the inner power that guides and restrains them.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 1
pages.original: The natural properties, and privileges of a reasonable soul are: That she seeth herself; that she can order, and compose herself: that she makes herself as she will herself: that she reaps her own fruits whatsoever, whereas plants, trees, unreasonable creatures, what fruit soever (be it either fruit properly, or analogically only) they bear, they bear them unto others, and not to themselves. Again; whensoever, and wheresoever, sooner or later, her life doth end, she hath her own end nevertheless. For it is not with her, as with dancers and players, who if they be interrupted in any part of their action, the whole action must needs be imperfect: but she in what part of time or action soever she be surprised, can make that which she hath in her hand whatsoever it be, complete and full, so that she may depart with that comfort, 'I have lived; neither want I anything of that which properly did belong unto me.' Again, she compasseth the whole world, and penetrateth into the vanity, and mere outside (wanting substance and solidity) of it, and stretcheth herself unto the infiniteness of eternity; and the revolution or restoration of all things after a certain period of time, to the same state and place as before, she fetcheth about, and doth comprehend in herself; and considers withal, and sees clearly this, that neither they that shall follow us, shall see any new thing, that we have not seen, nor they that went before, anything more than we: but that he that is once come to forty (if he have any wit at all) can in a manner (for that they are all of one kind) see all things, both past and future. As proper is it, and natural to the soul of man to love her neighbour, to be true and modest; and to regard nothing so much as herself: which is also the property of the law: whereby by the way it appears, that sound reason and justice comes all to one, and therefore that justice is the chief thing, that reasonable creatures ought to propose unto themselves as their end.
pages.familiar: The natural powers and privileges of a rational soul are these: it can see itself, arrange and steady itself, shape itself as it chooses, and gather its own results. Plants, trees, and animals produce whatever they produce for others, not for themselves. A rational soul, whenever and wherever life ends, can still reach its own proper fulfillment. It is not like a dancer or actor whose performance becomes incomplete if interrupted halfway through. At any moment, whatever it is doing can be made complete, so it can leave with the comfort of saying, “I have lived, and I lack nothing that truly belonged to me.” The soul can take in the whole world, see through its empty surface, and stretch its understanding across eternity. It can grasp the cycles by which things return to the same conditions, and recognize that those who come after us will see nothing fundamentally new, just as those before us saw nothing beyond what we see. Anyone with good sense who reaches middle age can understand the whole pattern of past and future, since human life keeps repeating its kinds of events. It is also natural for the human soul to love its neighbors, be truthful and modest, and value nothing above its own proper character. That is the nature of law as well. Sound reason and justice therefore come together, and justice is the chief purpose rational beings should set for themselves.
pages.abbreviated: A rational soul can understand and shape itself, fulfill its purpose at any moment, and leave life without lacking anything truly its own. It can grasp the recurring pattern of the world and recognizes that its proper nature is truthful, modest, neighbor-loving, and just, with justice as its chief aim.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 2
pages.original: A pleasant song or dance; the Pancratiast's exercise, sports that thou art wont to be much taken with, thou shalt easily contemn; if the harmonious voice thou shalt divide into so many particular sounds whereof it doth consist, and of every one in particular shall ask thyself; whether this or that sound is it, that doth so conquer thee. For thou wilt be ashamed of it. And so for shame, if accordingly thou shalt consider it, every particular motion and posture by itself: and so for the wrestler's exercise too. Generally then, whatsoever it be, besides virtue, and those things that proceed from virtue that thou art subject to be much affected with, remember presently thus to divide it, and by this kind of division, in each particular to attain unto the contempt of the whole. This thou must transfer and apply to thy whole life also.
pages.familiar: You can easily lose your fascination with a beautiful song, a dance, or a sport you usually love if you break it into its parts. Separate the song into individual notes and ask yourself whether any one note alone has such power over you. You will feel embarrassed by the answer. Do the same with each movement and pose in a dance, and with each part of an athlete's performance. In general, whenever something besides virtue and the actions that come from virtue has too much power over you, divide it into its separate parts until you can see the whole thing clearly and no longer be ruled by it. Apply the same practice to your entire life.
pages.abbreviated: Break apart songs, dances, sports, and other attractive things into their separate parts so their hold over you weakens and you see them clearly. Apply the same method to your whole life, reserving your strongest attachment for virtue and virtuous action.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 3
pages.original: That soul which is ever ready, even now presently (if need be) from the body, whether by way of extinction, or dispersion, or continuation in another place and estate to be separated, how blessed and happy is it! But this readiness of it, it must proceed, not from an obstinate and peremptory resolution of the mind, violently and passionately set upon Opposition, as Christians are wont; but from a peculiar judgment; with discretion and gravity, so that others may be persuaded also and drawn to the like example, but without any noise and passionate exclamations.
pages.familiar: How blessed is the soul that is ready, even now if necessary, to leave the body—whether life simply ends, or the soul disperses, or continues elsewhere in another condition. But this readiness should not come from a stubborn, dramatic, passionate urge to oppose life, as though making a spectacle of resistance.
