It should come from calm judgment, discretion, and dignity—quietly enough that others could be persuaded by the example rather than pushed away by shouting and emotional displays.
pages.abbreviated: Be ready to leave life whenever necessary, but let that readiness come from calm judgment, discretion, and dignity. Do not turn it into a stubborn, passionate spectacle of resistance.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 4
pages.original: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines; some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the proper and particular constitution of man?
pages.familiar: Have I helped someone with kindness? Then I have helped myself as well. Keep that thought ready whenever circumstances call for it, and return to it often. What is your work? To be good. How is that accomplished? By understanding certain principles—some about the nature of the universe, and others about the particular nature and responsibilities of a human being.
pages.abbreviated: Helping another through kindness is also helping yourself. Your work is to be good, which requires understanding both the universe and the nature and responsibilities of human beings.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 5
pages.original: Tragedies were at first brought in and instituted, to put men in mind of worldly chances and casualties: that these things in the ordinary course of nature did so happen: that men that were much pleased and delighted by such accidents upon this stage, would not by the same things in a greater stage be grieved and afflicted: for here you see what is the end of all such things; and that even they that cry out so mournfully to Cithaeron, must bear them for all their cries and exclamations, as well as others. And in very truth many good things are spoken by these poets; as that (for example) is an excellent passage: 'But if so be that I and my two children be neglected by the Gods, they have some reason even for that,' &c. And again, 'It will but little avail thee to storm and rage against the things themselves,' &c. Again, 'To reap one's life, as a ripe ear of corn;' and whatsoever else is to be found in them, that is of the same kind. After the tragedy, the ancient comedy was brought in, which had the liberty to inveigh against personal vices; being therefore through this her freedom and liberty of speech of very good use and effect, to restrain men from pride and arrogancy. To which end it was, that Diogenes took also the same liberty. After these, what were either the Middle, or New Comedy admitted for, but merely, (Or for the most part at least) for the delight and pleasure of curious and excellent imitation? 'It will steal away; look to it,' &c. Why, no man denies, but that these also have some good things whereof that may be one: but the whole drift and foundation of that kind of dramatical poetry, what is it else, but as we have said?
pages.familiar: Tragedy was first created to remind people that loss and disaster are part of the natural course of life. If people can watch such events onstage without being destroyed by grief, they should not be crushed when similar things happen in the larger theater of life. The story shows how these events end. Even those who cry out desperately against their fate must endure it, just like everyone else. The poets also offer useful wisdom: “If the gods have neglected me and my children, perhaps they have their reasons.” And: “Raging against what has happened will do you little good.” And: “Live out your life like a ripe ear of grain, ready to be gathered.” After tragedy came old comedy, which openly mocked personal faults. Its freedom helped restrain pride and arrogance; Diogenes used the same frankness. What purpose did middle and new comedy serve, except mostly to entertain through clever imitation? They too contain worthwhile lines, but what is the overall aim of that kind of drama, if not what we have described?
pages.abbreviated: Tragedy shows that loss and disaster belong to life and must ultimately be endured, while its wisdom teaches acceptance rather than rage against fate. Old comedy restrained pride by mocking faults; later comedy mainly entertained through imitation, though it still contained useful lines.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 6
pages.original: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?
pages.familiar: Can you not see clearly that no other way of living could suit the practice of a true philosopher better than the life you are already living?
pages.abbreviated: Recognize that no way of life could suit the practice of a true philosopher better than the life you already lead.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 7
pages.original: A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided from another man, is divided from the whole society. A branch is cut off by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation. But herein is the gift and mercy of God, the Author of this society, in that, once cut off we may grow together and become part of the whole again. But if this happen often the misery is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to be reunited and restored again: and however the branch which, once cut of afterwards was graffed in, gardeners can tell you is not like that which sprouted together at first, and still continued in the unity of the body.
pages.familiar: A branch cut away from the branch beside it is cut off from the whole tree. In the same way, a person who separates himself from another separates himself from the whole human community. A branch may be cut off by someone else, but a person who hates or rejects his neighbor cuts himself off by his own choice, without realizing that he has also divided himself from the whole body. Yet this is the mercy of the divine source of our society: what has been separated can grow together again and become part of the whole. The trouble is that the farther someone has gone in creating division, the harder reunion becomes. Gardeners know that a branch grafted back onto a tree is never quite like one that grew there from the beginning and remained united with it.
pages.abbreviated: Rejecting or hating another person separates you from the whole human community, as a severed branch is separated from its tree. Reunification remains possible through the divine source of society, but the farther division goes, the harder and less natural restoration becomes.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 8
pages.original: To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions. They that shall oppose thee in thy right courses, as it is not in their power to divert thee from thy good action, so neither let it be to divert thee from thy good affection towards them. But be it thy care to keep thyself constant in both; both in a right judgment and action, and in true meekness towards them, that either shall do their endeavour to hinder thee, or at least will be displeased with thee for what thou hast done. For to fail in either (either in the one to give over for fear, or in the other to forsake thy natural affection towards him, who by nature is both thy friend and thy kinsman) is equally base, and much savouring of the disposition of a cowardly fugitive soldier.
pages.familiar: Grow together with others like branches of the same tree through goodwill and affection, but not by surrendering your judgment. If people oppose you while you are doing what is right, they may not be able to stop your action; do not let them stop your goodwill toward them either. Remain steady in both: judge rightly, act rightly, and stay gentle toward those who try to obstruct you or resent what you have done. To fail in either way—to abandon the right course out of fear, or to abandon your natural affection for someone who is by nature your friend and fellow human being—is equally shameful, like a soldier who throws down his arms and runs away.
pages.abbreviated: Stay connected to others through goodwill without surrendering sound judgment. Continue doing what is right while remaining gentle toward those who oppose you; abandoning either right action or natural affection is equally shameful.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 9
pages.original: It is not possible that any nature should be inferior unto art, since that all arts imitate nature. If this be so; that the most perfect and general nature of all natures should in her operation come short of the skill of arts, is most improbable. Now common is it to all arts, to make that which is worse for the better's sake. Much more then doth the common nature do the same. Hence is the first ground of justice. From justice all other virtues have their existence. For justice cannot be preserved, if either we settle our minds and affections upon worldly things; or be apt to be deceived, or rash, and inconstant.
pages.familiar: Nature cannot be inferior to art, because every art imitates nature. It is even less likely that the greatest and most universal nature could carry out its work less skillfully than the arts do. Every craft improves something for the sake of what is better. The common nature does this all the more. This is the foundation of justice. All the other virtues grow from justice, and justice cannot survive if we become attached to worldly things, allow ourselves to be deceived, or act rashly and inconsistently.
pages.abbreviated: Universal nature cannot work less skillfully than human arts, which imitate it, and it orders things toward what is better; this grounds justice. All virtues depend on justice, which fails when attachment, deception, rashness, or inconsistency govern us.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 10
pages.original: The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all pursuing and flying cease.
pages.familiar: The things you struggle so hard to obtain or avoid do not come rushing toward you on their own; in a sense, you go toward them. Let your judgments and opinions about them become still. The things themselves stand quietly, without noise or disturbance. Then your frantic pursuit and avoidance will stop as well.
pages.abbreviated: The things you desperately pursue or avoid remain quiet; your own judgments make you rush toward or away from them. Still those judgments, and the frantic pursuit and avoidance will cease.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 11
pages.original: Then is the soul as Empedocles doth liken it, like unto a sphere or globe, when she is all of one form and figure: when she neither greedily stretcheth out herself unto anything, nor basely contracts herself, or lies flat and dejected; but shineth all with light, whereby she does see and behold the true nature, both that of the universe, and her own in particular.
pages.familiar: The soul is like the sphere Empedocles describes when it is whole and even in every direction. It does not stretch greedily toward anything, shrink cowardly away, or lie flattened and defeated. It shines with its own light, able to see the true nature of the universe and its own nature within it.
pages.abbreviated: A whole and balanced soul reaches greedily toward nothing, retreats from nothing, and is not flattened by defeat. It shines through its own power and sees both the universe and its own nature clearly.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 12
pages.original: Will any contemn me? let him look to that, upon what grounds he does it: my care shall be that I may never be found either doing or speaking anything that doth truly deserve contempt. Will any hate me? let him look to that. I for my part will be kind and loving unto all, and even unto him that hates me, whom-soever he be, will I be ready to show his error, not by way of exprobation or ostentation of my patience, but ingenuously and meekly: such as was that famous Phocion, if so be that he did not dissemble. For it is inwardly that these things must be: that the Gods who look inwardly, and not upon the outward appearance, may behold a man truly free from all indignation and grief. For what hurt can it be unto thee whatsoever any man else doth, as long as thou mayest do that which is proper and suitable to thine own nature? Wilt not thou (a man wholly appointed to be both what, and as the common good shall require) accept of that which is now seasonable to the nature of the universe?
pages.familiar: Will someone despise me? That is his concern; my concern is never to say or do anything that truly deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? Let him answer for that. I will remain kind and loving toward everyone, even toward the person who hates me. I will be ready to show him his mistake—not to shame him or display my patience, but honestly and gently, as Phocion is said to have done, if he was sincere. These qualities must be real within me, so that the gods, who see what is inside rather than the outward show, may find me free from anger and distress. What harm can another person's behavior do to you, as long as you can still act according to your own nature? As a person made to serve the common good, can you not accept what the nature of the universe now requires?
pages.abbreviated: Another person's contempt or hatred is their responsibility; yours is to do nothing contemptible and remain kind, even while correcting their mistake gently and sincerely. Their behavior cannot harm you if you continue acting according to your nature and accepting what the universe requires.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 13
pages.original: They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another: and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better part one to another.
pages.familiar: They despise one another, yet they keep trying to win one another's approval. While competing to surpass each other in wealth, status, and outward grandeur, they degrade and surrender the better part of themselves to one another.
pages.abbreviated: People who despise one another still compete for one another's approval through wealth, status, and display. In doing so, they degrade and surrender the better part of themselves to each other.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 14
pages.original: How rotten and insincere is he, that saith, I am resolved to carry myself hereafter towards you with all ingenuity and simplicity. O man, what doest thou mean! what needs this profession of thine? the thing itself will show it. It ought to be written upon thy forehead. No sooner thy voice is heard, than thy countenance must be able to show what is in thy mind: even as he that is loved knows presently by the looks of his sweetheart what is in her mind. Such must he be for all the world, that is truly simple and good, as he whose arm-holes are offensive, that whosoever stands by, as soon as ever he comes near him, may as it were smell him whether he will or no. But the affectation of simplicity is nowise laudable. There is nothing more shameful than perfidious friendship. Above all things, that must be avoided. However true goodness, simplicity, and kindness cannot so be hidden, but that as we have already said in the very eyes and countenance they will show themselves.
pages.familiar: How false and insincere someone sounds when he says, “From now on I will deal with you honestly and simply.” What do you mean? Why announce it? The quality itself should make the announcement. It should be written on your face. As soon as you speak, your expression should reveal your mind, just as someone who is loved can immediately read the feelings of the person they love from her face. A genuinely simple and good person should be that clear to everyone—like someone with an unpleasant odor, whose presence can be sensed the moment he comes near. Pretending to be simple is not admirable. Nothing is more shameful than treacherous friendship, and that must be avoided above all. True goodness, simplicity, and kindness cannot be completely concealed; they will show themselves in the eyes and face.
pages.abbreviated: Genuine honesty, simplicity, and goodness need no announcement because they reveal themselves in a person's face and conduct. Pretended simplicity and treacherous friendship are especially shameful, while real kindness cannot remain entirely hidden.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 15
pages.original: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our power to wipe them off. Remembering moreover, that this care and circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his own good and happiness.
pages.familiar: Happiness is an inner strength: the ability to remain steady toward things that are neither good nor bad by themselves. Look at everything, both separately and as a whole, and remember that things do not force opinions into us. They stand outside us, quiet and unchanged; we are the ones who form judgments about them. We can choose not to form those judgments, and if one slips in and hides somewhere, we can wipe it away. Remember, too, that this care will last only a little while, until your life ends. What prevents you from living well with everything around you? If something fits the order of nature, welcome it and let it please you. If it goes against your nature, pursue what does fit it, whether or not it wins you praise. No one should be blamed for seeking what truly makes them good and whole.
pages.abbreviated: Happiness is the inner steadiness to see external things as neither good nor bad in themselves, since our judgments—not the things—disturb us. Welcome what fits nature and pursue what makes you good and whole, whether or not it earns praise.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 16
pages.original: Of everything thou must consider from whence it came, of what things it doth consist, and into what it will be changed: what will be the nature of it, or what it will be like unto when it is changed; and that it can suffer no hurt by this change. And as for other men's either foolishness or wickedness, that it may not trouble and grieve thee; first generally thus; What reference have I unto these? and that we are all born for one another's good: then more particularly after another consideration; as a ram is first in a flock of sheep, and a bull in a herd of cattle, so am I born to rule over them. Begin yet higher, even from this: if atoms be not the beginning of all things, than which to believe nothing can be more absurd, then must we needs grant that there is a nature, that doth govern the universe. If such a nature, then are all worse things made for the better's sake; and all better for one another's sake. Secondly, what manner of men they be, at board, and upon their beds, and so forth. But above all things, how they are forced by their opinions that they hold, to do what they do; and even those things that they do, with what pride and self-conceit they do them. Thirdly, that if they do these things rightly, thou hast no reason to be grieved. But if not rightly, it must needs be that they do them against their wills, and through mere ignorance. For as, according to Plato's opinion, no soul doth willingly err, so by consequent neither doth it anything otherwise than it ought, but against her will. Therefore are they grieved, whensoever they hear themselves charged, either of injustice, or unconscionableness, or covetousness, or in general, of any injurious kind of dealing towards their neighbours. Fourthly, that thou thyself doest transgress in many things, and art even such another as they are. And though perchance thou doest forbear the very act of some sins, yet hast thou in thyself an habitual disposition to them, but that either through fear, or vainglory, or some such other ambitious foolish respect, thou art restrained. Fifthly, that whether they have sinned or no, thou doest not understand perfectly. For many things are done by way of discreet policy; and generally a man must know many things first, before he be able truly and judiciously to judge of another man's action. Sixthly, that whensoever thou doest take on grievously, or makest great woe, little doest thou remember then that a man's life is but for a moment of time, and that within a while we shall all be in our graves. Seventhly, that it is not the sins and transgressions themselves that trouble us properly; for they have their existence in their minds and understandings only, that commit them; but our own opinions concerning those sins. Remove then, and be content to part with that conceit of thine, that it is a grievous thing, and thou hast removed thine anger. But how should I remove it? How? reasoning with thyself that it is not shameful. For if that which is shameful, be not the only true evil that is, thou also wilt be driven whilest thou doest follow the common instinct of nature, to avoid that which is evil, to commit many unjust things, and to become a thief, and anything, that will make to the attainment of thy intended worldly ends. Eighthly, how many things may and do oftentimes follow upon such fits of anger and grief; far more grievous in themselves, than those very things which we are so grieved or angry for. Ninthly, that meekness is a thing unconquerable, if it be true and natural, and not affected or hypocritical. For how shall even the most fierce and malicious that thou shalt conceive, be able to hold on against thee, if thou shalt still continue meek and loving unto him; and that even at that time, when he is about to do thee wrong, thou shalt be well disposed, and in good temper, with all meekness to teach him, and to instruct him better? As for example; My son, we were not born for this, to hurt and annoy one another; it will be thy hurt not mine, my son: and so to show him forcibly and fully, that it is so in very deed: and that neither bees do it one to another, nor any other creatures that are naturally sociable. But this thou must do, not scoffingly, not by way of exprobation, but tenderly without any harshness of words. Neither must thou do it by way of exercise, or ostentation, that they that are by and hear thee, may admire thee: but so always that nobody be privy to it, but himself alone: yea, though there be more present at the same time. These nine particular heads, as so many gifts from the Muses, see that thou remember well: and begin one day, whilest thou art yet alive, to be a man indeed. But on the other side thou must take heed, as much to flatter them, as to be angry with them: for both are equally uncharitable, and equally hurtful. And in thy passions, take it presently to thy consideration, that to be angry is not the part of a man, but that to be meek and gentle, as it savours of more humanity, so of more manhood. That in this, there is strength and nerves, or vigour and fortitude: whereof anger and indignation is altogether void. For the nearer everything is unto unpassionateness, the nearer it is unto power. And as grief doth proceed from weakness, so doth anger. For both, both he that is angry and that grieveth, have received a wound, and cowardly have as it were yielded themselves unto their affections. If thou wilt have a tenth also, receive this tenth gift from Hercules the guide and leader of the Muses: that is a mad man's part, to look that there should be no wicked men in the world, because it is impossible. Now for a man to brook well enough, that there should be wicked men in the world, but not to endure that any should transgress against himself, is against all equity, and indeed tyrannical.
pages.familiar: For everything, consider where it came from, what it is made of, and what it will become. Ask what it will be like after it changes, and remember that this change cannot harm it. As for other people's foolishness or wrongdoing, keep asking: What does this have to do with me? We were made to help one another. Just as a ram leads a flock and a bull a herd, I was made to guide and care for those around me. Look at people more closely: how they behave in private, what beliefs drive them, and how proudly they act. If they do something rightly, there is no reason to be upset. If they do wrong, they do it unwillingly, through ignorance. No one knowingly chooses error; people act badly because they mistake it for good. They suffer when accused of injustice, greed, or cruelty. Remember that you also fail in many ways. Even when you avoid a particular sin, you may still carry the habit or impulse toward it, restrained only by fear, vanity, or ambition. You rarely know every fact behind another person's action, so you cannot judge perfectly. And when you are consumed by anger or grief, you forget that life is brief and that soon we will all be gone. The wrongdoing exists in the wrongdoer's mind; what torments you is your judgment about it. Change that judgment and you remove the anger. Tell yourself that the disgraceful thing is the only true evil. Otherwise, in chasing worldly success, you may excuse theft, injustice, and anything else that serves your aim. Also remember how often anger and grief lead to consequences worse than the original offense. Genuine gentleness cannot be defeated. Even someone fierce and malicious cannot keep fighting you if you remain calm and kind, correcting him when he is about to hurt you: We were not born to harm one another. This will injure you, not me. Show him patiently that this is true, as social creatures do not attack their own kind. Do it privately and tenderly, without mockery, harshness, or any wish to impress an audience. Remember these lessons while you still have time to become fully human. But do not flatter people any more than you rage at them; both are unkind and harmful. Anger is not strength. Gentleness shows greater humanity and greater courage. Power is nearer to calm than to fury. Grief comes from weakness, and so does anger: both surrender you to emotion. Finally, do not expect a world without bad people; that is madness. But to accept that bad people exist while refusing to tolerate any wrong done to you is unfair and tyrannical.
pages.abbreviated: Understand things by their origins, composition, and changes, and remember that other people's wrongdoing usually comes from ignorance while your distress comes from judging it. Remain gentle and correct harm privately, remembering your own faults, life's brevity, and that anger, grief, flattery, and worldly ambition can cause worse harm; accept that bad people exist without tolerating injustice.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 17
pages.original: Four several dispositions or inclinations there be of the mind and understanding, which to be aware of, thou must carefully observe: and whensoever thou doest discover them, thou must rectify them, saying to thyself concerning every one of them, This imagination is not necessary; this is uncharitable: this thou shalt speak as another man's slave, or instrument; than which nothing can be more senseless and absurd: for the fourth, thou shalt sharply check and upbraid thyself; for that thou doest suffer that more divine part in thee, to become subject and obnoxious to that more ignoble part of thy body, and the gross lusts and concupiscences thereof.
pages.familiar: Watch for four habits of mind, and correct them whenever you notice them. Tell yourself: This thought is unnecessary. This thought is unkind. This is something I am saying as another person's servant or instrument, which is foolish and absurd. And when you indulge the body's crude desires, rebuke yourself sharply for letting the better, more divine part of you become subject to the lower part.
pages.abbreviated: Correct unnecessary or unkind thoughts, thoughts that make you another person's instrument, and crude bodily desires that subordinate the better part of you to the lower.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 18
pages.original: What portion soever, either of air or fire there be in thee, although by nature it tend upwards, submitting nevertheless to the ordinance of the universe, it abides here below in this mixed body. So whatsoever is in thee, either earthy, or humid, although by nature it tend downwards, yet is it against its nature both raised upwards, and standing, or consistent. So obedient are even the elements themselves to the universe, abiding patiently wheresoever (though against their nature) they are placed, until the sound as it were of their retreat, and separation. Is it not a grievous thing then, that thy reasonable part only should be disobedient, and should not endure to keep its place: yea though it be nothing enjoined that is contrary unto it, but that only which is according to its nature? For we cannot say of it when it is disobedient, as we say of the fire, or air, that it tends upwards towards its proper element, for then goes it the quite contrary way. For the motion of the mind to any injustice, or incontinency, or to sorrow, or to fear, is nothing else but a separation from nature. Also when the mind is grieved for anything that is happened by the divine providence, then doth it likewise forsake its own place. For it was ordained unto holiness and godliness, which specially consist in an humble submission to God and His providence in all things; as well as unto justice: these also being part of those duties, which as naturally sociable, we are bound unto; and without which we cannot happily converse one with another: yea and the very ground and fountain indeed of all just actions.
pages.familiar: The fire and air within you naturally rise, yet they remain where the order of the universe has placed them in this mixed body. The earth and water within you naturally sink, yet they are lifted and held upward against their nature. Even the elements obey the whole, patiently staying wherever they are placed until the time comes to separate. Is it not shameful, then, for your reasoning mind alone to resist its place, when nothing required of it is contrary to its nature? When the mind moves toward injustice, lack of self-control, sorrow, or fear, it leaves its proper order. When it resents what has happened under the care of providence, it also abandons its place. Your mind was made for holiness, humility, justice, and cooperation with others. These are the foundations of right action and of living peacefully together. Accept what happens with humility, and act fairly toward everyone.
pages.abbreviated: Even the elements patiently remain where the universe places them, so the reasoning mind should not resist its proper order. Its nature is holiness, humility, justice, and cooperation: accept events humbly and act fairly toward everyone.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 19
pages.original: He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always. But this will not suffice except thou add also what ought to be this general end. For as the general conceit and apprehension of all those things which upon no certain ground are by the greater part of men deemed good, cannot be uniform and agreeable, but that only which is limited and restrained by some certain proprieties and conditions, as of community: that nothing be conceived good, which is not commonly and publicly good: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common and sociable. For he that doth direct all his own private motions and purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and by that means will be still the same man.
pages.familiar: Anyone who does not live by one enduring purpose cannot remain the same person throughout life. But it is not enough to have a purpose; you must know what it should be. Most people call many things good without any clear standard, so their opinions shift and conflict. A true good must be good for the community as well as for the individual. Your purpose, too, must be shared and humane. If you direct every private impulse and plan toward the common good, your actions will fit together, and you will remain consistently yourself.
pages.abbreviated: A person needs one enduring purpose to remain consistent, but that purpose must be clearly based on a good shared by both the individual and the community. Directing every private impulse toward the common good makes one's actions coherent and humane.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 20
pages.original: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse, and the great fright and terror that this was put into.
pages.familiar: Remember the country mouse and the city mouse, and how much fear and panic the city mouse's life created.
pages.abbreviated: Remember the country mouse and city mouse: the city mouse’s life brought far more fear and panic.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 21
pages.original: Socrates was wont to call the common conceits and opinions of men, the common bugbears of the world: the proper terror of silly children.
pages.familiar: Socrates used to call the common opinions of people the world's shared bogeymen: terrors that frighten foolish children.
pages.abbreviated: Socrates called popular opinions shared bogeymen—terrors that frighten foolish children.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 22
pages.original: The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were content to sit anywhere.
pages.familiar: At public events, the Spartans gave their foreign guests seats and benches in the shade, while they were content to sit wherever there was room.
pages.abbreviated: At public events, the Spartans gave foreign guests shade and good seats while accepting whatever places remained for themselves.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 23
pages.original: What Socrates answered unto Perdiccas, why he did not come unto him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he: that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.
pages.familiar: When Socrates was asked why he did not go to Perdiccas, he replied, I would rather avoid the worst kind of death: being unable to return the good someone has done for me.
pages.abbreviated: Socrates said he avoided Perdiccas because the worst death would be being unable to repay someone’s kindness.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 24
pages.original: In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the ancient worthies.
pages.familiar: An ancient Ephesian saying advised a person always to keep one of the great people of the past in mind.
pages.abbreviated: An ancient Ephesian saying advised always keeping one of the great people of the past in mind.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 25
pages.original: The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.
pages.familiar: The Pythagoreans used to begin each morning by looking up at the sky, reminding themselves of the beings that carried out their work steadily and without change. They also reminded themselves of order, purity, and unadorned simplicity—for no star or planet hides behind a covering.
pages.abbreviated: The Pythagoreans began each morning by viewing the stars, recalling the steady, orderly, pure, and simple beings that carried out their work without concealment.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 26
pages.original: How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw him thus decked.
pages.familiar: Think of Socrates wearing a rough animal skin after his wife, Xanthippe, took his clothes and carried them outside. When his companions saw him dressed that way, they felt embarrassed for him and withdrew out of respect. Consider how he looked, and what he said to them.
pages.abbreviated: Consider Socrates calmly wearing a rough animal skin after Xanthippe took his clothes, while his embarrassed companions withdrew respectfully, and recall his appearance and words.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 27
pages.original: In matter of writing or reading thou must needs be taught before thou can do either: much more in matter of life. 'For thou art born a mere slave, to thy senses and brutish affections;' destitute without teaching of all true knowledge and sound reason.
pages.familiar: You have to be taught before you can read or write; you need even more teaching to know how to live. You are born ruled by your senses and crude impulses, without instruction in real knowledge or sound judgment.
pages.abbreviated: Reading and writing require teaching, but living well requires even more; we are born governed by senses and crude impulses, without true knowledge or sound judgment.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 28
pages.original: 'My heart smiled within me.' 'They will accuse even virtue herself; with heinous and opprobrious words.'
pages.familiar: “My heart smiled within me.” Yet people will even attack virtue itself with vile and insulting accusations.
pages.abbreviated: Even while saying, “My heart smiled within me,” remember that people may attack virtue itself with vile insults.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 29
pages.original: As they that long after figs in winter when they cannot be had; so are they that long after children, before they be granted them.
pages.familiar: People who long for children before the time is right are like people craving figs in winter, when figs cannot be found.
pages.abbreviated: Wanting children before the right time is like craving figs in winter, when they cannot be found.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 30
pages.original: 'As often as a father kisseth his child, he should say secretly with himself' (said Epictetus,) 'tomorrow perchance shall he die.' But these words be ominous. No words ominous (said he) that signify anything that is natural: in very truth and deed not more ominous than this, 'to cut down grapes when they are ripe.' Green grapes, ripe grapes, dried grapes, or raisins: so many changes and mutations of one thing, not into that which was not absolutely, but rather so many several changes and mutations, not into that which hath no being at all, but into that which is not yet in being.
pages.familiar: Epictetus said that whenever a father kisses his child, he should quietly remind himself, “Tomorrow, perhaps, this child will die.” That sounds ominous, but it is not. Nothing natural is ominous. It is no more ominous than cutting grapes from the vine when they are ripe. First they are green grapes, then ripe grapes, then dried grapes or raisins: different changes in one thing, not a change into nothing, but into what it has not yet become.
pages.abbreviated: Epictetus advised remembering, even while kissing one’s child, that the child may die tomorrow. This is not ominous: natural things change from one form to another, as green grapes become ripe grapes and then raisins, rather than becoming nothing.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 31
pages.original: 'Of the free will there is no thief or robber:' out of Epictetus; Whose is this also: that we should find a certain art and method of assenting; and that we should always observe with great care and heed the inclinations of our minds, that they may always be with their due restraint and reservation, always charitable, and according to the true worth of every present object. And as for earnest longing, that we should altogether avoid it: and to use averseness in those things only, that wholly depend of our own wills. It is not about ordinary petty matters, believe it, that all our strife and contention is, but whether, with the vulgar, we should be mad, or by the help of philosophy wise and sober, said he.
pages.familiar: “No one can steal your free will.” Epictetus also said that we should develop a careful method for deciding what to accept as true. We should watch the movements of our minds closely, keeping our judgments measured, reserved, kind, and proportionate to the true value of each thing before us. We should avoid desperate longing altogether, and resist only what depends entirely on our own will. Believe me, our real struggle is not over small everyday matters. It is whether we will remain irrational like the crowd, or become wise and steady through philosophy.
pages.abbreviated: No one can steal your free will, but you must carefully test beliefs and keep judgments measured, kind, and proportionate. Avoid desperate longing and resist only what depends entirely on your will; the real struggle is whether to remain irrational like the crowd or become wise and steady through philosophy.

pages.label: Book XI · Section 32
pages.original: Socrates said, 'What will you have? the souls of reasonable, or unreasonable creatures? Of reasonable. But what? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect? or of those whose reason is vitiated and corrupted? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect. Why then labour ye not for such? Because we have them already. What then do ye so strive and contend between you?'
pages.familiar: Socrates asked, “What do you want—the souls of rational or irrational creatures?” “Rational.” “And do you want those whose reason is sound, or those whose reason is damaged and corrupt?” “Those whose reason is sound.” “Then why do you not work for that?” “Because we already have it.” “Then what are you fighting and arguing about?”
pages.abbreviated: Socrates argued that if people want rational beings with sound reason—and already possess them—then their fighting and arguing are pointless.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 1
pages.original: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness. And that will be, if thou shalt forget all that is past, and for the future, refer thyself wholly to the Divine Providence, and shalt bend and apply all thy present thoughts and intentions to holiness and righteousness. To holiness, in accepting willingly whatsoever is sent by the Divine Providence, as being that which the nature of the universe hath appointed unto thee, which also hath appointed thee for that, whatsoever it be. To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly. Now in this good course, let not other men's either wickedness, or opinion, or voice hinder thee: no, nor the sense of this thy pampered mass of flesh: for let that which suffers, look to itself. If therefore whensoever the time of thy departing shall come, thou shalt readily leave all things, and shalt respect thy mind only, and that divine part of thine, and this shall be thine only fear, not that some time or other thou shalt cease to live, but thou shalt never begin to live according to nature: then shalt thou be a man indeed, worthy of that world, from which thou hadst thy beginning; then shalt thou cease to be a stranger in thy country, and to wonder at those things that happen daily, as things strange and unexpected, and anxiously to depend of divers things that are not in thy power.
pages.familiar: Whatever you hope to achieve later, you can possess even now if you do not deprive yourself of your own happiness. You do that by letting go of the past, entrusting the future to divine providence, and directing all your present thoughts and intentions toward holiness and justice. Holiness means willingly accepting whatever providence sends, since the nature of the universe has assigned it to you—and has also made you for whatever it is. Justice means speaking plainly and truthfully, and acting fairly and thoughtfully. On this path, do not let other people’s wrongdoing, opinions, or criticism stop you. Do not let the demands of your pampered body stop you either; let the body deal with what happens to it. When the time comes to leave everything behind, leave it readily and care only for your mind and its divine part. Let your only fear be not that you will someday stop living, but that you will never begin living according to nature. Then you will truly be a human being, worthy of the world from which you came. You will no longer feel like a stranger in your own country, astonished by ordinary events or anxiously dependent on things outside your control.
pages.abbreviated: You can possess now whatever you hope to achieve later by releasing the past, entrusting the future to providence, and directing the present toward holiness and justice. Accept what providence assigns, speak truthfully, act fairly, ignore others’ wrongdoing and criticism, endure bodily demands, and leave life readily when the time comes; fear failing to live according to nature, not death, and you will belong peacefully to the world.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 2
pages.original: God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross. For with His simple and pure understanding, He pierceth into our inmost and purest parts, which from His, as it were by a water pipe and channel, first flowed and issued. This if thou also shalt use to do, thou shalt rid thyself of that manifold luggage, wherewith thou art round about encumbered. For he that does regard neither his body, nor his clothing, nor his dwelling, nor any such external furniture, must needs gain unto himself great rest and ease. Three things there be in all, which thou doest consist of; thy body, thy life, and thy mind. Of these the two former, are so far forth thine, as that thou art bound to take care for them. But the third alone is that which is properly thine. If then thou shalt separate from thyself, that is from thy mind, whatsoever other men either do or say, or whatsoever thou thyself hast heretofore either done or said; and all troublesome thoughts concerning the future, and whatsoever, (as either belonging to thy body or life:) is without the jurisdiction of thine own will, and whatsoever in the ordinary course of human chances and accidents doth happen unto thee; so that thy mind (keeping herself loose and free from all outward coincidental entanglements; always in a readiness to depart:) shall live by herself, and to herself, doing that which is just, accepting whatsoever doth happen, and speaking the truth always; if, I say, thou shalt separate from thy mind, whatsoever by sympathy might adhere unto it, and all time both past and future, and shalt make thyself in all points and respects, like unto Empedocles his allegorical sphere, 'all round and circular,' &c., and shalt think of no longer life than that which is now present: then shalt thou be truly able to pass the remainder of thy days without troubles and distractions; nobly and generously disposed, and in good favour and correspondency, with that spirit which is within thee.
pages.familiar: God sees our minds and understanding stripped bare of the body, its appearance, and every layer of earthly clutter. With a simple and pure understanding, God reaches into our deepest and clearest parts—the parts that first flowed from the divine source. If you learn to do the same, you can free yourself from the burdens that surround and weigh you down. Anyone who stops being ruled by concern for the body, clothing, home, and other outward possessions gains great peace. You consist of three things: your body, your life, and your mind. The first two are yours only in the sense that you are responsible for caring for them. The third is truly your own. Separate your mind from what other people do or say, from what you have done or said, from anxious thoughts about the future, and from everything connected with your body or circumstances that lies outside your will. Then your mind, released from outside entanglements and always ready to depart, can live by and for itself—doing what is just, accepting whatever happens, and always speaking the truth. Detach it from whatever sympathy has clung to it, from the past and the future, and make it complete and self-contained, like Empedocles’ perfectly rounded sphere. Think only about the life present now. Then you will be able to spend the rest of your days without turmoil or distraction, with dignity and generosity, at peace and in harmony with the spirit within you.
pages.abbreviated: God sees the pure mind beneath the body and its outward burdens, and you can gain peace by treating the body and life as responsibilities while keeping the mind truly your own. Detach it from others, past and future, bodily circumstances, and outside events so it can act justly, accept what happens, speak truthfully, and live in present harmony with the spirit within.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 3
pages.original: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own. For if any God or grave master standing by, should command any of us to think nothing by himself but what he should presently speak out; no man were able to endure it, though but for one day. Thus do we fear more what our neighbours will think of us, than what we ourselves.
pages.familiar: I have often wondered why, when each person cares most about himself, we pay more attention to other people's opinions of us than to our own. Imagine being ordered by some god or stern teacher to say aloud every thought that crossed your mind. No one could bear it for even a day. Yet that is how we live: fearing what our neighbors think more than what we think ourselves.
pages.abbreviated: Although each person cares most about himself, we fear others’ opinions more than our own. We could not endure having every thought spoken aloud, yet we effectively live under that fear.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 4
pages.original: how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever. But this thou mayest be sure of, that this (if it be so indeed) would never have been so ordered by the Gods, had it been fit otherwise. For certainly it was possible, had it been more just so and had it been according to nature, the nature of the universe would easily have borne it. But now because it is not so, (if so be that it be not so indeed) be therefore confident that it was not fit it should be so for thou seest thyself, that now seeking after this matter, how freely thou doest argue and contest with God. But were not the Gods both just and good in the highest degree, thou durst not thus reason with them. Now if just and good, it could not be that in the creation of the world, they should either unjustly or unreasonably oversee anything.
pages.familiar: Sometimes I wonder why the gods, who have arranged everything else with such wisdom and care, would allow good people who honored them deeply to die and disappear forever. But if things truly are this way, you can be certain they were not meant to be otherwise. If another arrangement had been just and natural, the universe could have supported it. Since it has not happened, it must not have been fitting. You can see how freely you question the gods about this. You would not dare do so if you did not believe they were perfectly just and good. And if they are just and good, they could not have overlooked anything unjust or unreasonable in creating the world.
pages.abbreviated: If good people die and disappear because the gods arranged the world that way, then that arrangement must have been just and natural. A perfectly just and good divine order could not have overlooked anything unreasonable.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 5
pages.original: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right, because it hath been used unto it.
pages.familiar: Train yourself to do even what seems impossible at first. The left hand usually lies unused, yet it can hold the reins more firmly than the right because it has practiced doing so.
pages.abbreviated: Practice can make even what first seems impossible possible, as the usually unused left hand can hold reins more firmly than the right when trained to do so.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 6
pages.original: Let these be the objects of thy ordinary meditation: to consider, what manner of men both for soul and body we ought to be, whensoever death shall surprise us: the shortness of this our mortal life: the immense vastness of the time that hath been before, and will he after us: the frailty of every worldly material object: all these things to consider, and behold clearly in themselves, all disguisement of external outside being removed and taken away. Again, to consider the efficient causes of all things: the proper ends and references of all actions: what pain is in itself; what pleasure, what death: what fame or honour, how every man is the true and proper ground of his own rest and tranquillity, and that no man can truly be hindered by any other: that all is but conceit and opinion. As for the use of thy dogmata, thou must carry thyself in the practice of them, rather like unto a pancratiastes, or one that at the same time both fights and wrestles with hands and feet, than a gladiator. For this, if he lose his sword that he fights with, he is gone: whereas the other hath still his hand free, which he may easily turn and manage at his will.
pages.familiar: Make these thoughts part of your regular reflection: What kind of person should I be in mind and body when death comes? How brief is this life, compared with the endless time before it and after it? How fragile are all material things? Look at them clearly, without the disguises we put over them. Consider what causes things, what each action is aimed at, and what pain, pleasure, death, fame, and honor really are. Remember that each person creates the conditions for his own peace, and that no one else can truly take it away; the rest is judgment and interpretation. Put your principles into practice like a fighter who can use both hands and feet, not like a swordsman who is helpless once his weapon is gone. Your mind remains capable of turning and responding.
pages.abbreviated: Regularly reflect on the kind of person you should be at death, life’s brevity, material fragility, and the true nature of pain, pleasure, death, fame, and honor. Put principles into practice flexibly, remembering that each person creates the conditions for his own peace and that the mind can always turn and respond.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 7
pages.original: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.
pages.familiar: Look at everything in the world by separating what it is made of, what shape or character it has, and what purpose it serves.
pages.abbreviated: Examine everything by separating its material, its form or character, and its purpose.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 8
pages.original: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
pages.familiar: How fortunate we are to have been given this ability: to do only what God approves, and to accept with peace whatever God sends us.
pages.abbreviated: We are fortunate to be able to do what God approves and peacefully accept whatever God sends.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 9
pages.original: Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.
pages.familiar: When something happens through the ordinary course of nature, do not blame the gods, because they cannot act wrongly, knowingly or unknowingly. Do not blame people either, because when they do wrong, it is through ignorance and against their better will. So there is no one to accuse.
pages.abbreviated: When nature takes its ordinary course, blame neither the gods, who cannot act wrongly, nor people, whose wrongdoing comes from ignorance and against their better will; therefore there is no one to accuse.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 10
pages.original: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!
pages.familiar: How strange and foolish it is to be surprised by anything that happens in this life according to nature's ordinary course.
pages.abbreviated: It is strange and foolish to be surprised by anything that happens according to nature’s ordinary course.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 11
pages.original: Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere casual confusion, void of all order and government. If an absolute and unavoidable necessity, why doest thou resist? If a placable and exorable Providence, make thyself worthy of the divine help and assistance. If all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou mayest govern thine own life and actions. But if thou beest carried away with the flood, it must be thy body perchance, or thy life, or some other thing that belongs unto them that is carried away: thy mind and understanding cannot. Or should it be so, that the light of a candle indeed is still bright and lightsome until it be put out: and should truth, and righteousness, and temperance cease to shine in thee whilest thou thyself hast any being?
pages.familiar: Either everything follows fate—an unavoidable necessity or a kind and responsive providence—or everything is random confusion. If necessity rules, why resist it? If providence can be moved, make yourself worthy of its help. If everything is confusion without any guide, then be glad that you possess reason and can govern your own life. The flood may carry away your body, your possessions, or even your life, but it cannot carry away your understanding. A candle shines until it is extinguished. So let truth, justice, and self-control continue to shine in you for as long as you live.
pages.abbreviated: If everything follows necessity, resistance is pointless; if providence responds, make yourself worthy of its help; and if all is confusion, use reason to govern yourself. Loss may carry away your body, possessions, or life, but it cannot take your understanding, so let truth, justice, and self-control shine while you live.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 12
pages.original: At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin indeed, as it seems to be? But if it be, what do I know but that he himself hath already condemned himself for it? And that is all one as if a man should scratch and tear his own face, an object of compassion rather than of anger. Again, that he that would not have a vicious man to sin, is like unto him that would not have moisture in the fig, nor children to welp nor a horse to neigh, nor anything else that in the course of nature is necessary. For what shall he do that hath such an habit? If thou therefore beest powerful and eloquent, remedy it if thou canst.
pages.familiar: When you think someone has done wrong, ask yourself: How do I know it is truly wrong, rather than merely appearing so? And if it is wrong, how do I know that person has not already condemned himself for it? Hurting himself with guilt is like tearing his own face; he deserves compassion more than anger. Expecting someone with a vicious habit never to act viciously is like expecting a fig to have no moisture, a child never to cry, or a horse never to neigh. What else can such a person do while ruled by that habit? If you have the power and the skill to help, then help him.
pages.abbreviated: Before condemning someone, ask whether the act is truly wrong and whether he has already condemned himself; guilt may hurt him more than anger would. A person ruled by a vicious habit will act according to it, so help him if you have the ability and skill.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 13
pages.original: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not. Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.
pages.familiar: If it isn’t right, don’t do it. If it isn’t true, don’t say it. Keep your purpose and resolve your own, free from pressure and compulsion.
pages.abbreviated: Do nothing wrong and say nothing untrue. Keep your purpose and resolve independent of pressure or compulsion.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 14
pages.original: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.
pages.familiar: Whenever something comes before you, consider its true nature. Examine it by separating what it is in form, what it is made of, what its real use or purpose is, and how long it is meant to last.
pages.abbreviated: Whenever something appears, examine its true nature: its form, material, purpose, and intended duration.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 15
pages.original: It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual appetites and affections. What is now the object of my mind, is it fear, or suspicion, or lust, or any such thing? To do nothing rashly without some certain end; let that be thy first care. The next, to have no other end than the common good. For, alas! yet a little while, and thou art no more: no more will any, either of those things that now thou seest, or of those men that now are living, be any more. For all things are by nature appointed soon to be changed, turned, and corrupted, that other things might succeed in their room.
pages.familiar: It is time to understand that something in you is better and more divine than your passions, cravings, and emotional impulses. What is occupying my mind right now: fear, suspicion, desire, or something else? First, make sure you do nothing without a clear purpose. Then make sure your purpose serves the common good. Soon you will be gone, and so will everything you now see and everyone who is alive today. Everything is naturally destined to change, decay, and make way for something else.
pages.abbreviated: Recognize that reason in you is higher than passion and ask what is occupying your mind. Act only with clear purpose, serve the common good, and remember that everything you see, including yourself, will change and pass away.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 16
pages.original: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.
pages.familiar: Remember that everything depends on your judgment, and every judgment depends on the mind. Remove the judgment, and you become safe and calm, like a ship that has entered the harbor: sheltered, steady, and beyond the reach of storms.
pages.abbreviated: Everything depends on judgment, and judgment depends on the mind. Remove the judgment, and you become safe and calm, like a ship sheltered in harbor.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 17
pages.original: No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end. Neither can he that is the author of that operation; for this very respect, because his operation is at an end, be said to suffer any evil. Likewise then, neither can the whole body of all our actions (which is our life) if in time it cease, be said to suffer any evil for this very reason, because it is at an end; nor he truly be said to have been ill affected, that did put a period to this series of actions. Now this time or certain period, depends of the determination of nature: sometimes of particular nature, as when a man dieth old; but of nature in general, however; the parts whereof thus changing one after another, the whole world still continues fresh and new. Now that is ever best and most seasonable, which is for the good of the whole. Thus it appears that death of itself can neither be hurtful to any in particular, because it is not a shameful thing (for neither is it a thing that depends of our own will, nor of itself contrary to the common good) and generally, as it is both expedient and seasonable to the whole, that in that respect it must needs be good. It is that also, which is brought unto us by the order and appointment of the Divine Providence; so that he whose will and mind in these things runs along with the Divine ordinance, and by this concurrence of his will and mind with the Divine Providence, is led and driven along, as it were by God Himself; may truly be termed and esteemed the θεοφόρητος, or divinely led and inspired.
pages.familiar: When any activity ends, even after only a short time, it has not suffered harm; it is simply finished. The person who carried it out has not suffered harm merely because the activity ended. In the same way, if the whole series of our actions—our life—comes to an end, it cannot be harmed simply because it is over. Nor can the person whose actions have ended be said to have been treated badly for that reason. The time and manner of this ending follow nature: sometimes an individual nature, as when someone dies in old age, and always the larger nature of the whole, whose parts continually change while the world remains renewed. What serves the whole is always best and most timely. Death, by itself, cannot harm anyone: it is not shameful, it does not depend on our choice, and it is not contrary to the common good. Since it is useful and timely for the whole, it must be good in that larger sense. It also comes through the order of divine providence. Someone whose will and mind move with that order, carried along by it as though guided by God, may truly be called divinely led.
pages.abbreviated: An activity is not harmed by ending, nor is a life or its agent harmed merely because its actions have ended. Death follows individual and universal nature, serves the whole, is neither shameful nor contrary to the common good, and is good in that larger order; those who accept this order are rightly called divinely led.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 18
pages.original: These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly, or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is equally against reason. Secondly, what like unto our bodies are whilest yet rude and imperfect, until they be animated: and from their animation, until their expiration: of what things they are compounded, and into what things they shall be dissolved. Thirdly, how vain all things will appear unto thee when, from on high as it were, looking down thou shalt contemplate all things upon earth, and the wonderful mutability, that they are subject unto: considering withal, the infinite both greatness and variety of things aerial and things celestial that are round about it. And that as often as thou shalt behold them, thou shalt still see the same: as the same things, so the same shortness of continuance of all those things. And, behold, these be the things that we are so proud and puffed up for.
pages.familiar: Keep three things ready in your mind. First, regarding your own actions: make sure you do nothing pointless and nothing contrary to justice and fairness. Regarding what happens to you from outside, remember that it comes either by chance or by providence; blaming either one is equally unreasonable. Second, consider what our bodies are like before they are formed and alive, and what they become from life until death: what they are made from and what they will break down into. Third, remember how insignificant everything appears when you look down on the earth from above and see how constantly it changes. Around it are countless and varied things in the air and sky, yet whenever you look, you see the same patterns and the same brief duration. These are the things we become so proud and inflated about.
pages.abbreviated: Keep three thoughts ready: make your actions purposeful and just; remember that external events come by chance or providence, and blaming either is unreasonable; and remember the body’s changing material nature and the earth’s small, shifting place in the universe. These are what people unjustly become proud of.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 19
pages.original: Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that hinders thee from casting of it away? When thou art grieved at anything, hast thou forgotten that all things happen according to the nature of the universe; and that him only it concerns, who is in fault; and moreover, that what is now done, is that which from ever hath been done in the world, and will ever be done, and is now done everywhere: how nearly all men are allied one to another by a kindred not of blood, nor of seed, but of the same mind. Thou hast also forgotten that every man's mind partakes of the Deity, and issueth from thence; and that no man can properly call anything his own, no not his son, nor his body, nor his life; for that they all proceed from that One who is the giver of all things: that all things are but opinion; that no man lives properly, but that very instant of time which is now present. And therefore that no man whensoever he dieth can properly be said to lose any more, than an instant of time.
pages.familiar: Let go of your judgments, and you are safe. What prevents you from letting them go? When something upsets you, have you forgotten that everything happens according to the nature of the universe, that blame belongs only to the person who did wrong, and that what has happened now has always happened in the world, will always happen, and is happening everywhere? Have you forgotten that people are connected not by blood or ancestry alone, but by sharing the same kind of mind? Every mind partakes of the divine and comes from it. No one can truly call anything their own—not a child, not a body, not even a life—because all of it comes from the one source that gives everything. Everything is a matter of judgment, and no one truly possesses more than the present moment. So when someone dies, they lose no more than that single instant.
pages.abbreviated: Release your judgments and you are safe, remembering that events follow universal nature and wrongdoing belongs only to the wrongdoer. All minds share a divine source, nothing is truly our own, and each person—including the dead—possesses only the present moment.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 20
pages.original: Let thy thoughts ever run upon them, who once for some one thing or other, were moved with extraordinary indignation; who were once in the highest pitch of either honour, or calamity; or mutual hatred and enmity; or of any other fortune or condition whatsoever. Then consider what's now become of all those things. All is turned to smoke; all to ashes, and a mere fable; and perchance not so much as a fable. As also whatsoever is of this nature, as Fabius Catulinus in the field; Lucius Lupus, and Stertinius, at Baiæ Tiberius at Capreæ and Velius Rufus, and all such examples of vehement prosecution in worldly matters; let these also run in thy mind at the same time; and how vile every object of such earnest and vehement prosecution is; and how much more agreeable to true philosophy it is, for a man to carry himself in every matter that offers itself; justly, and moderately, as one that followeth the Gods with all simplicity. For, for a man to be proud and high conceited, that he is not proud and high conceited, is of all kind of pride and presumption, the most intolerable.
pages.familiar: Think about people who were once consumed by outrage over some matter, raised to the heights of honor or crushed by disaster, locked in hatred and conflict, or caught up in any other extreme condition. Then ask what has become of all those things. They have turned to smoke, ashes, and a story—perhaps not even that. Think of all the people who pursued worldly affairs with fierce intensity, and how trivial the objects of that pursuit now appear. It is far more in keeping with true philosophy to meet each situation with justice and moderation, with the simple humility of someone who follows the divine order. To be proud that you are not proud is the most unbearable kind of pride.
pages.abbreviated: Outrage, honor, disaster, hatred, and intense worldly pursuits eventually become smoke, ashes, or barely a story. Philosophy calls for justice, moderation, humility, and following divine order; pride in lacking pride is still unbearable pride.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 21
pages.original: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore worship them.
pages.familiar: When people ask, “Where have you seen the gods, and how do you know they exist if you worship them so devotedly?” I answer first that, in some way, their presence is visible and evident in the world. Second, I have never seen my own soul, yet I respect and honor it. In the same way, through the daily experience of their power and care in my life and in the lives of others, I know that the gods exist, and so I worship them.
pages.abbreviated: The gods are evident through the world and through their power and care in daily life. Though I have never seen my own soul, I honor it, and similarly I know the gods through their effects and worship them.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 22
pages.original: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?
pages.familiar: A happy life consists in thoroughly understanding the true nature of everything—what it is made of and what gives it its form—and in devoting your whole heart and soul to doing what is just and speaking the truth. What more is needed than to enjoy your life as one good action follows immediately and naturally from the last, without interruption, even for a moment?
pages.abbreviated: A happy life understands the nature and formation of everything, devotes itself to justice and truth, and lets each good action follow naturally from the last without interruption.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 23
pages.original: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures. So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves (as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind, this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.
pages.familiar: There is only one sunlight, even when walls, mountains, and countless other things block it. There is one shared substance making up the whole world, even though it is enclosed and shaped into infinitely many different bodies. There is one shared soul, though it is divided among countless individual beings and natures. And there is one shared reasoning mind, even though it may seem divided among us.
