Other parts of the whole—sensitive life and physical matter—do not naturally recognize one another or belong to one another, since they are irrational, even when some contain a mind or reasoning faculty that guides them. But every reasoning mind naturally recognizes what belongs to its own kind and longs to unite with it. This shared affection, unity, and understanding cannot be blocked, divided, or trapped within separate individuals in the way other common things can.
pages.abbreviated: Just as sunlight, substance, soul, and reason are shared through many forms, every reasoning mind naturally recognizes and seeks union with its kind. This shared affection, unity, and understanding cannot be confined or divided like physical matter.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 24
pages.original: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again? Wouldst thou long be able to talk, to think and reason with thyself? Which of all these seems unto thee a worthy object of thy desire? Now if of all these thou doest find that they be but little worth in themselves, proceed on unto the last, which is, in all things to follow God and reason. But for a man to grieve that by death he shall be deprived of any of these things, is both against God and reason.
pages.familiar: What do you want—to live a long time? To keep enjoying sensations and appetites? To grow, then weaken again? To go on talking, thinking, and reasoning with yourself? Which of these truly deserves your desire? If you see that none of them is very valuable in itself, move on to the highest aim: to follow nature and reason in everything. Then grieving because death will take these things from you is contrary both to nature and to reason.
pages.abbreviated: Ask whether long life, pleasure, growth, or continued thought truly deserves desire. If not, pursue the highest aim—living according to nature and reason—and do not grieve when death takes those lesser things.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 25
pages.original: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl. After thou shalt rightly have considered these things with thyself; fancy not anything else in the world any more to be of any weight and moment but this, to do that only which thine own nature doth require; and to conform thyself to that which the common nature doth afford.
pages.familiar: Consider how tiny a piece of endless time each of us is given, and how quickly it disappears into the whole history of the world. Consider how small our share is of the common substance and the common soul, and how little patch of earth we crawl across. Once you have understood this clearly, let nothing else seem important except doing what your own nature requires and accepting what the nature of the whole provides.
pages.abbreviated: Our time, substance, soul, and place on earth are tiny portions of the whole. Once this is understood, let only fulfilling your nature’s requirements and accepting the whole’s provisions matter.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 26
pages.original: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
pages.familiar: What is the present condition of my mind? Everything depends on that. All other things lie outside my control; and whatever lies outside my control is, as far as I am concerned, no more alive than smoke.
pages.abbreviated: Everything depends on the present condition of the mind. All else lies outside your control and is, from your perspective, no more alive than smoke.

pages.label: Book XII · Section 27
pages.original: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any. And can death be terrible to him, to whom that only seems good, which in the ordinary course of nature is seasonable? to him, to whom, whether his actions be many or few, so they be all good, is all one; and who whether he behold the things of the world being always the same either for many years, or for few years only, is altogether indifferent? O man! as a citizen thou hast lived, and conversed in this great city the world. Whether just for so many years, or no, what is it unto thee? Thou hast lived (thou mayest be sure) as long as the laws and orders of the city required; which may be the common comfort of all. Why then should it be grievous unto thee, if (not a tyrant, nor an unjust judge, but) the same nature that brought thee in, doth now send thee out of the world? As if the praetor should fairly dismiss him from the stage, whom he had taken in to act a while. Oh, but the play is not yet at an end, there are but three acts yet acted of it? Thou hast well said: for in matter of life, three acts is the whole play. Now to set a certain time to every man's acting, belongs unto him only, who as first he was of thy composition, so is now the cause of thy dissolution. As for thyself; thou hast to do with neither. Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that dismisseth thee.
pages.familiar: One strong reason not to fear death is this: even people who believed pleasure was happiness and pain was misery often faced death with just as much calm as anyone else. How could death seem frightening to someone who considers good only what happens at the proper time in nature? To someone who knows that a life of many actions and a life of few actions are equal, as long as all those actions are good? To someone who is equally satisfied whether they have watched the world continue in its unchanging course for many years or for only a few? Human being, you have lived as a citizen in this great city, the world. Whether you have lived there for many years or only as long as you did, what difference does it make? You have lived as long as the laws of the city required—and that can comfort everyone. Why should it trouble you when the same nature that brought you into the world now sends you out—not a tyrant or an unjust judge, but nature itself? It is like being fairly dismissed from a play after being invited onto the stage for a while. But the play is not over yet; only three acts have been performed. Yes—but in a human life, three acts make the whole play. Only the one who first formed you and now dissolves you can decide how long your part will last. You have no control over either. So go willingly and be at peace, because the one who dismisses you is at peace too.
pages.abbreviated: Death need not frighten anyone who accepts what nature brings at the proper time and values good actions rather than their number or lifespan. We are citizens of the world for as long as its laws require, and nature—not a tyrant—both admits and dismisses us, so we should leave willingly and peacefully.
